-- Portability: date +/- integer days and date - date (a day count) are PostgreSQL/DuckDB style;
--   elsewhere use DATEADD / DATE_ADD for the offset and DATEDIFF / DATE_DIFF for the difference.

WITH implants AS (
  SELECT cl.claim_line_id, cl.claim_id, cl.beneficiary_id, cl.rendering_npi,
         cl.billing_npi, cl.cpt, cl.service_date, cl.paid_amount
  FROM claim_lines cl
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
    AND cl.cpt IN ('33249','33262','33263','33264','33270','33271')   -- verify against current CPT
),
event_claims AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT
      c.beneficiary_id, c.claim_id,
      e.event_type,                       -- 'MI' | 'CABG' | 'PCI' | 'NEW_HF_DX'
      c.service_date AS event_date
  FROM claim_lines c
  JOIN index_event_definition e
    ON (e.match_on = 'CPT'   AND e.code = c.cpt)
    OR (e.match_on = 'ICD10' AND e.code IN (SELECT icd10_code FROM claim_diagnosis d
                                            WHERE d.claim_id = c.claim_id))
  WHERE c.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
),
index_events AS (
  -- per implant and event type: one event date taken from claims dated BEFORE the implant day
  -- (the implant claim and other same-day claims often carry the indication code; later
  -- claims are ignored). First-diagnosis event types take the first claim, the rest the latest.
  SELECT i.claim_line_id, ev.event_type,
         CASE WHEN ev.event_type IN ('NEW_HF_DX')        -- list every first-occurrence event type here
              THEN MIN(ev.event_date)
              ELSE MAX(ev.event_date) END AS event_date
  FROM implants i
  JOIN event_claims ev ON ev.beneficiary_id = i.beneficiary_id
                      AND ev.event_date <  i.service_date
                      AND ev.claim_id  <> i.claim_id
  GROUP BY i.claim_line_id, ev.event_type
)
SELECT
    i.claim_line_id, i.beneficiary_id, i.rendering_npi, i.billing_npi,
    i.cpt AS implant_cpt, i.service_date AS implant_date, i.paid_amount,
    ie.event_type, ie.event_date,
    (i.service_date - ie.event_date) AS days_since_event,
    w.waiting_period_days,
    w.policy_id
FROM implants i
JOIN index_events ie ON ie.claim_line_id = i.claim_line_id
JOIN ncd_waiting_period w
  ON  w.event_type = ie.event_type
  AND i.service_date BETWEEN w.effective_date
                         AND COALESCE(w.retirement_date, DATE '9999-12-31')
WHERE (i.service_date - ie.event_date) < w.waiting_period_days
  -- exclusions that override the waiting period (e.g. secondary prevention after
  -- documented sustained VT/VF, or an existing device requiring replacement)
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM claim_diagnosis d
    JOIN waiting_period_exception_dx x ON x.icd10_code = d.icd10_code
    WHERE d.claim_id = i.claim_id
  )
ORDER BY days_since_event ASC, i.paid_amount DESC;
tests.threshold: Categorical against the loaded policy, and unusually consequential — which is exactly why the exception handling has to be right before anyone acts. Secondary prevention indications, generator replacements, and device upgrades all sit outside the waiting-period logic and will otherwise dominate the output. Confirm the waiting-period values against the current NCD for the service date rather than the current version; they have changed. Restrict the first run to primary prophylactic implants with a clean index event, and expand only once the exclusion lists are validated clinically. NEW_HF_DX is dated at the earliest heart-failure claim the warehouse holds, so a patient whose history starts recently (new to the plan) can look newly diagnosed: set a minimum period of prior enrolment before trusting that event type. An index event dated on the implant day itself is not counted. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: CD-01 (Coverage-criteria application — identify and apply the current NCD/LCD/LCA and Benefit Policy Manual criteria). Secondary: CD-02 (Coverage-policy change monitoring), PI-04 (Prepayment medical-review edits on high-risk codes/services).

failure_map.reading: No coverage-criteria crosswalk exists for this service. CD-01's crosswalk artifact does not exist.
CD-01 is per-service; a population of paid implants has no coverage-criteria determination on file.
Criteria were applied and a non-conforming case proceeded on clinical override with no documented basis.
The crosswalk encodes a superseded version of the NCD, so the control runs correctly against the wrong rule — CD-02 is the upstream failure.
Determinations were made but no retained crosswalk record shows which criteria were applied to which case.

tests.family_title: High-cost CPT concentration — spinal fusion, cardiac EP, and high-cost diagnostics
tests.name: Molecular pathology and genetic-test tier concentration
tests.hypothesis: Molecular pathology codes are tiered by complexity, with the top tiers paying many multiples of the base. Where enhanced documentation review for high-cost tests is absent, a laboratory can bill the highest tier as a default. CD-16 and PI-04 both cite the OIG molecular-pathology finding (CPT 81408) directly, so the vulnerability is already named in the control library — only the query is missing.
tests.check: For each billing laboratory, compute the share of molecular pathology claims billed at the top tier and the paid-per-test average, benchmark within the laboratory peer group, and flag concentration. Report the beneficiary-level panel count as a companion signal — many high-tier tests for one beneficiary in a short window is a distinct pattern.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 7 - Top-tier molecular pathology concentration by laboratory
-- Tier 1 molecular pathology: 81200-81383; Tier 2: 81400-81408 (81408 = highest tier,
-- the OIG-named code). Genomic sequencing procedures: 81410-81471. VERIFY current CPT.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :min_tests (50), :top_tier_share_cut (0.50)

WITH mp AS (
  SELECT
      cl.billing_npi, cl.ordering_npi, cl.beneficiary_id, cl.cpt,
      cl.service_date, cl.paid_amount,
      CASE WHEN cl.cpt IN ('81407','81408') THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END AS is_top_tier
  FROM claim_lines cl
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
    AND (cl.cpt BETWEEN '81200' AND '81408' OR cl.cpt BETWEEN '81410' AND '81471')
),
by_lab AS (
  SELECT
      billing_npi,
      COUNT(*)                          AS tests,
      AVG(is_top_tier)                  AS top_tier_share,
      SUM(paid_amount)                  AS paid_amount,
      SUM(paid_amount) / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0) AS paid_per_test,
      COUNT(DISTINCT beneficiary_id)    AS beneficiaries,
      COUNT(DISTINCT ordering_npi)      AS ordering_providers
  FROM mp
  GROUP BY billing_npi
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= :min_tests
)
SELECT
    billing_npi, tests, beneficiaries, ordering_providers,
    ROUND(top_tier_share, 3) AS top_tier_share,
    ROUND(paid_per_test, 2)  AS paid_per_test,
    ROUND(tests * 1.0 / NULLIF(beneficiaries, 0), 2) AS tests_per_beneficiary,
    paid_amount
FROM by_lab
WHERE top_tier_share > :top_tier_share_cut
ORDER BY paid_amount DESC;

-- Companion: beneficiaries receiving more than :panel_threshold distinct high-tier
-- molecular tests within :panel_window_days. Panel-stacking on a single beneficiary is a
-- different pattern from a lab's overall tier mix, and points at the ordering provider
-- rather than the lab.
tests.threshold: :top_tier_share_cut = 0.50 and :min_tests = 50 are starting cuts. Specialisation is the confound: a reference laboratory that exists to run rare-disease panels will legitimately show a high top-tier share, and the right comparison is against other reference laboratories, not against hospital labs. `tests_per_beneficiary` and the `ordering_providers` count are the more discriminating columns — a lab with a high tier share, few ordering providers and many tests per beneficiary is a materially different picture from one with the same tier share spread across a wide referral base. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: CD-16 (Enhanced documentation review for high-cost / high-risk tests and services). Secondary: PI-04 (Prepayment medical-review edits on high-risk codes/services), CB-21 (High-risk-code monitoring dashboard).

failure_map.reading: No enhanced review operates for high-cost diagnostics. CD-16's enhanced-review workpaper does not exist.
CD-16 is per-claim/sample; no sample was reviewed for this category in the period.
Reviews were performed and no denial, edit change or referral followed a sustained pattern.
Review is triggered by a per-claim dollar threshold that the individual test does not cross, so a high-volume, moderate-value pattern is never selected.
Reviews occurred but no workpaper records which claims were selected or what was concluded.

tests.family_title: High-cost CPT concentration — spinal fusion, cardiac EP, and high-cost diagnostics
tests.name: High-cost diagnostic with no treating relationship — ordering-NPI fan-out
tests.hypothesis: Where valid-order verification is absent, or verifies only that an ordering NPI field is populated, a small number of ordering providers can generate a very large volume of high-cost diagnostics for beneficiaries they have no treating relationship with. The signature is an ordering NPI with many distinct beneficiaries and few or no corresponding evaluation encounters.
tests.check: For each ordering provider on high-cost diagnostic claims, count distinct beneficiaries ordered for, count how many of those beneficiaries had any evaluation encounter with that provider in the lookback, and report the no-encounter ratio and the distinct-laboratory fan-out.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 8 - Ordering-provider fan-out on high-cost diagnostics
-- Deliberately scoped to DIAGNOSTICS. The DMEPOS/telemedicine order-to-encounter test is
-- family 6; keep them separate so the paired controls stay distinct.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :encounter_lookback_days (180), :min_orders (25),
--         :no_encounter_cut (0.80)
-- Portability: date +/- integer days and date - date (a day count) are PostgreSQL/DuckDB style;
--   elsewhere use DATEADD / DATE_ADD for the offset and DATEDIFF / DATE_DIFF for the difference.

WITH orders AS (
  SELECT
      cl.ordering_npi, cl.beneficiary_id, cl.billing_npi AS lab_npi,
      cl.claim_line_id, cl.service_date, cl.paid_amount,
      CASE WHEN EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM claim_lines e
        WHERE e.beneficiary_id = cl.beneficiary_id
          AND e.rendering_npi  = cl.ordering_npi
          AND e.claim_type IN ('PROFESSIONAL','TELEHEALTH')
          AND e.cpt BETWEEN '99202' AND '99215'
          AND e.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
          AND e.service_date BETWEEN cl.service_date - :encounter_lookback_days
                                 AND cl.service_date
      ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS has_treating_encounter
  FROM claim_lines cl
  JOIN high_cost_code_register hc ON hc.hcpcs = cl.cpt AND hc.category = 'DIAGNOSTIC'
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
    AND cl.ordering_npi IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT
    o.ordering_npi, pr.specialty, pr.peer_region,
    COUNT(*)                                   AS orders,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.beneficiary_id)           AS distinct_beneficiaries,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.lab_npi)                  AS distinct_labs,
    ROUND(1 - AVG(o.has_treating_encounter), 3) AS no_encounter_ratio,
    SUM(o.paid_amount)                         AS paid_amount
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN provider pr ON pr.npi = o.ordering_npi
GROUP BY o.ordering_npi, pr.specialty, pr.peer_region
HAVING COUNT(*) >= :min_orders
   AND (1 - AVG(o.has_treating_encounter)) > :no_encounter_cut
ORDER BY paid_amount DESC;
tests.threshold: :no_encounter_cut = 0.80 and :min_orders = 25 are starting cuts. The :encounter_lookback_days window is the sensitive parameter: 180 days is generous for a diagnostic order, but a shorter window will flag legitimate follow-up ordering and a longer one will miss the pattern entirely. Ordering providers with high fan-out across many distinct laboratories are the strongest candidates — a single-lab relationship usually has a mundane explanation. Note that pathologists, radiologists and hospitalists order legitimately without an E&M encounter; exclude those specialties or the output is a list of them. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: CD-08 (Valid-order verification — signed order on file, source-verified ordering-provider identity). Secondary: PI-20 (Provider NPI/credential-footprint consistency monitoring), CD-16 (Enhanced documentation review for high-cost tests).

failure_map.reading: No order verification operates for diagnostics. CD-08's signed-order-plus-verified-identity artifact does not exist.
CD-08 is per-service; a population of paid high-cost diagnostics has no verification record.
Tests were performed on a requisition with no signed order subsequently obtained.
The check confirms the ordering NPI is present and valid but never source-verifies it against PECOS/NPPES nor tests for a treating relationship — so stolen and rented NPIs pass.
Orders exist but are not retrievable within the retention requirement.

tests.family_title: High-cost CPT concentration — spinal fusion, cardiac EP, and high-cost diagnostics
tests.name: Prepayment review coverage rate on high-cost codes
tests.hypothesis: This test measures the control, not the claims. Where prepayment medical-review edits are absent or configured too narrowly, high-cost codes adjudicate straight through with no review touch at all. The finding is a coverage rate: what share of high-cost paid dollars passed through any prepayment review, and which codes have a rate of effectively zero.
tests.check: For each high-cost register code, compute paid dollars, the count of claims that hit any prepayment review edit, and the resulting denial rate. Flag codes with material spend and a review-touch rate near zero.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 9 - Prepayment review coverage on high-cost codes
-- Requires the edit-hit / medical-review log. If you cannot produce this query at all,
-- that inability IS the PI-04 finding - record it as such.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :min_paid (250000), :min_review_rate (0.01)

WITH spend AS (
  SELECT
      hc.hcpcs, hc.category, hc.risk_source,
      COUNT(cl.claim_line_id) AS paid_lines,
      SUM(cl.paid_amount)     AS paid_amount,
      COUNT(DISTINCT cl.billing_npi) AS billing_entities
  FROM high_cost_code_register hc
  LEFT JOIN claim_lines cl
    ON  cl.cpt = hc.hcpcs
    AND cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  GROUP BY hc.hcpcs, hc.category, hc.risk_source
),
reviewed AS (
  SELECT
      mr.hcpcs,
      COUNT(*)                                          AS reviewed_claims,
      SUM(CASE WHEN mr.outcome = 'DENIED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS denied_claims
  FROM medical_review_log mr
  WHERE mr.review_type = 'PREPAYMENT'
    AND mr.review_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
  GROUP BY mr.hcpcs
)
SELECT
    s.hcpcs, s.category, s.risk_source,
    s.paid_lines, s.paid_amount, s.billing_entities,
    COALESCE(r.reviewed_claims, 0) AS reviewed_claims,
    ROUND(COALESCE(r.reviewed_claims, 0) * 1.0 / NULLIF(s.paid_lines, 0), 4) AS review_rate,
    ROUND(COALESCE(r.denied_claims, 0)   * 1.0 / NULLIF(r.reviewed_claims, 0), 3) AS denial_rate_when_reviewed
FROM spend s
LEFT JOIN reviewed r ON r.hcpcs = s.hcpcs
WHERE s.paid_amount >= :min_paid
  AND COALESCE(r.reviewed_claims, 0) * 1.0 / NULLIF(s.paid_lines, 0) < :min_review_rate
ORDER BY s.paid_amount DESC;

-- Read denial_rate_when_reviewed alongside the review rate. A code with a LOW review
-- rate and a HIGH denial rate among those reviewed is the strongest possible argument
-- for expanding the edit: the reviews you did do are finding problems.
tests.threshold: :min_paid = 250,000 and :min_review_rate = 0.01 are placeholders for your own materiality. The output is a control finding by construction and should go to the edit-change board (CB-17), not into any provider review queue. The most useful single number this query produces is `denial_rate_when_reviewed` on a low-review-rate code — a high denial rate on a small sample is the cleanest available evidence that the review population should be larger, and it is an argument made entirely from the payer's own operating data. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: PI-04 (Prepayment medical-review edits on high-risk codes/services). Secondary: CB-17 (Prepayment edit maintenance & tuning), CD-16 (Enhanced documentation review for high-cost tests).

failure_map.reading: No prepayment medical-review edits operate on high-cost codes. PI-04's edit-hit & denial report does not exist.
Edits are configured but produced no hits in the period, and no one noticed.
Review hits were released to payment under throughput pressure without clinical adjudication.
Edits are scoped so narrowly that they touch a negligible share of the code's volume — measurable directly by this query's review_rate.
Reviews occur but no log ties a reviewed claim to a reviewer and an outcome, so the coverage rate cannot be evidenced at all.

tests.family_title: High-cost CPT concentration — spinal fusion, cardiac EP, and high-cost diagnostics
tests.name: Post-payment review blind spot — high-cost codes never sampled
tests.hypothesis: The mirror of test 9 on the detective side. Where post-payment medical review operates as a series of targeted projects without portfolio coverage tracking, large categories of high-cost spend go years without ever entering a sample. The absence is invisible precisely because each individual project looks reasonable.
tests.check: For each high-cost code, find the date it was last included in any post-payment review project, compute elapsed time and unreviewed paid dollars since, and rank by exposure.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 10 - High-cost spend with no post-payment review coverage
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :stale_days (730)

WITH last_review AS (
  SELECT
      mr.hcpcs,
      MAX(mr.review_date) AS last_reviewed,
      MAX(mr.project_id)  AS last_project
  FROM medical_review_log mr
  WHERE mr.review_type = 'POSTPAYMENT'
  GROUP BY mr.hcpcs
),
spend AS (
  SELECT
      hc.hcpcs, hc.category, hc.risk_source,
      SUM(cl.paid_amount)     AS paid_amount,
      COUNT(cl.claim_line_id) AS paid_lines
  FROM high_cost_code_register hc
  JOIN claim_lines cl
    ON  cl.cpt = hc.hcpcs
    AND cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  GROUP BY hc.hcpcs, hc.category, hc.risk_source
)
SELECT
    s.hcpcs, s.category, s.risk_source,
    s.paid_lines, s.paid_amount,
    lr.last_reviewed, lr.last_project,
    CASE WHEN lr.last_reviewed IS NULL THEN NULL
         ELSE CURRENT_DATE - lr.last_reviewed END AS days_since_review,
    CASE WHEN lr.last_reviewed IS NULL THEN 'NEVER_REVIEWED'
         WHEN CURRENT_DATE - lr.last_reviewed > :stale_days THEN 'STALE'
         ELSE 'CURRENT' END AS coverage_class
FROM spend s
LEFT JOIN last_review lr ON lr.hcpcs = s.hcpcs
WHERE lr.last_reviewed IS NULL
   OR CURRENT_DATE - lr.last_reviewed > :stale_days
ORDER BY s.paid_amount DESC;
tests.threshold: :stale_days = 730 (two years) is a reasonable opening definition of stale for a high-cost code, but the right value depends on how fast your coding and coverage landscape moves — high-cost diagnostics turn over far faster than surgical procedures, and a single global value will misclassify one of them. The NEVER_REVIEWED bucket, sorted by paid dollars, is the output that matters and usually needs no threshold discussion at all. This is a review-planning input for PI-05 and a portfolio-coverage argument for governance — it is not evidence about any provider. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: PI-05 (Post-payment medical review with valid sampling & extrapolation). Secondary: PI-10 (Root-cause corrective-action workflow), CB-19 (Coding audit program with statistically valid sampling).

failure_map.reading: No post-payment medical review programme exists. PI-05's sampling plan and extrapolation memo do not exist.
Projects are defined but none ran in the period.
Reviews identified errors and no recovery or corrective action followed (PI-09, PI-10).
Project selection is driven entirely by external referrals, so portfolio coverage is never assessed and whole categories of spend are structurally excluded.
Reviews occurred but no log records which codes were in scope, so coverage cannot be demonstrated.

tests.family_title: High-cost CPT concentration — spinal fusion, cardiac EP, and high-cost diagnostics
tests.name: Facility-professional claim pairing mismatch on high-cost procedures
tests.hypothesis: A high-cost procedure normally generates both a facility claim and a professional claim. Where the coordination/setting control is absent, one side can appear without the other — a facility claim with no surgeon, or a surgeon's claim with no facility — which points variously at services not rendered, at claims submitted under the wrong entity, or at a setting misstatement.
tests.check: For each high-cost procedure on a facility claim, look for a corresponding professional claim for the same beneficiary and date, and vice versa. Report both directions separately; they mean different things.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 11 - Facility and professional claims that should pair, and do not
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :pairing_window_days (1)
-- Portability: date +/- integer days and date - date (a day count) are PostgreSQL/DuckDB style;
--   elsewhere use DATEADD / DATE_ADD for the offset and DATEDIFF / DATE_DIFF for the difference.

-- 11a: facility claim with no professional claim
SELECT
    'FACILITY_WITHOUT_PROFESSIONAL' AS mismatch_type,
    f.claim_id, f.beneficiary_id, f.facility_npi AS entity_npi,
    f.cpt, f.service_date, f.paid_amount
FROM claim_lines f
JOIN high_cost_code_register hc ON hc.hcpcs = f.cpt
WHERE f.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
  AND f.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  AND f.claim_type IN ('OUTPATIENT','ASC','INPATIENT')
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM claim_lines p
    WHERE p.beneficiary_id = f.beneficiary_id
      AND p.cpt            = f.cpt
      AND p.claim_type     = 'PROFESSIONAL'
      AND p.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
      AND p.service_date BETWEEN f.service_date - :pairing_window_days
                             AND f.service_date + :pairing_window_days
  )

UNION ALL

-- 11b: professional claim with no facility claim, where the POS asserts a facility
SELECT
    'PROFESSIONAL_WITHOUT_FACILITY' AS mismatch_type,
    p.claim_id, p.beneficiary_id, p.billing_npi AS entity_npi,
    p.cpt, p.service_date, p.paid_amount
FROM claim_lines p
JOIN high_cost_code_register hc ON hc.hcpcs = p.cpt
WHERE p.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
  AND p.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  AND p.claim_type = 'PROFESSIONAL'
  AND p.place_of_service IN ('19','21','22','24')     -- hospital / ASC settings
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM claim_lines f
    WHERE f.beneficiary_id = p.beneficiary_id
      AND f.cpt            = p.cpt
      AND f.claim_type IN ('OUTPATIENT','ASC','INPATIENT')
      AND f.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
      AND f.service_date BETWEEN p.service_date - :pairing_window_days
                             AND p.service_date + :pairing_window_days
  )
ORDER BY paid_amount DESC;
tests.threshold: :pairing_window_days = 1 absorbs the common case where facility and professional claims carry service dates a day apart. Before drawing any conclusion, establish your baseline pairing rate — if it is not well above 90% you have a claim-linkage problem rather than a services problem, and the entire output is noise. Carve-out arrangements, professional-component-only billing, and capitated facility payment all break the pairing legitimately, so exclude those arrangements explicitly rather than discovering them one review at a time. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: CD-17 (Coordination-of-benefits / setting documentation control). Secondary: CB-15 (Duplicate claim / line detection), CB-13 (Place-of-service / facility-vs-non-facility rate edit).

failure_map.reading: No cross-setting reconciliation exists. CD-17's COB documentation artifact does not exist.
CD-17 is per-claim; no reconciliation ran for high-cost procedures in the period.
Mismatches were identified and closed without establishing which claim was correct.
The control checks benefit-period overlap only and never tests whether the expected companion claim exists at all.
No retained reconciliation output.

tests.family_title: High-cost CPT concentration — spinal fusion, cardiac EP, and high-cost diagnostics
tests.name: Site-of-service migration toward the higher-paying setting
tests.hypothesis: The same procedure pays differently across inpatient, hospital outpatient, ASC and office settings. Where the place-of-service control operates as a rate edit but nobody monitors utilisation shift, a provider or system can migrate a procedure into the higher-paying setting over time with every individual claim coded correctly. Each claim is right; the pattern is the finding.
tests.check: For each high-cost procedure, compute the setting mix by provider and by market across successive periods, and flag providers whose mix has shifted materially toward the higher-paying setting relative to the market trend.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 12 - Setting-mix shift toward the higher-paying site of service
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :shift_threshold (0.15), :min_cases_per_quarter (5)
-- Portability: DATE_TRUNC is PostgreSQL/Snowflake/DuckDB style; elsewhere use DATETRUNC (SQL Server),
--   TRUNC(date, 'MM') (Oracle) or DATE_TRUNC(date, MONTH) (BigQuery).
-- Portability: MIN_BY / MAX_BY are DuckDB/Snowflake/Databricks functions; elsewhere use
--   ROW_NUMBER() ... = 1 or FIRST_VALUE over the same ordering.
-- Portability: JOIN ... USING (...) is not accepted by SQL Server; write the ON equalities out there.

WITH setting_mix AS (
  SELECT
      cl.rendering_npi, cl.cpt, pr.peer_region,
      DATE_TRUNC('quarter', cl.service_date) AS service_quarter,
      COUNT(*) AS cases,
      AVG(CASE WHEN cl.place_of_service IN ('21','22') THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) AS hospital_share,
      SUM(cl.paid_amount) AS paid_amount
  FROM claim_lines cl
  JOIN provider pr ON pr.npi = cl.rendering_npi
  JOIN high_cost_code_register hc ON hc.hcpcs = cl.cpt
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  GROUP BY cl.rendering_npi, cl.cpt, pr.peer_region, DATE_TRUNC('quarter', cl.service_date)
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= :min_cases_per_quarter
),
market AS (
  SELECT cpt, peer_region, service_quarter,
         AVG(hospital_share) AS market_hospital_share
  FROM setting_mix
  GROUP BY cpt, peer_region, service_quarter
),
paired AS (
  SELECT
      s.rendering_npi, s.cpt, s.peer_region,
      MIN(s.service_quarter) AS first_quarter,
      MAX(s.service_quarter) AS last_quarter,
      MIN_BY(s.hospital_share, s.service_quarter) AS first_hospital_share,
      MAX_BY(s.hospital_share, s.service_quarter) AS last_hospital_share,
      MIN_BY(m.market_hospital_share, s.service_quarter) AS first_market_share,
      MAX_BY(m.market_hospital_share, s.service_quarter) AS last_market_share,
      SUM(s.paid_amount) AS paid_amount
  FROM setting_mix s
  JOIN market m USING (cpt, peer_region, service_quarter)
  GROUP BY s.rendering_npi, s.cpt, s.peer_region
)
SELECT
    rendering_npi, cpt, peer_region, first_quarter, last_quarter,
    ROUND(first_hospital_share, 3) AS first_hospital_share,
    ROUND(last_hospital_share, 3)  AS last_hospital_share,
    ROUND(last_hospital_share - first_hospital_share, 3) AS provider_shift,
    ROUND(last_market_share  - first_market_share, 3)    AS market_shift,
    ROUND((last_hospital_share - first_hospital_share)
        - (last_market_share  - first_market_share), 3)  AS excess_shift,
    paid_amount
FROM paired
WHERE (last_hospital_share - first_hospital_share)
    - (last_market_share  - first_market_share) > :shift_threshold
ORDER BY excess_shift DESC, paid_amount DESC;

-- MIN_BY/MAX_BY are Snowflake/BigQuery/Databricks. In Postgres use
-- (array_agg(x ORDER BY q))[1] and (array_agg(x ORDER BY q DESC))[1];
-- in SQL Server use FIRST_VALUE/LAST_VALUE windows.
tests.threshold: :shift_threshold = 0.15 excess shift — that is, 15 percentage points of migration beyond what the provider's own market did over the same interval. Netting off the market trend is the whole point: site-of-service migration is often driven by hospital acquisition of physician practices, ASC capacity, or payer policy, none of which is a provider finding, and all of which move the market together. A provider moving with their market is not a signal; a provider moving against it is. Even then this is a contracting and payment-policy conversation before it is a program-integrity one. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: CB-13 (Place-of-service / facility-vs-non-facility rate edit). Secondary: CB-21 (High-risk-code monitoring dashboard), CB-17 (Prepayment edit maintenance & tuning). See gap note G4 — no control monitors setting-mix *shift* as distinct from POS coding accuracy.

failure_map.reading: No monitoring of setting mix exists in any form.
CB-13 is specified continuous; no POS-vs-rate exception reporting covers the period.
The shift was observed and no contracting, payment-policy or review response followed.
CB-13 validates the rate paid for the POS asserted on each claim — which is correct and insufficient, because a correctly-coded migration is invisible to it.
No retained reporting of setting mix over time.

tests.family_title: High-cost CPT concentration — spinal fusion, cardiac EP, and high-cost diagnostics
tests.name: Referral concentration into an entity with ownership or payment ties
tests.hypothesis: Where kickback-detection analytics are absent, financial relationships between referring physicians and the entities performing high-cost procedures are invisible in transaction-level views. The signature is referral concentration that correlates with an ownership stake or a payment stream — physician-owned distributorships in spinal implants are the canonical high-cost instance, and PI-23 is written for exactly this cross-reference.
tests.check: For each referring provider, compute the share of their high-cost referrals going to a single entity, join to ownership-disclosure and Open Payments data, and report where high concentration coincides with a disclosed financial relationship.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 13 - Referral concentration correlated with a financial relationship
-- Open Payments (42 CFR 403 Subpart I) and your own ownership-disclosure data are the
-- reference sources. This test surfaces a QUESTION about a relationship; it does not
-- characterise the relationship. Anti-kickback conclusions require legal analysis.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :min_referrals (20), :concentration_cut (0.75)

WITH referrals AS (
  SELECT
      cl.ordering_npi AS referring_npi,
      cl.billing_npi  AS performing_entity_npi,
      COUNT(*)            AS referrals,
      SUM(cl.paid_amount) AS referred_paid
  FROM claim_lines cl
  JOIN high_cost_code_register hc ON hc.hcpcs = cl.cpt
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
    AND cl.ordering_npi IS NOT NULL
    AND cl.ordering_npi <> cl.billing_npi
  GROUP BY cl.ordering_npi, cl.billing_npi
),
totals AS (
  SELECT referring_npi, SUM(referrals) AS total_referrals, SUM(referred_paid) AS total_paid
  FROM referrals GROUP BY referring_npi
  HAVING SUM(referrals) >= :min_referrals
)
SELECT
    r.referring_npi, r.performing_entity_npi,
    r.referrals, t.total_referrals,
    ROUND(r.referrals * 1.0 / NULLIF(t.total_referrals, 0), 3) AS concentration_share,
    r.referred_paid,
    own.ownership_pct,
    op.total_open_payments_value,
    op.payment_categories
FROM referrals r
JOIN totals t ON t.referring_npi = r.referring_npi
LEFT JOIN ownership_disclosure own
       ON own.owner_npi = r.referring_npi AND own.entity_npi = r.performing_entity_npi
LEFT JOIN open_payments_summary op
       ON op.physician_npi = r.referring_npi AND op.paying_entity_npi = r.performing_entity_npi
WHERE r.referrals * 1.0 / NULLIF(t.total_referrals, 0) > :concentration_cut
  AND (own.ownership_pct IS NOT NULL OR op.total_open_payments_value IS NOT NULL)
ORDER BY r.referred_paid DESC;

-- Run WITHOUT the financial-relationship filter first to see the concentration
-- distribution. High concentration alone is extremely common and entirely lawful - 
-- it is the conjunction with a financial tie that makes a case worth a look.
tests.threshold: :concentration_cut = 0.75 and :min_referrals = 20 are starting cuts, and this is the test where thresholds matter least and framing matters most. Referral concentration is normal: geography, hospital affiliation, sub-specialty and network design all produce it lawfully, and so does simple professional trust. The query is built so that concentration alone never surfaces — a disclosed ownership stake or an Open Payments relationship must also be present. Even then the output is a question for counsel and the SIU, not a conclusion: physician ownership is lawful under multiple safe harbours and disclosure is evidence of compliance, not of its opposite. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: PI-23 (MSO/investment-disguised kickback detection — cross-reference referral volume against ownership and Open Payments data). Secondary: PI-22 (Entity-network cash-loop detection), PE-05 (Beneficial-ownership network/graph analysis).

failure_map.reading: No cross-reference between referral volume and financial-relationship data exists. PI-23's correlation report does not exist.
PI-23 is annual/on-trigger; no report was produced in the period.
Correlations were identified and no SIU review, referral or legal assessment followed.
The analysis uses ownership-disclosure data only and never joins Open Payments, so relationships structured as consulting or royalty payments are invisible.
The analysis was run but neither the correlation output nor its disposition is retained.

tests.family_title: High-cost CPT concentration — spinal fusion, cardiac EP, and high-cost diagnostics
tests.name: Severity capture drift on high-cost admissions (CC/MCC rate vs peers)
tests.hypothesis: Inpatient payment scales with severity: the same base procedure pays materially more when a complication or comorbidity is coded. Where DRG coding accuracy review is absent or samples only discharge status, a facility's severity capture can drift upward without any individual claim looking wrong. The signature is a CC/MCC rate above peers on the same base DRG family, and a rate that has moved.
tests.check: For each facility and base DRG family covering high-cost procedures, compute the share of admissions coded with a CC or MCC, benchmark within the peer group, and report both the level and the period-over-period change.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 14 - CC/MCC capture rate on high-cost admissions vs peers
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :min_admissions (50), :min_peer_n (15), :z_threshold (2.5)
-- Portability: DATE_TRUNC is PostgreSQL/Snowflake/DuckDB style; elsewhere use DATETRUNC (SQL Server),
--   TRUNC(date, 'MM') (Oracle) or DATE_TRUNC(date, MONTH) (BigQuery).
-- Portability: JOIN ... USING (...) is not accepted by SQL Server; write the ON equalities out there.

WITH admissions AS (
  SELECT
      i.facility_npi, f.facility_type, f.peer_region,
      d.base_drg_family,
      DATE_TRUNC('year', i.discharge_date) AS discharge_year,
      COUNT(*) AS admissions,
      AVG(CASE WHEN d.severity_level IN ('CC','MCC') THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) AS cc_mcc_rate,
      SUM(i.paid_amount) AS paid_amount
  FROM inpatient_claim i
  JOIN drg_reference d ON d.drg_code = i.drg_code
  JOIN facility f      ON f.npi      = i.facility_npi
  WHERE i.discharge_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND i.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
    AND d.base_drg_family IN (SELECT base_drg_family FROM high_cost_drg_family)
  GROUP BY i.facility_npi, f.facility_type, f.peer_region, d.base_drg_family,
           DATE_TRUNC('year', i.discharge_date)
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= :min_admissions
),
admissions_yoy AS (
  -- year-on-year change computed before the z filter, so a facility that is newly high
  -- (not high the year before) still carries its prior-year rate
  SELECT a.*,
         ROUND(a.cc_mcc_rate - LAG(a.cc_mcc_rate) OVER (
             PARTITION BY a.facility_npi, a.base_drg_family ORDER BY a.discharge_year), 3)
           AS yoy_change
  FROM admissions a
),
peer AS (
  SELECT facility_type, peer_region, base_drg_family, discharge_year,
         AVG(cc_mcc_rate) AS peer_mean, STDDEV(cc_mcc_rate) AS peer_sd, COUNT(*) AS peer_n
  FROM admissions
  GROUP BY facility_type, peer_region, base_drg_family, discharge_year
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= :min_peer_n
)
SELECT
    a.facility_npi, a.facility_type, a.peer_region, a.base_drg_family, a.discharge_year,
    a.admissions,
    ROUND(a.cc_mcc_rate, 3) AS cc_mcc_rate,
    ROUND(p.peer_mean, 3)   AS peer_mean,
    ROUND((a.cc_mcc_rate - p.peer_mean) / NULLIF(p.peer_sd, 0), 2) AS z_score,
    a.yoy_change,
    a.paid_amount
FROM admissions_yoy a
JOIN peer p USING (facility_type, peer_region, base_drg_family, discharge_year)
WHERE (a.cc_mcc_rate - p.peer_mean) / NULLIF(p.peer_sd, 0) > :z_threshold
ORDER BY z_score DESC;
tests.threshold: :z_threshold = 2.5 with :min_admissions = 50. Case mix is the confound and it is a serious one: a tertiary referral centre treats sicker patients and will show a genuinely higher CC/MCC rate, which is why the peer group must control for facility type, not just region. Read `yoy_change` as the more interesting column — a facility that has always been high is probably describing its population, while one that moved sharply is describing a change in its coding, and a coding change has a cause worth knowing. Improved documentation is a legitimate cause. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: CB-14 (DRG & discharge-status coding accuracy review). Secondary: CB-19 (Coding audit program with statistically valid sampling), PI-01 (Routine claims-aberrancy analytics).

failure_map.reading: No DRG coding accuracy review exists. CB-14's discharge-status audit sample does not exist.
CB-14 is monthly; no sample was drawn in the period.
Severity findings were identified and no rebilling, recovery or education followed.
The review covers discharge status and transfer logic only, never severity capture, so CC/MCC drift is structurally out of scope. This is the defining defect for this test.
Audit occurred but the sample and its conclusions are not retained in reviewable form.

tests.family_title: High-cost CPT concentration — spinal fusion, cardiac EP, and high-cost diagnostics
tests.name: Composite high-cost outlier score feeding the review queue
tests.hypothesis: Any single test in this family produces too many candidates and too little confidence to act on alone. Where provider risk-scoring is absent, review effort is allocated by whoever shouts loudest. The composite — a provider appearing in several independent tests — is far more discriminating than any one of them, and building it is what PI-02 exists to do.
tests.check: Union the provider-level outputs of tests 1, 3, 7, 8, 12, 13 and 14 into a signal table, count distinct signals per provider, weight by exposure, and rank. Report which signals each provider triggered so the queue is explainable.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 15 - Composite outlier score across the family's provider-level tests
-- Populate analytics_signal from the other tests in this pack: one row per
-- (provider, signal_name, run_date, exposure_amount). Keep signal_name stable - 
-- the whole value of this table is that it accumulates across runs.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :min_signals (2)
-- Portability: STRING_AGG is PostgreSQL/SQL Server/DuckDB style; elsewhere use LISTAGG (Oracle,
--   Snowflake, Redshift) or GROUP_CONCAT (MySQL).

WITH signals AS (
  SELECT
      s.provider_npi,
      s.signal_name,
      s.exposure_amount,
      s.run_date
  FROM analytics_signal s
  WHERE s.run_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND s.family = 'high_cost_cpt_concentration'
),
scored AS (
  SELECT
      provider_npi,
      COUNT(DISTINCT signal_name)                  AS distinct_signals,
      SUM(exposure_amount)                         AS total_exposure,
      -- string_agg / listagg / array_join depending on dialect
      STRING_AGG(DISTINCT signal_name, ', ')       AS signals_triggered
  FROM signals
  GROUP BY provider_npi
)
SELECT
    sc.provider_npi, pr.specialty, pr.peer_region,
    sc.distinct_signals,
    sc.total_exposure,
    sc.signals_triggered,
    -- deliberately simple: signal count first, exposure as the tie-break.
    -- Do not weight signals differently until you have outcome data to justify it.
    RANK() OVER (ORDER BY sc.distinct_signals DESC, sc.total_exposure DESC) AS review_rank
FROM scored sc
LEFT JOIN provider pr ON pr.npi = sc.provider_npi
WHERE sc.distinct_signals >= :min_signals
ORDER BY review_rank;
tests.threshold: :min_signals = 2 is the whole threshold, and it should stay crude. The temptation is to weight signals by perceived severity or to fit a model; resist it until you have outcome data — review dispositions, overturn rates, recovery outcomes — to fit against, because a weighting scheme invented in advance encodes assumptions you cannot defend and will be asked to defend. Signal count first, exposure as tie-break, and `signals_triggered` carried through so every position in the queue can be explained to the provider it concerns. That explainability is a control property, not a nicety. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: PI-02 (Provider risk-scoring & review-prioritization model). Secondary: PI-01 (Routine claims-aberrancy analytics), CB-21 (High-risk-code monitoring dashboard).

failure_map.reading: No risk-scoring or prioritisation exists. PI-02's risk-ranked review queue does not exist and review effort is allocated ad hoc.
PI-02 is monthly; no scoring cycle ran.
A ranked queue exists and reviews are selected outside it without recorded justification.
The model runs on a single signal, so it reproduces that signal's false positives rather than filtering them — the point of a composite is defeated.
Scores are generated but neither the inputs nor the resulting queue are retained, so prioritisation decisions cannot be reconstructed.

tests.family_title: High-cost CPT concentration — spinal fusion, cardiac EP, and high-cost diagnostics
tests.name: Device credit and warranty replacement not reflected on the claim
tests.hypothesis: When a device is replaced under warranty or recall, the credit received from the manufacturer must reduce the claim — reported through the relevant modifiers and condition codes. Where the overpayment identification and return workflow does not cover device credits, replacement procedures are billed at full value with no credit reported, and the resulting retained overpayment carries False Claims Act exposure under the 60-day rule.
tests.check: Identify device replacement procedures — a device implant preceded by a removal or explant of the same device family — and test whether the claim carries a credit modifier or condition code. Report replacements with no credit reported.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 16 - Device replacement with no credit reported
-- Credit reporting uses modifiers FB (no cost) and FC (partial credit) and condition
-- codes 49/50 on institutional claims. Confirm current reporting requirements.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :replacement_window_days (30)
-- Portability: date +/- integer days and date - date (a day count) are PostgreSQL/DuckDB style;
--   elsewhere use DATEADD / DATE_ADD for the offset and DATEDIFF / DATE_DIFF for the difference.

WITH replacements AS (
  SELECT
      impl.claim_id, impl.claim_line_id, impl.beneficiary_id,
      impl.billing_npi, impl.facility_npi,
      impl.cpt AS implant_cpt, impl.service_date AS implant_date, impl.paid_amount,
      rem.cpt AS removal_cpt, rem.service_date AS removal_date,
      dev.device_family
  FROM claim_lines impl
  JOIN device_procedure_map dev ON dev.hcpcs = impl.cpt AND dev.procedure_role = 'IMPLANT'
  JOIN claim_lines rem
    ON  rem.beneficiary_id = impl.beneficiary_id
    AND rem.service_date BETWEEN impl.service_date - :replacement_window_days
                             AND impl.service_date
    AND rem.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  JOIN device_procedure_map dev2
    ON  dev2.hcpcs = rem.cpt
    AND dev2.procedure_role = 'REMOVAL'
    AND dev2.device_family  = dev.device_family
  WHERE impl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND impl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
)
SELECT
    r.*,
    CASE WHEN EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM claim_lines c
      WHERE c.claim_id = r.claim_id
        AND (c.modifier_1 IN ('FB','FC') OR c.modifier_2 IN ('FB','FC'))
    ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS has_credit_modifier,
    CASE WHEN EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM claim_condition_code cc
      WHERE cc.claim_id = r.claim_id AND cc.condition_code IN ('49','50')
    ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS has_credit_condition_code
FROM replacements r
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM claim_lines c
        WHERE c.claim_id = r.claim_id
          AND (c.modifier_1 IN ('FB','FC') OR c.modifier_2 IN ('FB','FC')))
  AND NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM claim_condition_code cc
        WHERE cc.claim_id = r.claim_id AND cc.condition_code IN ('49','50'))
ORDER BY r.paid_amount DESC;
tests.threshold: Categorical once a replacement is correctly identified — and identifying the replacement is the hard part, since it depends entirely on `device_procedure_map` correctly pairing implant and removal codes within a device family. Build that mapping before the first run. Not every replacement generates a credit: devices outside warranty, replacements for a changed clinical indication, and upgrades all legitimately carry no credit, so the output is a question about whether a credit was received, answerable only from the provider's own purchasing records. That makes this a provider-inquiry list rather than an overpayment list. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: PI-07 (60-day self-identified overpayment report-&-return workflow). Secondary: CB-17 (Prepayment edit maintenance & tuning), PI-09 (Overpayment recovery tracking). See gap note G3 — no control names device credit reporting.

failure_map.reading: No workflow identifies device-credit overpayments. PI-07's refund and 60-day timestamp do not exist for this category.
The 60-day workflow exists generally but has never been applied to device credits.
Credits were received and the corresponding claim adjustment was not made within the 60-day window.
The workflow relies on self-identification with no analytic trigger, so a credit that nobody flags never enters it.
Adjustments were made but no record ties the refund to the credit that prompted it or evidences the 60-day timing.

tests.family_title: Eligibility integrity and services not rendered
tests.name: Payment after date of death — fee-for-service and capitation
tests.hypothesis: Where the Death Master File match is absent, run late, or matched only against eligibility rather than against payments, claims and — more importantly — monthly capitation continue after death. Capitation is the larger exposure by an order of magnitude in a managed-care programme, because it pays silently every month with no service to trigger a review.
tests.check: Test both payment streams against the recorded date of death: FFS claim lines with a service date after death, and capitation payments for a coverage month beginning after death. Split each by whether the payment was made before or after the death record loaded — the two have different remediations.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 1 - FFS and capitation paid after date of death
-- Generalises family 1's test 5 beyond home health to all service types, and adds the
-- capitation leg. Where both families are in use, THIS test supersedes that one.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :grace_days (0)

-- 1a: fee-for-service
SELECT
    'FFS' AS payment_stream,
    cl.claim_line_id AS payment_id, cl.beneficiary_id,
    cl.billing_npi, cl.hcpcs, cl.service_date AS coverage_date,
    b.date_of_death, (cl.service_date - b.date_of_death) AS days_after_death,
    cl.paid_amount,
    CASE WHEN cl.payment_date > b.death_record_load_date
         THEN 'PAID_AFTER_DEATH_KNOWN' ELSE 'PAID_BEFORE_DEATH_KNOWN' END AS timing_class
FROM claim_lines cl
JOIN beneficiary b ON b.beneficiary_id = cl.beneficiary_id
WHERE b.date_of_death IS NOT NULL
  AND cl.service_date > b.date_of_death + :grace_days
  AND cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
  AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'

UNION ALL

-- 1b: capitation - usually the larger exposure and the one nobody looks at
SELECT
    'CAPITATION' AS payment_stream,
    cap.capitation_id AS payment_id, cap.beneficiary_id,
    cap.plan_npi AS billing_npi, CAST(NULL AS VARCHAR) AS hcpcs,
    cap.coverage_month_start AS coverage_date,
    b.date_of_death, (cap.coverage_month_start - b.date_of_death) AS days_after_death,
    cap.paid_amount,
    CASE WHEN cap.payment_date > b.death_record_load_date
         THEN 'PAID_AFTER_DEATH_KNOWN' ELSE 'PAID_BEFORE_DEATH_KNOWN' END AS timing_class
FROM capitation_payment cap
JOIN beneficiary b ON b.beneficiary_id = cap.beneficiary_id
WHERE b.date_of_death IS NOT NULL
  AND cap.coverage_month_start > b.date_of_death
  AND cap.coverage_month_start BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
ORDER BY days_after_death DESC, paid_amount DESC;
tests.threshold: :grace_days = 0 for most services — but not all. A claim dated the day of death is usually legitimate (the patient was treated, then died), and some facility and hospice claims legitimately span the date of death, so exclude the death date itself and handle span-dated claims on their end date rather than their start. The `timing_class` split is what makes this actionable: PAID_BEFORE_DEATH_KNOWN is a recovery workflow question, PAID_AFTER_DEATH_KNOWN is a control failure — the payer already had the information and paid anyway. Report the two separately or the control finding is diluted by unavoidable data latency. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: MD-08 (Deceased-enrollee detection via SSA Death Master File match). Secondary: MD-06 (Enrollee eligibility verification), MD-16 (T-MSIS monthly submission + data-quality validation).

failure_map.reading: No DMF match runs. MD-08's DMF-match exception disposition does not exist.
MD-08 is monthly; the match did not run for one or more months. Establish what was paid in the gap.
Matches were dispositioned as false positives in bulk without a documented identity-resolution step.
The match updates eligibility but never sweeps paid claims or capitation, so it prevents future payment without recovering past payment — the defining defect.
The match runs but no dated exception output or per-case disposition is retained.

tests.family_title: Eligibility integrity and services not rendered
tests.name: Services and capitation during incarceration
tests.hypothesis: Federal financial participation is unavailable for most services to an inmate of a public institution. Where the corrections-roster match is absent or runs only against eligibility, both FFS claims and capitation continue through a custody period. Note the 2026 change: the CAA 2024 requires states to *suspend* rather than terminate eligibility, which makes the payment-side control more important, not less — the person stays enrolled, so only a payment control stops the money.
tests.check: Interval-join FFS claims and capitation months against the corrections roster, excluding the inpatient-hospitalisation exception where FFP remains available, and excluding boundary days.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 2 - Claims and capitation inside a custody window
-- Generalises family 1's test 6 beyond home health and adds capitation.
-- SSA §1905(a)(29)(A); 42 CFR 435.1009-.1010; CAA 2024 suspend-not-terminate (eff. 1/1/2026).
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end

SELECT
    'FFS' AS payment_stream,
    cl.claim_line_id AS payment_id, cl.beneficiary_id, cl.billing_npi,
    cl.hcpcs, cl.service_date AS coverage_date, cl.paid_amount,
    inc.book_date, inc.release_date, inc.facility_id
FROM claim_lines cl
JOIN incarceration_roster inc
  ON  inc.beneficiary_id = cl.beneficiary_id
  AND cl.service_date >  inc.book_date                       -- exclude the booking day
  AND cl.service_date <  COALESCE(inc.release_date, DATE '9999-12-31')
WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
  AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  -- the inpatient exception: FFP remains available for an inmate admitted as an
  -- inpatient to a medical institution for >24 hours. Exclude those stays.
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM institutional_stay st
    WHERE st.beneficiary_id = cl.beneficiary_id
      AND st.facility_type  = 'INPATIENT_HOSPITAL'
      AND cl.service_date BETWEEN st.admit_date AND COALESCE(st.discharge_date, DATE '9999-12-31')
      AND COALESCE(st.discharge_date, CURRENT_DATE) - st.admit_date >= 1
  )

UNION ALL

SELECT
    'CAPITATION' AS payment_stream,
    cap.capitation_id, cap.beneficiary_id, cap.plan_npi,
    CAST(NULL AS VARCHAR), cap.coverage_month_start, cap.paid_amount,
    inc.book_date, inc.release_date, inc.facility_id
FROM capitation_payment cap
JOIN incarceration_roster inc
  ON  inc.beneficiary_id = cap.beneficiary_id
  -- capitation month fully inside custody: a partial month is not a finding
  AND cap.coverage_month_start >= inc.book_date
  AND cap.coverage_month_end   <= COALESCE(inc.release_date, DATE '9999-12-31')
WHERE cap.coverage_month_start BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
ORDER BY paid_amount DESC;
tests.threshold: Categorical, with three carve-outs that must be built in before anyone acts: the inpatient-hospitalisation exception (FFP continues for an inmate admitted as a hospital inpatient), the boundary days around booking and release, and partial capitation months — a person booked on the 20th was legitimately covered for nineteen days. Without these the output is dominated by correct payments. Corrections-roster data quality is the other constraint: matching is usually on name and date of birth rather than a shared identifier, so treat matches as candidates requiring identity resolution, and record the match rule you used. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: MD-22 (Incarceration/institutional-status match — suspend claims/capitation during incarceration). Secondary: MD-06 (Enrollee eligibility verification), CD-17 (Coordination-of-benefits / setting documentation control).

failure_map.reading: No corrections-data feed exists. MD-22's monthly exception report does not exist.
MD-22 is monthly; the roster match did not run, or ran without the paid-claims join its design specifies.
Conflicts were closed on an unverified assertion of early release.
The match suspends future capitation only and never tests already-paid claims. Under suspend-not-terminate this is a larger defect than it was before 2026.
Match runs but no dated exception report with dispositions is retained.

tests.family_title: Eligibility integrity and services not rendered
tests.name: Concurrent enrollment — duplicate capitation in the same coverage month
tests.hypothesis: A beneficiary should generate one capitation payment per coverage month. Where concurrent-enrollment detection is absent, an identity enrolled in two managed care plans — or in two states, or in both managed care and fee-for-service — generates duplicate payment every month until someone notices. Nothing in the claim stream signals it, because no claim is wrong.
tests.check: Net each reversal and adjustment against the payment it belongs to, then group the payments still standing by beneficiary and coverage month and flag any month with more than one, reporting whether the duplication is across plans, across states, or across delivery systems. Add the FFS-alongside-capitation case, which is the same failure in a different shape.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 3 - More than one capitation payment for one beneficiary-month
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end

-- Reversals and adjustments are netted against the payment they belong to BEFORE counting,
-- in two steps:
--   1. a row that carries adjusts_capitation_id (a reversal or a retroactive rate adjustment
--      that names its payment) is added to that payment and is not a payment of its own;
--   2. a negative row with no reference cancels one payment of the same amount for the same
--      beneficiary, month and plan.
-- What is left is the set of payments still standing for the month.
WITH cap AS (
  SELECT c.capitation_id, c.beneficiary_id, c.coverage_month_start, c.plan_npi, c.state_code,
         c.paid_amount, c.adjusts_capitation_id
  FROM capitation_payment c
  WHERE c.coverage_month_start BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
),
referenced AS (
  SELECT adjusts_capitation_id AS capitation_id, SUM(paid_amount) AS adjustment_amount
  FROM cap
  WHERE adjusts_capitation_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY adjusts_capitation_id
),
netted AS (
  SELECT c.capitation_id, c.beneficiary_id, c.coverage_month_start, c.plan_npi, c.state_code,
         ROUND(c.paid_amount + COALESCE(r.adjustment_amount, 0), 2) AS net_amount
  FROM cap c
  LEFT JOIN referenced r ON r.capitation_id = c.capitation_id
  WHERE c.adjusts_capitation_id IS NULL
),
numbered AS (                -- number equal amounts so one reversal cancels exactly one payment
  SELECT n.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY n.beneficiary_id, n.coverage_month_start, n.plan_npi,
                                         ABS(n.net_amount),
                                         CASE WHEN n.net_amount > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
                            ORDER BY n.capitation_id) AS seq
  FROM netted n
  WHERE n.net_amount <> 0
),
standing AS (
  SELECT p.*
  FROM numbered p
  WHERE p.net_amount > 0
    AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM numbered v
                    WHERE v.net_amount < 0
                      AND v.beneficiary_id       = p.beneficiary_id
                      AND v.coverage_month_start = p.coverage_month_start
                      AND v.plan_npi             = p.plan_npi
                      AND ABS(v.net_amount)      = p.net_amount
                      AND v.seq                  = p.seq)
),
bene_month AS (
  SELECT
      s.beneficiary_id,
      s.coverage_month_start,
      COUNT(*)                            AS payment_count,           -- payments still standing
      COUNT(DISTINCT s.plan_npi)          AS distinct_plans,
      COUNT(DISTINCT s.state_code)        AS distinct_states,
      SUM(s.net_amount)                   AS total_paid,              -- net of reversals and adjustments
      STRING_AGG(DISTINCT s.plan_npi, ', ') AS plans                  -- LISTAGG on Oracle and Snowflake
  FROM standing s
  GROUP BY s.beneficiary_id, s.coverage_month_start
)
SELECT
    bm.*,
    CASE
      WHEN distinct_states > 1 THEN 'CROSS_STATE'
      WHEN distinct_plans  > 1 THEN 'CROSS_PLAN'
      ELSE 'SAME_PLAN_DUPLICATE'
    END AS duplication_class,
    -- FFS paid in the same month as capitation: the same failure in another shape
    (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(cl.paid_amount), 0)
       FROM claim_lines cl
      WHERE cl.beneficiary_id = bm.beneficiary_id
        AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
        AND cl.payment_arrangement = 'FFS'
        -- last day of the month: PostgreSQL and DuckDB interval syntax; elsewhere use
        -- DATEADD(day, -1, DATEADD(month, 1, month_start)) or LAST_DAY(month_start)
        AND cl.service_date BETWEEN bm.coverage_month_start
                                AND bm.coverage_month_start + INTERVAL '1 month' - INTERVAL '1 day'
    ) AS ffs_paid_same_month
FROM bene_month bm
WHERE payment_count > 1                  -- more than one payment still standing after netting
ORDER BY total_paid DESC;

-- Run a second pass for beneficiaries with capitation AND material FFS spend in the same
-- month even where capitation is singular - carve-out services are legitimate, so build
-- the carve-out code list first and exclude it, or this pass is unusable.
tests.threshold: Categorical for duplicate capitation, but the identity question sits underneath it: cross-state and cross-plan duplication usually means one person holds two enrollment records, and confirming that is identity resolution, not analytics. Retroactive enrollment adjustments and mid-month plan changes both generate legitimate multiple payments in a month — check how your capitation table records adjustments and reversals before treating a count above one as duplication, because a payment and its reversal will otherwise read as two payments. The query nets them in two ways: a row that names the payment it adjusts (adjusts_capitation_id) is added to that payment, and an unreferenced negative row cancels one payment of the same amount in the same plan and month. A partial reversal or a positive adjustment that carries no reference cannot be matched and still counts, so populate the reference where your source has one. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: MD-09 (Concurrent multi-state MCO enrollment detection). Secondary: MD-07 (Interstate duplicate-enrollment matching via PARIS), MD-16 (T-MSIS submission + data-quality validation).

failure_map.reading: No concurrent-enrollment scan exists. MD-09's concurrent-enrollment alert log does not exist.
MD-09 is monthly; no scan ran for the period.
Alerts were raised and neither enrollment was terminated nor capitation recovered.
The scan compares enrollment records within the state only, so cross-state duplication — the case MD-09 is named for — is structurally invisible.
Alerts generated with no retained disposition record.

tests.family_title: Eligibility integrity and services not rendered
tests.name: Interstate duplicate enrollment — claims in two states in one period
tests.hypothesis: PARIS matching exists to find beneficiaries enrolled in more than one state. Where the quarterly match is absent or matches are never resolved to a termination, the duplicate persists. GAO has an open recommendation on exactly this. A payer with multi-state data can see the pattern directly: service claims in two states within a window too short to represent a genuine relocation.
tests.check: For each beneficiary identity, find claim or capitation activity in more than one state within a rolling window, and rank by the overlap duration and the paid amount in the overlapping period.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 4 - Activity in two states within one window (PARIS-style)
-- Requires either multi-state data or a matched identity across states. Where you hold
-- only one state's data, this test is not runnable - and MD-07's PARIS interface is the
-- control that exists precisely because of that limitation.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :overlap_window_days (60)

WITH activity AS (
  SELECT beneficiary_identity_hash, state_code,
         MIN(service_date) AS first_activity,
         MAX(service_date) AS last_activity,
         COUNT(*)          AS events,
         SUM(paid_amount)  AS paid_amount
  FROM (
      SELECT cl.beneficiary_identity_hash, cl.state_code, cl.service_date, cl.paid_amount
      FROM claim_lines cl
      WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
        AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
      UNION ALL
      SELECT cap.beneficiary_identity_hash, cap.state_code,
             cap.coverage_month_start, cap.paid_amount
      FROM capitation_payment cap
      WHERE cap.coverage_month_start BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
  ) u
  GROUP BY beneficiary_identity_hash, state_code
)
SELECT
    a.beneficiary_identity_hash,
    a.state_code AS state_a, b.state_code AS state_b,
    a.first_activity AS a_first, a.last_activity AS a_last,
    b.first_activity AS b_first, b.last_activity AS b_last,
    a.events + b.events         AS combined_events,
    a.paid_amount + b.paid_amount AS combined_paid,
    -- days of genuine overlap between the two states' activity spans
    LEAST(a.last_activity, b.last_activity)
      - GREATEST(a.first_activity, b.first_activity) AS overlap_days
FROM activity a
JOIN activity b
  ON  b.beneficiary_identity_hash = a.beneficiary_identity_hash
  AND b.state_code > a.state_code                  -- each state pair once
  AND a.first_activity <= b.last_activity
  AND b.first_activity <= a.last_activity
WHERE LEAST(a.last_activity, b.last_activity)
      - GREATEST(a.first_activity, b.first_activity) > :overlap_window_days
ORDER BY combined_paid DESC;
tests.threshold: :overlap_window_days = 60 is deliberately generous. Relocation is normal, and a genuine move produces exactly this pattern for a short transition period while the old state's coverage runs out — so a short overlap is expected and the signal is duration. Border-region beneficiaries who legitimately receive care across a state line will also appear; consider excluding adjacent-state pairs in border counties, or at least stratifying by them. Identity matching drives everything here, so record the hash rule you used and treat every hit as a candidate for resolution. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: MD-07 (Interstate duplicate-enrollment matching via PARIS — resolve & terminate). Secondary: MD-09 (Concurrent multi-state MCO enrollment detection), PI-21 (Beneficiary-side integrity analytics).

failure_map.reading: No PARIS participation or matching. MD-07's match-resolution and termination log does not exist.
MD-07 is quarterly; one or more quarterly matches did not run.
Matches were received and never worked to a resolution — the GAO open recommendation is specifically about resolution, not matching.
Matches are received but the workflow has no path to terminate the duplicate enrollment, so identification never converts to action.
Matching occurs but no log records which matches were resolved and how.

tests.family_title: Eligibility integrity and services not rendered
tests.name: Eligibility verification completeness at determination and redetermination
tests.hypothesis: 42 CFR Part 435 Subpart J requires verification of specified eligibility data elements through electronic data sources. Where the verification control is absent or partial, determinations are made with elements unverified — and the resulting eligibility errors are the largest single component of the Medicaid improper payment rate. The signature is in the eligibility system, not the claim stream: determinations with no verification record per required element.
tests.check: For each determination and redetermination in the period, check for a verification record against each required data element, and report completeness by element, by worker, and by office. Then quantify the downstream payment exposure attached to incomplete determinations.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 5 - Verification completeness per required eligibility data element
-- 42 CFR 435.940-.965. The required element list is program- and state-specific;
-- drive it from a reference table rather than hardcoding.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end

WITH determinations AS (
  SELECT d.determination_id, d.beneficiary_id, d.determination_date,
         d.determination_type,             -- 'INITIAL' | 'REDETERMINATION'
         d.worker_id, d.office_id, d.outcome
  FROM eligibility_determination d
  WHERE d.determination_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND d.outcome = 'APPROVED'
),
required AS (
  -- the element list is not filtered here: each determination is tested against the elements
  -- in force on ITS OWN date (see the WHERE below), not on the reporting period
  SELECT re.element_name, re.verification_source, re.applies_to_type,
         re.effective_date, re.termination_date
  FROM required_verification_element re
)
SELECT
    d.determination_id, d.beneficiary_id, d.determination_date,
    d.determination_type, d.worker_id, d.office_id,
    r.element_name, r.verification_source,
    v.verification_id IS NOT NULL AS is_verified,
    v.verified_date,
    -- downstream exposure attached to this determination
    (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(cl.paid_amount), 0) FROM claim_lines cl
      WHERE cl.beneficiary_id = d.beneficiary_id
        AND cl.service_date >= d.determination_date
        AND cl.service_date <  d.determination_date + 365
        AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID') AS paid_12mo_after
FROM determinations d
CROSS JOIN required r
LEFT JOIN eligibility_verification v
       ON  v.determination_id = d.determination_id
       AND v.element_name     = r.element_name
WHERE (r.applies_to_type = 'ALL' OR r.applies_to_type = d.determination_type)
  AND r.effective_date <= d.determination_date
  AND COALESCE(r.termination_date, DATE '9999-12-31') >= d.determination_date
  AND v.verification_id IS NULL
ORDER BY paid_12mo_after DESC;

-- Roll up by element_name first, then by office_id, then by worker_id. An element
-- missing across every office is a SYSTEM configuration problem; one missing in a single
-- office is a training or workload problem. Fix the right thing.
tests.threshold: Completeness is categorical against the required-element list, and the required-element list is where the judgement sits — build it from 42 CFR 435 Subpart J and your own state plan, not from an assumption. Two cautions. First, reasonable-compatibility rules mean an element can be properly resolved without a successful electronic match, so absence of a verification record is not necessarily absence of verification — check how your system records the reasonable-compatibility path. Second, and more important: this test's output must never be used to disenroll anyone. It identifies a control weakness in how determinations were made, not a conclusion that any individual is ineligible. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: MD-06 (Enrollee eligibility verification via authoritative electronic data sources). Secondary: MD-12 (PERM / MEQC eligibility & claims sampling), MD-13 (Improper-payment corrective action plans).

failure_map.reading: No electronic verification operates. MD-06's per-element verification record does not exist.
MD-06 is per-determination; a population of approved determinations has no verification records.
Verification failed or returned no match and the determination proceeded without the documented reasonable-compatibility or self-attestation path.
Verification runs against a data source that is stale or does not cover the population, so it returns 'no match' routinely and workers learn to override it.
Verification occurred inside a vendor system with no record surfaced into the case file.

tests.family_title: Eligibility integrity and services not rendered
tests.name: Claims paid outside the beneficiary's coverage span
tests.hypothesis: The simplest eligibility test there is, and the one most often assumed to be handled by adjudication. Where eligibility spans are loaded late, retroactively adjusted, or held inconsistently between the eligibility system and the claims system, claims pay for dates on which the person was not enrolled. PERM measures this as an eligibility error; the payer can measure it directly.
tests.check: Join every paid claim line to the beneficiary's eligibility spans and flag service dates falling in no span, distinguishing claims that were outside the span at adjudication from those made non-conforming by a later retroactive change.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 6 - Service dates with no covering eligibility span
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end

SELECT
    cl.claim_line_id, cl.beneficiary_id, cl.billing_npi,
    cl.hcpcs, cl.service_date, cl.paid_amount, cl.payment_date,
    -- nearest spans either side, to characterise the gap
    (SELECT MAX(e.span_end) FROM eligibility_span e
      WHERE e.beneficiary_id = cl.beneficiary_id AND e.span_end < cl.service_date)
      AS prior_span_end,
    (SELECT MIN(e.span_start) FROM eligibility_span e
      WHERE e.beneficiary_id = cl.beneficiary_id AND e.span_start > cl.service_date)
      AS next_span_start,
    CASE WHEN EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM eligibility_span_history h
      WHERE h.beneficiary_id = cl.beneficiary_id
        AND h.change_date > cl.payment_date
        AND cl.service_date BETWEEN h.old_span_start AND COALESCE(h.old_span_end, DATE '9999-12-31')
    ) THEN 'RETROACTIVE_CHANGE' ELSE 'INELIGIBLE_AT_ADJUDICATION' END AS gap_class
FROM claim_lines cl
WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
  AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM eligibility_span e
    WHERE e.beneficiary_id = cl.beneficiary_id
      AND cl.service_date BETWEEN e.span_start
                              AND COALESCE(e.span_end, DATE '9999-12-31')
  )
ORDER BY gap_class, cl.paid_amount DESC;
tests.threshold: Categorical, and the `gap_class` split is the entire value of the test. RETROACTIVE_CHANGE claims were correct when paid and became non-conforming afterward — that is a recovery and reconciliation question, and in the case of a retroactive *termination* it may also be a beneficiary-notice question worth asking about. INELIGIBLE_AT_ADJUDICATION is the control finding: the eligibility data the claims system held was wrong or absent at the moment it mattered. Merging the two makes both uninterpretable. Expect a large RETROACTIVE_CHANGE bucket in any programme with retroactive eligibility; that is the system working as designed, not a finding. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: MD-12 (PERM / MEQC eligibility & claims sampling with error-rate measurement). Secondary: MD-06 (Enrollee eligibility verification), MD-16 (T-MSIS submission + data-quality validation).

failure_map.reading: No eligibility-error measurement operates outside the federal PERM cycle. MD-12's sampled-case workpapers do not exist for the period.
The MEQC pilot or equivalent did not run in its cycle.
Errors were measured and no corrective action plan followed (MD-13).
Sampling covers claims accuracy only and never tests the eligibility determination behind the claim, so the eligibility error category is out of scope by construction.
Sampling occurred but workpapers do not evidence the eligibility basis tested.

tests.family_title: Eligibility integrity and services not rendered
tests.name: Phantom encounter — a service with no surrounding care footprint
tests.hypothesis: A real clinical encounter usually leaves a footprint: a referral before it, a prescription or follow-up after it, other claims from the same provider for the same person. Where proof-of-service capture is absent, billing for services never rendered produces claims that are isolated — a single high-value encounter with a provider the beneficiary has no other relationship with, and nothing before or after.
tests.check: For each paid encounter, count the beneficiary's other claims with the same provider in a surrounding window and any downstream activity (pharmacy, referral, follow-up). Flag isolated high-value encounters and rank providers by the share of their volume that is isolated.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 7 - Isolated encounters with no surrounding care footprint
-- A prioritisation signal, not evidence. Isolated encounters are legitimately common
-- (urgent care, one-off consults, screening). The PROVIDER-level rate is the signal.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :footprint_window_days (90), :min_paid (200), :min_isolated (3)

WITH encounters AS (
  SELECT
      cl.claim_line_id, cl.beneficiary_id, cl.rendering_npi, cl.billing_npi,
      cl.hcpcs, cl.service_date, cl.paid_amount,
      (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM claim_lines o
        WHERE o.beneficiary_id = cl.beneficiary_id
          AND o.rendering_npi  = cl.rendering_npi
          AND o.claim_line_id <> cl.claim_line_id
          AND o.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
          AND o.service_date BETWEEN cl.service_date - :footprint_window_days
                                 AND cl.service_date + :footprint_window_days)
        AS same_provider_claims,
      (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pharmacy_claim rx
        WHERE rx.beneficiary_id = cl.beneficiary_id
          AND rx.fill_date BETWEEN cl.service_date AND cl.service_date + :footprint_window_days)
        AS downstream_rx,
      (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM claim_lines f
        WHERE f.beneficiary_id = cl.beneficiary_id
          AND f.rendering_npi <> cl.rendering_npi
          AND f.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
          AND f.service_date BETWEEN cl.service_date AND cl.service_date + :footprint_window_days)
        AS downstream_other_provider
  FROM claim_lines cl
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
    AND cl.paid_amount >= :min_paid
),
isolated AS (
  SELECT * FROM encounters
  WHERE same_provider_claims = 0
    AND downstream_rx = 0
    AND downstream_other_provider = 0
)
SELECT
    e.rendering_npi, pr.specialty,
    COUNT(*)                                  AS isolated_encounters,
    SUM(e.paid_amount)                        AS isolated_paid,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM encounters a WHERE a.rendering_npi = e.rendering_npi) AS total_encounters,
    ROUND(COUNT(*) * 1.0 /
          NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM encounters a WHERE a.rendering_npi = e.rendering_npi), 0), 3)
      AS isolated_rate
FROM isolated e
LEFT JOIN provider pr ON pr.npi = e.rendering_npi
GROUP BY e.rendering_npi, pr.specialty
HAVING COUNT(*) >= :min_isolated
ORDER BY isolated_rate DESC, isolated_paid DESC;
tests.threshold: There is no defensible absolute threshold here — the isolated-encounter rate varies enormously by specialty, and urgent care, screening, telehealth-only and mobile services are legitimately isolated most of the time. Benchmark the rate within specialty and treat only the extreme tail as a candidate. Two structural caveats: a beneficiary who receives care under another payer will look isolated in your data, and a footprint window that is too short manufactures isolation. This is the weakest test in the family on its own and one of the more useful ones as an input to a composite. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: CD-09 (Proof-of-delivery / proof-of-service capture and retention). Secondary: PI-06 (Medical review for benefit integrity), CD-03 (Reasonable-and-necessary documentation).

failure_map.reading: No proof-of-service capture operates for this service category. CD-09's complete POD record does not exist outside DMEPOS.
The control is defined but no proof-of-service evidence was captured for a population of paid services.
Proof-of-service was accepted in a form that does not independently evidence the encounter (e.g. the provider's own billing record).
CD-09 is scoped to DMEPOS delivery only, so professional services have no equivalent control at all — see gap note G1.
Services were rendered and documented but no retained artifact independently evidences delivery.

tests.family_title: Eligibility integrity and services not rendered
tests.name: Benefit-integrity workflow coverage — leads that never became cases
