                                   ORDER BY d.service_date) AS prior_date
  FROM (
    SELECT cl.beneficiary_id, cl.hcpcs, cl.service_date,
           MIN(cl.claim_line_id)        AS claim_line_id,     -- first line of the day stands for the event
           MIN(cl.billing_npi)          AS billing_npi,
           SUM(cl.paid_amount)          AS paid_amount,       -- all lines of the day
           MIN(su.expected_supply_days) AS expected_supply_days
    FROM claim_lines cl
    JOIN supply_utilisation_reference su ON su.hcpcs = cl.hcpcs
    -- date minus integer days (PostgreSQL, DuckDB, Oracle); elsewhere use DATEADD(day, -365, start_date)
    WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start - 365 AND :period_end
      AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
      AND cl.claim_type = 'DMEPOS'
    GROUP BY cl.beneficiary_id, cl.hcpcs, cl.service_date
  ) d
) x
WHERE x.service_date >= :period_start
  AND x.prior_date IS NOT NULL
  AND x.service_date - x.prior_date < x.expected_supply_days
ORDER BY finding, paid_amount DESC;

-- Companion roll-up the check asks for: by supplier, COUNT(*) and SUM(paid_amount) of the
-- ACCELERATED_RESUPPLY rows above, so a supplier-level pattern shows beside the single claims.
tests.threshold: Reasonable useful lifetime is set by policy and is not a tunable; expected utilisation for consumables is, and it should come from the item's own labelled use rate rather than an assumption. Two exclusions carry this test: documented loss, theft and irreparable damage justify early replacement lawfully, and a change in the beneficiary's clinical condition justifies a change of item. Build `replacement_justification` capture before running, or the output will be dominated by legitimate replacements. For 11b, roll up to the supplier — a single early shipment is a logistics artifact, a supplier whose whole book ships at 70% of the expected interval has an auto-ship programme. Same-day lines for one code are treated as one supply event and the expected interval is not scaled by the units supplied, so a double-quantity shipment followed by a normal interval reads as on time. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: CD-10 (Continued-need / recertification documentation control for ongoing services, including DME rental). Secondary: CB-08 (Quantity / frequency-limit edits), PA-07 (Continued-medical-necessity re-documentation). See gap note G2 — no control names replacement timing or resupply cadence.

failure_map.reading: No control tests replacement or resupply timing. CD-10's continued-need record does not address replacement intervals.
CD-10 is per-interval; recertifications supporting replacement were not performed.
Early replacements were approved on a supplier's assertion of damage with no supporting record.
The control documents continued need for the item category but never tests whether a replacement was due, so early replacement passes a control designed for a different question.
No retained justification for replacements inside the useful lifetime.

tests.family_title: DMEPOS and telemedicine — the order-to-encounter gap
tests.name: High-denial item categories with no documentation checklist in use
tests.hypothesis: Certain item categories generate insufficient-documentation errors repeatedly — the OIG intermittent urinary catheter finding cited by both CD-05 and PA-08 is the current example. Where the category documentation checklist is absent, the same documentation gap recurs indefinitely. The signature is a category with a high and *stable* denial or error rate: stability is what distinguishes a systemic documentation gap from a transient problem.
tests.check: Compute denial and post-payment error rates by item category over successive periods, identify categories with persistently high rates, and reconcile against which categories actually have a checklist deployed and education delivered.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 12 - Persistent category error rates versus checklist and education coverage
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :error_rate_cut (0.15), :min_claims (100)

WITH category_period AS (
  SELECT
      ec.item_category,
      DATE_TRUNC('quarter', cl.service_date) AS period,
      COUNT(*) AS claims,
      AVG(CASE WHEN cl.adjudication_status = 'DENIED'
                AND cl.denial_reason_group = 'INSUFFICIENT_DOCUMENTATION'
               THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) AS insufficient_doc_denial_rate,
      SUM(cl.paid_amount) AS paid_amount
  FROM claim_lines cl
  JOIN item_category_map ec ON ec.hcpcs = cl.hcpcs
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
  GROUP BY ec.item_category, DATE_TRUNC('quarter', cl.service_date)
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= :min_claims
),
persistent AS (
  SELECT item_category,
         COUNT(*) AS periods,
         AVG(insufficient_doc_denial_rate) AS mean_rate,
         MIN(insufficient_doc_denial_rate) AS min_rate,
         SUM(paid_amount) AS paid_amount
  FROM category_period
  GROUP BY item_category
  HAVING MIN(insufficient_doc_denial_rate) > :error_rate_cut     -- high in EVERY period
     AND COUNT(*) >= 3
)
SELECT
    p.item_category, p.periods,
    ROUND(p.mean_rate, 3) AS mean_insufficient_doc_rate,
    ROUND(p.min_rate, 3)  AS worst_case_floor,
    p.paid_amount,
    chk.checklist_id, chk.deployed_date,
    edu.last_education_date,
    CASE
      WHEN chk.checklist_id IS NULL AND edu.last_education_date IS NULL
        THEN 'NO_CHECKLIST_NO_EDUCATION'
      WHEN chk.checklist_id IS NULL THEN 'NO_CHECKLIST'
      WHEN edu.last_education_date IS NULL THEN 'NO_EDUCATION'
      ELSE 'BOTH_IN_PLACE_STILL_FAILING'
    END AS remediation_status
FROM persistent p
LEFT JOIN documentation_checklist chk ON chk.item_category = p.item_category
LEFT JOIN category_education edu      ON edu.item_category = p.item_category
ORDER BY p.paid_amount DESC;
tests.threshold: :error_rate_cut = 0.15 applied to the *minimum* across periods rather than the mean is the design choice that matters here — requiring the rate to be high in every period filters out categories having a bad quarter and isolates the ones with a structural documentation gap. `remediation_status` is the finding: NO_CHECKLIST_NO_EDUCATION is a straightforward CD-05 and CD-15 gap, while BOTH_IN_PLACE_STILL_FAILING is the more interesting result, because it means the controls exist and do not work — an effectiveness question rather than a coverage one. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: CD-05 (Item/service-category documentation-eligibility checklist). Secondary: PA-08 (Item-category documentation-eligibility checklists for PA), CD-15 (Targeted documentation education for high-risk categories).

failure_map.reading: No category checklists exist. CD-05's category eligibility checklist does not exist.
Checklists exist but are not applied at claim preparation for the affected categories.
The checklist is completed as a formality without the underlying documentation being obtained.
The checklist exists and the error rate has not moved — BOTH_IN_PLACE_STILL_FAILING — meaning the checklist does not reflect what reviewers actually require.
Checklists are used but not retained with the claim, so their use cannot be evidenced on review.

tests.family_title: DMEPOS and telemedicine — the order-to-encounter gap
tests.name: Medical-necessity rationale absent at the coverage determination
tests.hypothesis: Where the reasonable-and-necessary documentation control at the determination point is absent, prior authorisations are affirmed without a recorded clinical rationale. The consequence is asymmetric and worth naming: it produces both improper payments (affirmations that should not have been made) and improper denials (rejections with no articulated basis, which cannot be meaningfully appealed).
tests.check: For each coverage determination, test for a recorded medical-necessity rationale and a named reviewing clinician. Report by decision direction so affirmations and non-affirmations are visible separately.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 13 - Determinations with no recorded medical-necessity rationale
-- SSA 1862(a)(1)(A). Params: :period_start, :period_end

SELECT
    r.pa_request_id, r.beneficiary_id, r.hcpcs, r.request_date,
    r.decision, r.decision_date,
    r.reviewing_clinician_npi,
    ra.rationale_id, ra.rationale_recorded_date,
    p.credential AS reviewer_credential,
    CASE
      WHEN ra.rationale_id IS NULL              THEN 'NO_RATIONALE_RECORDED'
      WHEN r.reviewing_clinician_npi IS NULL    THEN 'NO_NAMED_REVIEWER'
      WHEN p.credential IS NULL                 THEN 'REVIEWER_CREDENTIAL_UNKNOWN'
    END AS determination_defect,
    -- exposure differs by direction: affirmations carry payment risk,
    -- non-affirmations carry beneficiary-access risk
    CASE WHEN r.decision = 'AFFIRMED' THEN 'PAYMENT_RISK'
         ELSE 'ACCESS_RISK' END AS risk_direction,
    (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(cl.paid_amount), 0) FROM claim_lines cl
      WHERE cl.beneficiary_id = r.beneficiary_id
        AND cl.hcpcs = r.hcpcs
        AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
        AND cl.service_date BETWEEN r.decision_date AND r.decision_date + 365) AS paid_following
FROM pa_request r
LEFT JOIN pa_rationale ra ON ra.pa_request_id = r.pa_request_id
LEFT JOIN provider p      ON p.npi = r.reviewing_clinician_npi
WHERE r.decision_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
  AND (ra.rationale_id IS NULL
       OR r.reviewing_clinician_npi IS NULL
       OR p.credential IS NULL)
ORDER BY risk_direction, paid_following DESC;
tests.threshold: Categorical, and the `risk_direction` split is the reason to run it. An affirmation with no rationale is a payment-integrity finding. A non-affirmation with no rationale is a beneficiary-access finding, and it is the more serious of the two in its consequences for the person involved — an unarticulated denial cannot be meaningfully appealed. Report both, and resist the pull to work only the payment side because it is the one with a dollar figure attached. PA-19's requirement that no denial rest solely on an algorithm is the adjacent control worth testing at the same time. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: PA-06 (Reasonable-and-necessary documentation control at the medical-necessity determination). Secondary: PA-03 (Complete PA package assembly & validation), CD-03 (Reasonable-and-necessary documentation).

failure_map.reading: No rationale is recorded at determination. PA-06's medical-necessity rationale record does not exist.
PA-06 is per-request; a population of decisions carries no rationale.
Rationale fields were completed with template text carrying no case-specific reasoning.
A rationale is recorded but not by a clinician qualified to make the determination, which is the condition PA-19 addresses.
Determinations were reasoned but the reasoning is not retained in the case record.

tests.family_title: DMEPOS and telemedicine — the order-to-encounter gap
tests.name: DMEPOS supplier standards — surety bond and accreditation currency
tests.hypothesis: DMEPOS suppliers must maintain accreditation and a surety bond as conditions of enrollment. Where verification is performed once at enrollment and never revisited, suppliers bill while unaccredited or unbonded — PE-17's stated failure mode is 'unaccountable DMEPOS suppliers', and the bond exists precisely to make recovery possible when it goes wrong.
tests.check: For each supplier with paid DMEPOS claims, test accreditation status and surety bond currency as at each service date, and quantify claims paid while either was lapsed.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 14 - Claims paid while accreditation or surety bond was lapsed
-- 42 CFR 424.57(c),(d); SSA §1834(a)(16). Params: :period_start, :period_end, :minimum_bond_amount
-- A supplier with no accreditation or bond record at all is labelled NO_..._RECORD. A supplier
-- that holds records, none of which covers the service date, is labelled
-- ACCREDITATION_NOT_IN_FORCE_ON_SERVICE_DATE or BOND_NOT_IN_FORCE_ON_SERVICE_DATE. Those two
-- labels say nothing about when cover stopped: it may have lapsed inside the period, years
-- earlier, or not yet have started. Read the earliest and latest claim dates beside them.

WITH acc_n AS (SELECT supplier_npi, COUNT(*) AS n FROM supplier_accreditation GROUP BY supplier_npi),
     bond_n AS (SELECT supplier_npi, COUNT(*) AS n FROM surety_bond GROUP BY supplier_npi)
SELECT
    s.supplier_npi, s.supplier_name_hash,
    acc.accreditation_org, acc.accreditation_start, acc.accreditation_end,
    bond.bond_amount, bond.bond_effective, bond.bond_expiry, bond.surety_name_hash,
    COUNT(cl.claim_line_id) AS claims_during_lapse,
    SUM(cl.paid_amount)     AS paid_during_lapse,
    MIN(cl.service_date)    AS earliest_lapsed_claim,
    MAX(cl.service_date)    AS latest_lapsed_claim,
    CASE
      WHEN acc.accreditation_org IS NULL AND COALESCE(an.n, 0) = 0 THEN 'NO_ACCREDITATION_RECORD'
      WHEN bond.bond_amount IS NULL AND COALESCE(bn.n, 0) = 0      THEN 'NO_BOND_RECORD'
      WHEN bond.bond_amount < :minimum_bond_amount                 THEN 'BOND_BELOW_MINIMUM'
      WHEN acc.accreditation_org IS NULL                           THEN 'ACCREDITATION_NOT_IN_FORCE_ON_SERVICE_DATE'
      ELSE 'BOND_NOT_IN_FORCE_ON_SERVICE_DATE'
    END AS supplier_standard_defect
FROM dmepos_supplier s
JOIN claim_lines cl
  ON  cl.billing_npi = s.supplier_npi
  AND cl.claim_type  = 'DMEPOS'
  AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  AND cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
LEFT JOIN acc_n an ON an.supplier_npi = s.supplier_npi
LEFT JOIN bond_n bn ON bn.supplier_npi = s.supplier_npi
LEFT JOIN supplier_accreditation acc
       ON  acc.supplier_npi = s.supplier_npi
       AND cl.service_date BETWEEN acc.accreditation_start
                               AND COALESCE(acc.accreditation_end, DATE '9999-12-31')
LEFT JOIN surety_bond bond
       ON  bond.supplier_npi = s.supplier_npi
       AND cl.service_date BETWEEN bond.bond_effective
                               AND COALESCE(bond.bond_expiry, DATE '9999-12-31')
WHERE acc.accreditation_org IS NULL
   OR bond.bond_amount IS NULL
   OR bond.bond_amount < :minimum_bond_amount
GROUP BY s.supplier_npi, s.supplier_name_hash, acc.accreditation_org,
         acc.accreditation_start, acc.accreditation_end, bond.bond_amount,
         bond.bond_effective, bond.bond_expiry, bond.surety_name_hash, an.n, bn.n
ORDER BY paid_during_lapse DESC;

-- Companion worth running: suppliers sharing a surety_name_hash AND an address hash.
-- A single surety writing bonds for a cluster of co-located suppliers is a network
-- signal, and connects this test to family 5's ownership-graph work.
tests.threshold: :minimum_bond_amount = 50,000 per 42 CFR 424.57(d); confirm the current figure and any category-specific variations. Certain supplier types are exempt from the bond requirement — pharmacies and some professional practitioners among them — so build the exemption list before running or those will dominate NO_BOND_RECORD. Join on the accreditation and bond records effective for the *service date* rather than current status, or you will report every claim from a supplier whose accreditation lapsed last month as retrospectively defective. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: PE-17 (DMEPOS surety bond & accreditation verification). Secondary: PE-14 (Revalidation cycle enforcement + auto-deactivation), PE-02 (PECOS/enrollment-of-record data reconciliation).

failure_map.reading: No bond or accreditation verification. PE-17's bond + accreditation on file artifact does not exist.
PE-17 is per application/cycle; a population of active suppliers has no current verification.
A lapse was identified and billing privileges continued pending renewal.
Verification occurs at enrollment only and is never re-checked, so a lapse mid-cycle is invisible until revalidation — potentially three years.
Verification performed with no retained record of the bond or accreditation evidence reviewed.

tests.family_title: DMEPOS and telemedicine — the order-to-encounter gap
tests.name: ABN not issued where non-affirmation or denial was likely
tests.hypothesis: This is the beneficiary-protection test in this family. An Advance Beneficiary Notice tells a person, before an item is furnished, that it may not be covered and that they may become liable. Where ABN issuance is absent, beneficiaries are billed after the fact for items they had no notice were at risk. The predictable situations are visible in the data: item categories and circumstances with high denial rates, furnished with no ABN.
tests.check: Identify furnished items in circumstances with a historically high denial rate — or where a non-affirmation had already been issued — and test whether a signed ABN exists. Report the beneficiary liability that resulted.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 15 - Items furnished without an ABN where denial was foreseeable
-- CMS Form CMS-R-131; SSA §1879. Params: :period_start, :period_end, :denial_rate_cut (0.30), :min_claims

WITH category_denial_rate AS (
  SELECT ic.item_category,
         AVG(CASE WHEN cl.adjudication_status = 'DENIED' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) AS denial_rate,
         COUNT(*) AS claims
  FROM claim_lines cl
  JOIN item_category_map ic ON ic.hcpcs = cl.hcpcs
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start - 365 AND :period_start - 1
  GROUP BY ic.item_category
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= :min_claims
),
foreseeable AS (
  SELECT
      cl.claim_line_id, cl.claim_id, cl.beneficiary_id, cl.billing_npi AS supplier_npi,
      cl.hcpcs, ic.item_category, cl.service_date,
      cl.adjudication_status, cl.beneficiary_liability_amount,
      cdr.denial_rate AS prior_year_category_denial_rate,
      CASE WHEN EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM pa_request r
        WHERE r.beneficiary_id = cl.beneficiary_id
          AND r.hcpcs = cl.hcpcs
          AND r.decision = 'NON_AFFIRMED'
          AND r.decision_date < cl.service_date
      ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS prior_non_affirmation
  FROM claim_lines cl
  JOIN item_category_map ic       ON ic.hcpcs = cl.hcpcs
  LEFT JOIN category_denial_rate cdr ON cdr.item_category = ic.item_category
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND (COALESCE(cdr.denial_rate, 0) > :denial_rate_cut
         OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pa_request r2
                    WHERE r2.beneficiary_id = cl.beneficiary_id
                      AND r2.hcpcs = cl.hcpcs
                      AND r2.decision = 'NON_AFFIRMED'
                      AND r2.decision_date < cl.service_date))
)
SELECT
    f.*,
    abn.abn_id, abn.signed_date, abn.option_selected
FROM foreseeable f
LEFT JOIN abn_record abn ON abn.claim_id = f.claim_id
WHERE abn.abn_id IS NULL
ORDER BY f.prior_non_affirmation DESC, f.beneficiary_liability_amount DESC;
tests.threshold: :denial_rate_cut = 0.30 on the prior year's category denial rate is a starting definition of 'foreseeable', and it is a genuinely contestable one — a supplier is not obliged to anticipate every denial, and issuing ABNs routinely as a blanket practice is itself improper. The stronger and less arguable subset is `prior_non_affirmation = 1`: the item was already non-affirmed for this beneficiary and furnished anyway with no notice. Work that population first. Note this test's output is not an overpayment; it is beneficiary liability that may have been improperly created, which is a different remedy and a different conversation. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: PA-13 (ABN issuance when non-affirmation/denial is likely, before furnishing the item/service). Secondary: PA-06 (R&N documentation at the medical-necessity determination), PA-12 (Specific denial-reason communication).

failure_map.reading: No ABN workflow. PA-13's signed CMS-R-131 does not exist.
The workflow exists but no ABNs were issued for foreseeable-denial categories in the period.
The item was furnished without notice and the beneficiary billed after denial.
ABNs are issued as a blanket practice on every item, which is itself improper and provides no meaningful notice.
ABNs were issued but signed copies are not retained, so liability cannot be substantiated.

tests.family_title: DMEPOS and telemedicine — the order-to-encounter gap
tests.name: Items delivered during an inpatient or institutional stay
tests.hypothesis: Equipment furnished to a beneficiary who is an inpatient is generally the facility's responsibility and not separately payable, and equipment cannot be delivered to a home the beneficiary is not living in. Where the setting coordination control is absent, DMEPOS claims fall inside inpatient and skilled-nursing stays — sometimes a timing artifact, sometimes billing for items that were never received.
tests.check: Interval-join paid DMEPOS claims against inpatient, SNF and hospice stays, excluding the discharge day and the day before it, when delivery in anticipation of discharge is legitimate and expected.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 16 - DMEPOS service dates inside an institutional stay
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :predischarge_grace_days (2)

SELECT
    d.claim_line_id, d.beneficiary_id, d.billing_npi AS supplier_npi,
    d.hcpcs, d.service_date, d.units, d.paid_amount,
    st.facility_type, st.facility_npi, st.admit_date, st.discharge_date,
    (d.service_date - st.admit_date) AS days_into_stay,
    (COALESCE(st.discharge_date, CURRENT_DATE) - d.service_date) AS days_before_discharge,
    ec.item_category
FROM claim_lines d
JOIN institutional_stay st
  ON  st.beneficiary_id = d.beneficiary_id
  AND d.service_date >  st.admit_date
  -- delivery in anticipation of discharge is legitimate: exclude the grace window
  AND d.service_date <  COALESCE(st.discharge_date, DATE '9999-12-31') - :predischarge_grace_days
LEFT JOIN item_category_map ec ON ec.hcpcs = d.hcpcs
WHERE d.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
  AND d.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  AND d.claim_type = 'DMEPOS'
  AND st.facility_type IN ('INPATIENT_HOSPITAL','SNF','IRF','LTCH','HOSPICE')
  -- exclude item categories legitimately furnished during a stay
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM institutional_stay_carveout co
                  WHERE co.item_category = ec.item_category)
ORDER BY d.paid_amount DESC;
tests.threshold: :predischarge_grace_days = 2 is the parameter that matters most, and it should probably be longer for items requiring fitting or home setup — a wheelchair or hospital bed delivered several days before discharge is good discharge planning, not a finding. Set the grace window by item category rather than globally. The carve-out list is equally load-bearing: prosthetics, orthotics and certain supplies are legitimately furnished during a stay. `days_into_stay` is the ranking column to use — an item dated in the middle of a long admission has fewer innocent explanations than one dated near either boundary. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: CD-17 (Coordination-of-benefits / setting documentation control). Secondary: CD-09 (Proof-of-delivery capture and retention), PA-18 (POD / service-vs-affirmation post-payment match).

failure_map.reading: No cross-setting check for DMEPOS. CD-17's COB documentation artifact does not cover equipment.
CD-17 is per-claim; no setting check ran for DMEPOS claims in the period.
Conflicts were identified at adjudication and paid on override.
The check tests benefit-period overlap for services but excludes DMEPOS claim types from its scope entirely.
No retained record of setting conflicts and their disposition.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Risk-adjusted cost-per-beneficiary peer z-score
tests.hypothesis: If routine aberrancy analytics are absent, run only on raw totals, or run without risk adjustment, a provider whose per-beneficiary cost sits far above its specialty and regional peers can bill at that level indefinitely without anyone asking why. Almost every scheme in the case base eventually shows up here, because almost every scheme ends in money: whether the mechanism is upcoding, phantom services, unnecessary services or unit-splitting, the terminal signature is the same — this provider costs more per patient than providers doing the same work on comparable patients. That generality is the test's strength and its weakness. It catches nearly everything and explains nearly nothing, which is why it is a triage instrument and never a finding.
tests.check: For each rendering or billing provider, compute total paid dollars divided by the count of distinct beneficiaries served in the period. Normalise for case mix using whatever risk score your population already carries (HCC, CDPS, CRG, ACG). Group providers into peer cells by specialty/taxonomy and region, compute the cell mean and standard deviation, and express each provider as a z-score. Return the upper tail with enough context columns — panel size, claim count, dollars — that a reviewer can see immediately whether the outlier is a real volume story or a small-denominator artifact.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 1 - Risk-adjusted cost-per-beneficiary peer z-score (the MEVIA-style core test)
-- Pattern only. Run on your own warehouse. Output = review candidates, not dispositions.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :min_panel_size (30), :min_peer_cell (20), :z_cut (2.5)
-- Portability: STDDEV here is the sample standard deviation; the standard SQL name is STDDEV_SAMP.

WITH provider_panel AS (
  SELECT
      cl.billing_npi,
      cl.rendering_npi,
      pr.specialty_taxonomy,                       -- from YOUR enrollment-of-record, not the claim
      pr.region_code,                              -- county, MSA or rating region - pick one and keep it
      COUNT(DISTINCT cl.beneficiary_id)            AS panel_size,
      COUNT(*)                                     AS line_count,
      SUM(cl.paid_amount)                          AS paid_total,
      -- risk weight of the panel: mean of whatever risk score you already compute.
      -- If you have none, run the test UNADJUSTED and label it so - do not invent one here.
      AVG(bx.risk_score)                           AS mean_risk_score
  FROM claim_lines cl
  LEFT JOIN beneficiary_risk bx
         ON bx.beneficiary_id = cl.beneficiary_id
        AND bx.risk_year      = EXTRACT(YEAR FROM cl.service_date)
  JOIN provider_reference pr
         ON pr.npi = cl.rendering_npi
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  GROUP BY cl.billing_npi, cl.rendering_npi, pr.specialty_taxonomy, pr.region_code
),
adjusted AS (
  SELECT
      *,
      paid_total / NULLIF(panel_size, 0)                                AS cost_per_bene,
      -- risk-adjusted: divide by the panel's mean risk score so a sicker panel is not an outlier
      (paid_total / NULLIF(panel_size, 0)) / NULLIF(mean_risk_score, 0) AS adj_cost_per_bene
  FROM provider_panel
  WHERE panel_size >= :min_panel_size              -- small denominators produce fake outliers
),
peer AS (
  SELECT
      specialty_taxonomy,
      region_code,
      COUNT(*)                        AS peer_n,
      AVG(adj_cost_per_bene)          AS peer_mean,
      STDDEV(adj_cost_per_bene)       AS peer_sd
  FROM adjusted
  GROUP BY specialty_taxonomy, region_code
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= :min_peer_cell                -- a peer group of four is not a peer group
)
SELECT
    a.rendering_npi,
    a.billing_npi,
    a.specialty_taxonomy,
    a.region_code,
    a.panel_size,
    a.line_count,
    a.paid_total,
    ROUND(a.cost_per_bene, 2)                                     AS cost_per_bene,
    ROUND(a.adj_cost_per_bene, 2)                                 AS adj_cost_per_bene,
    ROUND(p.peer_mean, 2)                                         AS peer_mean,
    p.peer_n,
    ROUND((a.adj_cost_per_bene - p.peer_mean)
          / NULLIF(p.peer_sd, 0), 2)                              AS z_score,
    ROUND(a.adj_cost_per_bene / NULLIF(p.peer_mean, 0), 2)        AS ratio_to_peer_mean
FROM adjusted a
JOIN peer p
  ON p.specialty_taxonomy = a.specialty_taxonomy
 AND p.region_code        = a.region_code
WHERE (a.adj_cost_per_bene - p.peer_mean) / NULLIF(p.peer_sd, 0) > :z_cut
ORDER BY z_score DESC, a.paid_total DESC;

-- Read the ratio column before the z-score. A z of 4.0 in a tight peer group can be a
-- 15% cost difference; a z of 2.6 in a loose one can be triple the peer mean. The z tells
-- you how unusual, the ratio tells you how much money. Reviewers respond to the ratio.
tests.threshold: :z_cut = 2.5 is the conventional starting point, but it is the least defensible number in this pack — a z-score assumes an approximately normal peer distribution, and healthcare cost distributions are right-skewed with heavy tails, so a fixed z will over-flag in some specialties and under-flag in others. Measure your own distribution per peer cell before adopting any cut, and see test 4 for the robust cross-check. :min_panel_size = 30 and :min_peer_cell = 20 matter more than the cut itself: most spurious outliers in practice are denominator artifacts, not statistical extremes. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: **PI-01 — routine claims-aberrancy analytics (peer-outlier / statistical).** This test is PI-01 executing. A hit is not by itself a control finding: the control finding is what the *absence* of hits, or the absence of anyone looking at them, tells you. Secondary PI-02 (risk-scoring and review prioritisation) is where the hit is supposed to go next; MD-14 (SURS) is the Medicaid statutory equivalent.

failure_map.reading: No peer-outlier analytics run at all — the first time this query is executed it produces years of accumulated tail, which is itself the finding. Expect a large initial hit list and resist the urge to tune it down; triage by dollars first.

An outlier report exists in the PI plan but has not been produced for the period under review, or is produced and never distributed. Check the report's last run date before concluding anything about the providers.

The analytics run but named provider groups are excluded from the population — high-volume systems, contracted networks, or providers with an existing relationship. Compare the query's provider count against the paid-claims provider count for the same period; the gap is the bypass.

The test runs on raw totals with no risk adjustment or no peer grouping, so the top of the list is simply the largest practices. If your top 20 outliers are also your top 20 by volume, the test is measuring size, not aberrancy.

Outliers were identified but no record exists of what was done with them — no disposition, no reviewer, no date. See test 10; an outlier program with no disposition trail cannot demonstrate it operated.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Peer-group construction integrity — taxonomy misassignment and thin peer cells
tests.hypothesis: Every peer-comparison test inherits the quality of the enrollment record that defines the peer group. If a provider's specialty taxonomy in the enrollment file is wrong, stale, or self-reported and never verified, that provider is compared against the wrong peers — and the comparison fails in whichever direction the error runs. A high-cost specialist coded as a generalist becomes a permanent outlier and consumes review capacity forever; a generalist coded into a high-cost specialty becomes permanently invisible, which is the more dangerous direction and the one no one checks. Thin peer cells do the same damage by a different route: in a cell of six, one member's own values dominate the mean it is being compared against.
tests.check: Three passes. First, a coherence pass: for each provider, compare the specialty taxonomy on the enrollment record against the specialty implied by its own billing — the procedure mix it actually submits — and flag providers whose billed mix sits far from the mix of the other providers in their recorded specialty. Second, a structural pass: count peer cells by size and report what share of providers and of dollars sit in cells too small to support a peer statistic at all. Third, a list of providers with no reference row or no recorded specialty, who cannot be placed in any peer group. Report all three before publishing any outlier list.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 2 - Peer-group construction integrity: is the peer group real?
-- Three independent passes. Run ALL of them before you publish any outlier ranking.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :min_peer_cell (20), :mix_divergence_cut (0.60), :min_mix_providers (5)
-- Portability: GROUP BY 1 in pass B is an ordinal; repeat the CASE expression where ordinals are not accepted.

-- PASS A - taxonomy coherence: does the recorded specialty match the billed procedure mix?
WITH provider_mix AS (
  SELECT
      cl.rendering_npi,
      pr.specialty_taxonomy                  AS recorded_specialty,
      cl.hcpcs_cpt,
      SUM(cl.paid_amount)                    AS code_paid
  FROM claim_lines cl
  JOIN provider_reference pr ON pr.npi = cl.rendering_npi
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
    -- a missing specialty has no peer mix to be measured against, so it is not scored
    -- here at all; those providers are listed by pass C
    AND pr.specialty_taxonomy IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY cl.rendering_npi, pr.specialty_taxonomy, cl.hcpcs_cpt
),
provider_total AS (
  SELECT rendering_npi, recorded_specialty, SUM(code_paid) AS prov_paid
  FROM provider_mix
  GROUP BY rendering_npi, recorded_specialty
),
specialty_code AS (
  SELECT recorded_specialty, hcpcs_cpt, SUM(code_paid) AS spec_code_paid
  FROM provider_mix
  GROUP BY recorded_specialty, hcpcs_cpt
),
specialty_total AS (
  SELECT recorded_specialty, COUNT(*) AS spec_providers, SUM(prov_paid) AS spec_paid
  FROM provider_total
  GROUP BY recorded_specialty
),
compared AS (
  -- leave-one-out: the reference mix is the specialty WITHOUT this provider, so a provider
  -- cannot pull the reference towards its own mix and hide behind it
  SELECT
      pm.rendering_npi,
      pm.recorded_specialty,
      st.spec_providers,
      pm.code_paid / NULLIF(pt.prov_paid, 0)                                      AS prov_share,
      (sc.spec_code_paid - pm.code_paid) / NULLIF(st.spec_paid - pt.prov_paid, 0) AS peer_share
  FROM provider_mix pm
  JOIN provider_total pt
    ON pt.rendering_npi = pm.rendering_npi AND pt.recorded_specialty = pm.recorded_specialty
  JOIN specialty_code sc
    ON sc.recorded_specialty = pm.recorded_specialty AND sc.hcpcs_cpt = pm.hcpcs_cpt
  JOIN specialty_total st
    ON st.recorded_specialty = pm.recorded_specialty
),
scored AS (
  SELECT
      rendering_npi,
      recorded_specialty,
      spec_providers,
      -- total variation distance between this provider's mix and the mix of the other
      -- providers in its specialty: 0 = identical, 1 = no overlap at all. The first SUM
      -- covers the codes the provider billed; "1 - SUM(peer_share)" adds the peer mass on
      -- codes the provider never billed, so the result is a true 0..1 metric. Not scored
      -- in a specialty with fewer than :min_mix_providers providers.
      CASE WHEN spec_providers >= :min_mix_providers
           THEN 0.5 * (SUM(ABS(prov_share - peer_share)) + 1 - SUM(peer_share))
      END                                    AS mix_divergence
  FROM compared
  GROUP BY rendering_npi, recorded_specialty, spec_providers
)
SELECT
    rendering_npi,
    recorded_specialty,
    spec_providers,
    ROUND(mix_divergence, 3)                 AS mix_divergence,
    CASE WHEN spec_providers < :min_mix_providers THEN 'TOO_THIN_TO_COMPARE'
         ELSE 'DIVERGENT' END                AS mix_status
FROM scored
WHERE spec_providers < :min_mix_providers
   OR mix_divergence > :mix_divergence_cut
ORDER BY mix_status, mix_divergence DESC;

-- TOO_THIN_TO_COMPARE is a statement about the specialty, not the provider: with two or
-- three providers the reference mix is one or two practices, and a distance from it says
-- which of them is the odd one only by assumption. Those providers are listed, not scored.

-- PASS B - structural: how much of the population cannot be peer-compared at all?
WITH cell AS (
  SELECT pr.specialty_taxonomy, pr.region_code,
         COUNT(DISTINCT cl.rendering_npi) AS peer_n,
         SUM(cl.paid_amount)              AS cell_paid
  FROM claim_lines cl
  JOIN provider_reference pr ON pr.npi = cl.rendering_npi
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  GROUP BY pr.specialty_taxonomy, pr.region_code
)
SELECT
    CASE WHEN peer_n < :min_peer_cell THEN 'UNCOMPARABLE' ELSE 'COMPARABLE' END AS cell_status,
    COUNT(*)                                    AS cells,
    SUM(peer_n)                                 AS providers,
    SUM(cell_paid)                              AS paid_dollars,
    ROUND(100.0 * SUM(cell_paid)
          / SUM(SUM(cell_paid)) OVER (), 1)     AS pct_of_dollars
FROM cell
GROUP BY 1;

-- PASS C - providers with no usable specialty: no reference row, or a NULL specialty.
-- In most warehouses this is a larger group than anyone expects, and every one of them is
-- invisible to every peer test in this family.
SELECT
    cl.rendering_npi,
    CASE WHEN pr.npi IS NULL THEN 'NO_REFERENCE_ROW' ELSE 'NULL_SPECIALTY' END AS specialty_gap,
    COUNT(*)                                    AS line_count,
    SUM(cl.paid_amount)                         AS paid_dollars
FROM claim_lines cl
LEFT JOIN provider_reference pr ON pr.npi = cl.rendering_npi
WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
  AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  AND (pr.npi IS NULL OR pr.specialty_taxonomy IS NULL)
GROUP BY cl.rendering_npi,
         CASE WHEN pr.npi IS NULL THEN 'NO_REFERENCE_ROW' ELSE 'NULL_SPECIALTY' END
ORDER BY paid_dollars DESC;

-- Pass C does not check that a populated specialty is a valid code. If you hold a
-- taxonomy code list, add a third gap value for codes that are not on it.
tests.threshold: :mix_divergence_cut = 0.60 on total variation distance is a deliberately loose start — it flags providers whose billed mix shares less than about 40% of its mass with the other providers in its recorded specialty (the provider's own billing is left out of the reference mix). Legitimate sub-specialisation will trip it, so treat pass A output as a data-quality worklist, not an integrity finding. :min_mix_providers = 5 is the smallest specialty in which pass A scores anyone; below it the providers are listed as too thin to compare, because a reference mix built from one or two other practices cannot say which practice is the odd one. It is a judgement, not a rule. :min_peer_cell = 20 is a judgement, not a rule; the honest way to set it is to compute, per cell size, how much a single provider's own value moves its peer mean, and set the floor where that leverage becomes acceptable to you. If pass B shows more than a quarter of dollars in uncomparable cells, fix the peer construction — broaden the region, collapse taxonomy to a parent level — before running test 1 at all. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: **PE-02 — PECOS/enrollment-of-record data reconciliation cycle.** The specialty taxonomy that defines every peer group in this family lives on the enrollment record, and PE-02 is the control that keeps that record accurate. A large pass-A list is a PE-02 finding, not a provider finding. MD-16 (T-MSIS submission and data-quality validation) is the Medicaid analogue where provider attributes flow to CMS; PI-01 is the downstream consumer that silently inherits the error.

failure_map.reading: No reconciliation cycle exists between the enrollment record and any authoritative source, so specialty is whatever was typed at enrollment and never revisited. Expect divergence to correlate with enrollment age.
A reconciliation cycle is documented at a quarterly cadence but the last exception report predates the period under review. Check the report date first.
Reconciliation covers new enrollments only, so the long-tenured providers — the ones with the largest paid totals — are exactly the ones never re-verified.
The cycle checks that a taxonomy value is present and syntactically valid, not that it is right. Presence checks pass while the peer groups stay wrong; pass A is the test that distinguishes them.
Exceptions were identified but there is no record of resolution — no updated record, no provider contact, no closure date — so the same divergences reappear next cycle.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Outlier decomposition — is it price, volume, or panel?
tests.hypothesis: A cost-per-beneficiary outlier is an identity with three factors: dollars per beneficiary equals services per beneficiary times dollars per service, over a panel of a given size. Those three factors point at three completely different control failures. High services per beneficiary with normal price is a utilisation or medical-necessity question. Normal services with high price per service is a coding question — upcoding, modifier abuse, place-of-service. A tiny panel with enormous per-head spend is usually either a genuine complex-care practice or a phantom-panel scheme. If the risk-scoring and prioritisation model ranks outliers by z-score alone and never decomposes them, every flag arrives at the reviewer's desk with no hypothesis attached, and review capacity is spent rediscovering the same three distinctions by hand.
tests.check: For each flagged provider from test 1, compute the three factors and express each as its own peer ratio. Assign a driver label to whichever factor carries the largest share of the deviation. Route the flag by label: price-driven flags to the coding family (family 2), volume-driven flags to utilisation review, panel-driven flags to eligibility and identity checks (family 4).
tests.sql:
-- TEST 3 - Decompose the outlier so the flag names its own driver
-- Runs on the output population of TEST 1. Review candidates, not dispositions.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :min_panel_size (30)

WITH prov AS (
  SELECT
      cl.rendering_npi,
      pr.specialty_taxonomy,
      pr.region_code,
      COUNT(DISTINCT cl.beneficiary_id)                     AS panel_size,
      COUNT(*)                                              AS service_count,
      SUM(cl.paid_amount)                                   AS paid_total,
      SUM(cl.paid_amount) / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0)             AS price_per_service,
      COUNT(*) * 1.0 / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT cl.beneficiary_id), 0) AS services_per_bene
  FROM claim_lines cl
  JOIN provider_reference pr ON pr.npi = cl.rendering_npi
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  GROUP BY cl.rendering_npi, pr.specialty_taxonomy, pr.region_code
  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT cl.beneficiary_id) >= :min_panel_size
),
peer AS (
  SELECT specialty_taxonomy, region_code,
         AVG(price_per_service)  AS peer_price,
         AVG(services_per_bene)  AS peer_svc,
         AVG(panel_size)         AS peer_panel
  FROM prov
  GROUP BY specialty_taxonomy, region_code
),
ratios AS (
  SELECT
      p.rendering_npi, p.specialty_taxonomy, p.panel_size, p.paid_total,
      p.price_per_service / NULLIF(pe.peer_price, 0) AS price_r,
      p.services_per_bene / NULLIF(pe.peer_svc,   0) AS volume_r,
      p.panel_size        / NULLIF(pe.peer_panel, 0) AS panel_r
  FROM prov p
  JOIN peer pe
    ON pe.specialty_taxonomy = p.specialty_taxonomy
   AND pe.region_code        = p.region_code
)
SELECT
    p.rendering_npi,
    p.specialty_taxonomy,
    p.panel_size,
    p.paid_total,
    ROUND(p.price_r,  2)                                     AS price_ratio,
    ROUND(p.volume_r, 2)                                     AS volume_ratio,
    ROUND(p.panel_r,  2)                                     AS panel_ratio,
    -- the driver is the factor with the largest peer ratio; a tie is reported as MIXED
    CASE
      WHEN p.price_r  > p.volume_r AND p.price_r  > p.panel_r  THEN 'PRICE_DRIVEN'
      WHEN p.volume_r > p.price_r  AND p.volume_r > p.panel_r  THEN 'VOLUME_DRIVEN'
      WHEN p.panel_r  > p.price_r  AND p.panel_r  > p.volume_r THEN 'PANEL_DRIVEN'
      ELSE 'MIXED'
    END                                                      AS primary_driver,
    CASE WHEN p.panel_r < 0.5
              AND p.paid_total / NULLIF(p.panel_size, 0)
                > 2 * (SELECT AVG(paid_total / NULLIF(panel_size,0)) FROM prov)
         THEN 'SMALL_PANEL_HIGH_SPEND'                       -- look at family 4 before family 2
    END                                                      AS panel_flag
FROM ratios p
ORDER BY p.paid_total DESC;

-- The driver label is a routing hint, not a conclusion. A provider can be high on both
-- factors, and the interesting cases usually are. Keep both ratios on the record.
tests.threshold: There is no threshold in this test and that is deliberate — it runs on a population already selected by test 1 and its job is to explain, not to select. The one number worth tuning is the small-panel rule (panel below half the peer average with per-head spend above twice the population average); set it from your own distribution, and expect legitimate complex-care and transplant practices to sit in it permanently, which is a reason to maintain a documented exclusion list rather than to soften the rule. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: **PI-02 — provider risk-scoring and review-prioritisation model.** Decomposition is what turns a ranking into a prioritised queue: the model's job is not to say who is highest but to say who is highest *and why*, so review capacity goes to the right reviewer. A prioritisation model that emits an undifferentiated ranked list is operating but not doing its work. CB-19 (coding audit program) is where price-driven flags should land.

failure_map.reading: No prioritisation model exists; outliers are worked in whatever order they were produced, or by dollars alone, so cheap-to-resolve coding issues and expensive investigations compete for the same queue.

A risk-scoring model is documented but the score is not attached to the flags reviewers actually receive — a common gap where the model lives in an analytics environment and the queue lives in a case system.

Scores are computed but review order is set by referral source or by who complained, and the score is reconstructed afterwards to justify the order. Compare score rank against actual work-start sequence.
The model ranks on a single composite with no driver decomposition, so the queue is ordered but uninformative. If reviewers routinely re-triage flags on receipt, the model is not doing the work.

The score exists at the moment of triage but is not persisted with the case, so no one can later reconstruct why this provider was reviewed and that one was not — which is the record you need when the selection itself is challenged.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Estimator fragility — parametric z-score versus robust median/MAD
tests.hypothesis: A z-score built on the mean and standard deviation of a peer cell is computed from statistics that the outliers themselves contaminate. In a small or heavily skewed cell, a handful of extreme providers inflate both the mean and the standard deviation, pulling the cut-off up behind them — so the worst actors raise the bar they have to clear, and the moderately aberrant providers just below them disappear entirely. This is masking, and it is not a hypothetical: it is the ordinary behaviour of a parametric estimator on a right-skewed distribution. If the analytics governance regime never requires an estimator to be validated before deployment, this failure is invisible, because the model produces a plausible-looking list either way.
tests.check: Compute the same outlier ranking twice — once with mean and standard deviation, once with median and median absolute deviation — and compare the two lists. Report providers that appear in the robust list but not the parametric one; those are the candidates the conventional test masked. Report the peer cells where the two rankings disagree most, because those are the cells where the parametric assumption is failing and every future run on that cell is suspect.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 4 - Estimator fragility: does a robust statistic find providers the z-score misses?
-- A model-validation test, not a provider test. Its output is a list of MODEL findings.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :min_panel_size (30), :z_cut (2.5), :robust_cut (3.5)
-- Portability: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP is the SQL-standard median; where it is missing use MEDIAN() or an approximate quantile function. STDDEV is STDDEV_SAMP.
-- Cost here is RAW cost per beneficiary with no risk adjustment: the output compares two
-- estimators on the same input. It is not a provider outlier list (test 1 is).

WITH prov AS (
  SELECT cl.rendering_npi, pr.specialty_taxonomy, pr.region_code,
         SUM(cl.paid_amount) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT cl.beneficiary_id), 0) AS cost_per_bene
  FROM claim_lines cl
  JOIN provider_reference pr ON pr.npi = cl.rendering_npi
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  GROUP BY cl.rendering_npi, pr.specialty_taxonomy, pr.region_code
  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT cl.beneficiary_id) >= :min_panel_size
),
stats AS (
  SELECT
      specialty_taxonomy, region_code,
      AVG(cost_per_bene)                                                   AS peer_mean,
      STDDEV(cost_per_bene)                                                AS peer_sd,
      PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY cost_per_bene)           AS peer_median
  FROM prov
  GROUP BY specialty_taxonomy, region_code
),
mad AS (
  -- median absolute deviation: the robust analogue of the standard deviation. The mean
  -- absolute deviation is carried as the fallback for cells where more than half the
  -- providers share one cost, which makes the MAD exactly zero.
  SELECT p.specialty_taxonomy, p.region_code,
         PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ABS(p.cost_per_bene - s.peer_median))
           AS peer_mad,
         AVG(ABS(p.cost_per_bene - s.peer_median)) AS peer_meanad
  FROM prov p
  JOIN stats s ON s.specialty_taxonomy = p.specialty_taxonomy
              AND s.region_code        = p.region_code
  GROUP BY p.specialty_taxonomy, p.region_code
),
scored AS (
  SELECT
      p.rendering_npi, p.specialty_taxonomy, p.region_code, p.cost_per_bene,
      (p.cost_per_bene - s.peer_mean) / NULLIF(s.peer_sd, 0)               AS z_par,
      -- 0.6745 rescales MAD so the robust score is on the same footing as a z-score; when
      -- MAD = 0 the score uses 1.253314 * mean absolute deviation (same scale for a normal
      -- cell); if that is also 0 the robust score is undefined and is reported as such.
      -- The fallback is DISCONTINUOUS: the mean absolute deviation is far larger than a
      -- near-zero MAD, so the same provider scores much lower in a perfectly uniform cell
      -- than in an almost uniform one. Read scores from zero-MAD cells as a floor.
      CASE
        WHEN m.peer_mad > 0
          THEN 0.6745 * (p.cost_per_bene - s.peer_median) / m.peer_mad
        WHEN m.peer_meanad > 0
          THEN (p.cost_per_bene - s.peer_median) / (1.253314 * m.peer_meanad)
      END                                                                  AS z_rob
  FROM prov p
  JOIN stats s ON s.specialty_taxonomy = p.specialty_taxonomy AND s.region_code = p.region_code
  JOIN mad   m ON m.specialty_taxonomy = p.specialty_taxonomy AND m.region_code = p.region_code
)
SELECT
    rendering_npi,
    specialty_taxonomy,
    region_code,
    ROUND(cost_per_bene, 2)                                                AS cost_per_bene,
    ROUND(z_par, 2)                                                        AS z_parametric,
    ROUND(z_rob, 2)                                                        AS z_robust,
    CASE
      WHEN z_rob > :robust_cut AND z_par <= :z_cut
        THEN 'MASKED_BY_PARAMETRIC'          -- the parametric test missed this provider
      WHEN z_par > :z_cut AND z_rob <= :robust_cut
        THEN 'PARAMETRIC_ONLY'               -- likely a skew artifact, not an outlier
      WHEN z_par > :z_cut AND z_rob IS NULL
        THEN 'ROBUST_UNDEFINED'              -- no spread in the cell to scale by
      ELSE 'AGREE'
    END                                                                    AS estimator_agreement
FROM scored
WHERE z_par > :z_cut
   OR z_rob > :robust_cut
ORDER BY estimator_agreement, z_robust DESC;

-- Cell-level companion: rank peer cells by disagreement rate. A cell where the two
-- estimators disagree on most of the tail should not be scored parametrically at all.
tests.threshold: :robust_cut = 3.5 on the rescaled robust score is the standard convention and is roughly comparable in strictness to a parametric z of 2.5-3.0 on well-behaved data; the pairing matters more than either number, because the point of the test is the disagreement, not the ranking. Note honestly that neither estimator is right in general — the robust version resists contamination but is less sensitive in genuinely normal cells. The defensible position is to compute both, publish the union for triage, and record which estimator produced each flag. One known limit: when more than half a cell shares exactly one cost the MAD is zero and the score falls back to the mean absolute deviation, and that fallback is discontinuous. On the seeded data a provider 20 percent above a perfectly uniform cell scores about 2.7, under the cut, while the same gap above a cell that is only nearly uniform scores between 15 and 46. Treat a score from a zero-MAD cell as a lower bound and review such cells by hand. The test also runs on raw cost per beneficiary with no risk adjustment, so its rows are estimator disagreements to investigate, not provider outliers. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: **AG-01 — AI governance to NIST AI RMF, including model inventory, intended-use statements, pre-deployment testing and a human-in-the-loop gate before adverse action.** A peer-group outlier model is a model, whether or not anyone calls it AI, and estimator choice is a pre-deployment testing question. This is the first test in the pack paired to AG-01, and it is the natural one: the finding is about the detection model, not about any provider. Nothing here should reach a provider.

failure_map.reading: No model inventory exists, so the outlier statistic is not registered as a model at all and no one owns its assumptions. The estimator was chosen once, by whoever wrote the first query, and has never been revisited.
An inventory and intended-use statement exist on paper but the outlier model is not in them — analytics built inside the PI unit routinely escape a governance regime aimed at procured AI systems.

The model is registered and governed, but production runs use a locally modified threshold or a different peer definition than the registered version. Compare the parameters in the registered spec against the parameters in the last production run.
Pre-deployment testing was performed but only for reproducibility and runtime, not for estimator validity or masking. A model can pass every engineering test and still be measuring the wrong thing.

No record of which model version and which thresholds produced a given historical flag list, so past selections cannot be reconstructed or defended — the single most common analytics-governance gap and the hardest to remediate after the fact.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Pharmacy cost-per-beneficiary outlier and high-cost drug concentration
tests.hypothesis: Pharmacy is the surface where a peer-cost outlier is most informative, because the unit of production is standardised: a drug is the same drug everywhere, so a pharmacy whose cost per beneficiary is far above its peers is either dispensing a different mix or dispensing more of it. Where routine pharmacy and PDE analytics are absent, the recurring patterns — non-dispensed prescriptions, a small pharmacy with an improbable concentration in one high-cost specialty drug, an independent whose beneficiaries mostly live nowhere near it — all show up in the same aggregate first. Concentration is the discriminating column: legitimate high-cost pharmacies are high cost across a broad mix; scheme pharmacies are high cost because of one or two codes.
tests.check: For each pharmacy (service-provider NPI), compute paid dollars per distinct beneficiary, prescriptions per beneficiary, and the share of paid dollars accounted for by its single largest drug. Compare against peers grouped by pharmacy type — chain, independent, mail-order, long-term-care, specialty — because those groups have genuinely different cost structures and pooling them makes the test meaningless. Report cost z-score and top-drug concentration side by side.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 5 - Pharmacy cost-per-beneficiary outlier with concentration context
-- Pattern only. Review candidates, not dispositions. No PHI leaves your environment.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :min_bene (25), :z_cut (2.5), :conc_cut (0.40)
-- Portability: STDDEV here is the sample standard deviation; the standard SQL name is STDDEV_SAMP.

WITH rx AS (
  SELECT
      p.service_provider_npi                          AS pharmacy_npi,
      ph.pharmacy_type,                               -- chain / independent / mail / LTC / specialty
      ph.region_code,
      COUNT(DISTINCT p.beneficiary_id)                AS bene_count,
      COUNT(*)                                        AS fill_count,
      SUM(p.total_paid_amount)                        AS paid_total
  FROM pharmacy_claims p                              -- PDE / NCPDP-derived table in your warehouse
  JOIN pharmacy_reference ph ON ph.npi = p.service_provider_npi
  WHERE p.date_of_service BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND p.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  GROUP BY p.service_provider_npi, ph.pharmacy_type, ph.region_code
  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.beneficiary_id) >= :min_bene
),
top_drug AS (
  SELECT pharmacy_npi, ndc_or_drug_name, drug_paid,
         drug_paid / SUM(drug_paid) OVER (PARTITION BY pharmacy_npi) AS drug_share,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY pharmacy_npi ORDER BY drug_paid DESC) AS rn
  FROM (
    SELECT p.service_provider_npi AS pharmacy_npi,
           p.ndc_or_drug_name,
           SUM(p.total_paid_amount) AS drug_paid
    FROM pharmacy_claims p
    WHERE p.date_of_service BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
      AND p.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
    GROUP BY p.service_provider_npi, p.ndc_or_drug_name
  ) d
),
peer AS (
  SELECT pharmacy_type, region_code,
         AVG(paid_total / NULLIF(bene_count, 0))    AS peer_mean,
         STDDEV(paid_total / NULLIF(bene_count, 0)) AS peer_sd
  FROM rx
  GROUP BY pharmacy_type, region_code
)
SELECT
    r.pharmacy_npi,
    r.pharmacy_type,
    r.bene_count,
    r.fill_count,
    ROUND(r.fill_count * 1.0 / NULLIF(r.bene_count, 0), 2)                 AS fills_per_bene,
    r.paid_total,
    ROUND(r.paid_total / NULLIF(r.bene_count, 0), 2)                       AS cost_per_bene,
    ROUND(((r.paid_total / NULLIF(r.bene_count, 0)) - pe.peer_mean)
          / NULLIF(pe.peer_sd, 0), 2)                                      AS z_score,
    td.ndc_or_drug_name                                                    AS top_drug,
    ROUND(td.drug_share, 3)                                                AS top_drug_share,
    CASE WHEN td.drug_share > :conc_cut THEN 'CONCENTRATED' ELSE 'BROAD_MIX' END AS mix_profile
FROM rx r
JOIN peer pe ON pe.pharmacy_type = r.pharmacy_type AND pe.region_code = r.region_code
LEFT JOIN top_drug td ON td.pharmacy_npi = r.pharmacy_npi AND td.rn = 1
WHERE ((r.paid_total / NULLIF(r.bene_count, 0)) - pe.peer_mean)
      / NULLIF(pe.peer_sd, 0) > :z_cut
ORDER BY z_score DESC, r.paid_total DESC;

-- Companion pass worth running alongside: distance between the beneficiary's residence
-- ZIP and the pharmacy ZIP, aggregated to a median per pharmacy. Use ZIP-level centroids
-- only - never beneficiary addresses - and report the median, never the rows.
tests.threshold: :conc_cut = 0.40 (a single drug carrying more than 40% of a pharmacy's paid dollars) is a starting point that will legitimately capture specialty and infusion pharmacies, which is why pharmacy_type must be in the peer key rather than in the threshold. :min_bene = 25 excludes the tiny-denominator noise that dominates any pharmacy ranking. The most useful tuning move is to run the test with and without the highest-cost therapeutic class excluded: if the outlier list is unchanged, the signal is structural rather than drug-specific. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: **MC-10 — routine claims and PDE analytics for aberrant provider/pharmacy billing.** This test is MC-10 executing on the pharmacy side. MC-13 (desk and on-site pharmacy audits for non-dispensed or phantom prescriptions) is the follow-on control that converts a flag into evidence, and the pairing matters: an analytics control with no audit capability behind it generates lists no one can resolve.

failure_map.reading: No routine pharmacy analytics run; pharmacy oversight is complaint-driven or delegated entirely to the PBM with no payer-side view. Ask who last looked at a pharmacy-level cost distribution and when.

Analytics are contractually required of the PBM or delegated entity and are not being produced, or are produced and not shared with the plan. The plan retains the control even where the work is delegated.

Analytics exclude the pharmacies with the strongest business relationship — chain contracts, an affiliated mail-order or specialty pharmacy — which is precisely the population where a payer-side view adds most.

The analytics pool all pharmacy types into one peer group, so specialty and infusion pharmacies permanently occupy the top of the list and crowd out everything else. If your outlier list is the same every quarter, the peer key is wrong.
Flags were generated but the audit trail stops there — no record of which flags went to MC-13 audits, what those audits found, or why the rest were closed.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Beneficiary-side utilisation outlier and cross-provider concentration
tests.hypothesis: Every test so far ranks providers. The same arithmetic run from the member side finds a different and complementary population: beneficiaries whose utilisation is far above risk-matched peers, or who are receiving the same service category from an implausible number of unrelated providers. That pattern has two very different explanations and the data cannot distinguish them — it is the signature of a beneficiary being used as a billing vehicle by multiple providers, and it is equally the signature of a genuinely complex patient with fragmented care and no case management. Where overutilisation monitoring is absent, neither one is seen, and the second is the more common. Treating this test as a fraud test rather than a care-coordination test is the standing error in this space.
tests.check: For each beneficiary, count distinct billing entities per service category, total paid dollars, and services per month enrolled; compare against peers matched on risk score band and eligibility category. Return the tail, but route it by shape: many providers with low per-provider volume points at fragmentation or at recruitment; few providers with very high volume points at the provider side and belongs back in test 1.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 6 - Beneficiary-side utilisation outlier: read this as a care question first
-- Output is a REVIEW population for care management and integrity review jointly.
-- Never route beneficiary-level output to a payment or eligibility action.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :min_months (6), :z_cut (3.0), :provider_cut (8)
-- Portability: STDDEV here is the sample standard deviation; the standard SQL name is STDDEV_SAMP.

WITH bene AS (
  SELECT
      cl.beneficiary_id,
      br.risk_band,                                   -- decile or band of your existing risk score
      br.eligibility_category,
      br.months_enrolled,
      COUNT(DISTINCT cl.billing_npi)                          AS distinct_billers,
      COUNT(DISTINCT cl.service_category)                     AS distinct_categories,
      COUNT(*)                                                AS service_count,
      SUM(cl.paid_amount)                                     AS paid_total,
      SUM(cl.paid_amount) / NULLIF(br.months_enrolled, 0)     AS paid_per_month
  FROM claim_lines cl
  JOIN beneficiary_risk br ON br.beneficiary_id = cl.beneficiary_id
                          AND br.risk_year = EXTRACT(YEAR FROM cl.service_date)
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
    AND br.months_enrolled >= :min_months
  GROUP BY cl.beneficiary_id, br.risk_band, br.eligibility_category, br.months_enrolled
),
peer AS (
  SELECT risk_band, eligibility_category,
         AVG(paid_per_month)    AS peer_mean,
         STDDEV(paid_per_month) AS peer_sd,
         AVG(distinct_billers)  AS peer_billers
  FROM bene
  GROUP BY risk_band, eligibility_category
)
SELECT
    b.beneficiary_id,                                  -- pseudonymise before ANY export
    b.risk_band,
    b.eligibility_category,
    b.months_enrolled,
    b.distinct_billers,
    b.distinct_categories,
    b.service_count,
    b.paid_total,
    ROUND((b.paid_per_month - p.peer_mean) / NULLIF(p.peer_sd, 0), 2) AS z_score,
    ROUND(b.distinct_billers / NULLIF(p.peer_billers, 0), 2)          AS biller_ratio,
    CASE
      WHEN b.distinct_billers >= :provider_cut
       AND b.paid_total / NULLIF(b.distinct_billers, 0)
           < (SELECT AVG(paid_total) FROM bene)
        THEN 'FRAGMENTED_MANY_LOW'      -- care-coordination or recruitment pattern
      ELSE 'CONCENTRATED_FEW_HIGH'      -- send back to the provider-side tests
    END                                                               AS shape
FROM bene b
JOIN peer p ON p.risk_band = b.risk_band
           AND p.eligibility_category = b.eligibility_category
WHERE (b.paid_per_month - p.peer_mean) / NULLIF(p.peer_sd, 0) > :z_cut
   OR b.distinct_billers >= :provider_cut
ORDER BY z_score DESC;

-- Aggregate before you report. The reportable artifact from this test is counts and rates
-- by shape and risk band, plus a referral list to care management - not a row dump.
tests.threshold: :z_cut = 3.0 is deliberately tighter than the provider-side 2.5, because beneficiary cost distributions are far more skewed — a small number of members legitimately account for a large share of spend, and flagging them adds nothing anyone did not already know. :provider_cut = 8 distinct billing entities in a period is a starting point only and varies enormously by eligibility category; dual-eligible and LTSS populations will exceed it routinely and should be banded separately rather than excluded. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: **MC-14 — opioid overutilisation monitoring and drug-management programme.** MC-14 is the library's only beneficiary-level overutilisation control, and it is drug-specific; this test is its generalisation to service utilisation, which is why gap note G3 recommends a broader control. PI-21 (beneficiary-side integrity analytics) covers the recruitment interpretation; MD-14 (SURS) is the Medicaid utilisation-control hook. The beneficiary-protection framing of MC-14 — the member is a subject of care, not a suspect — should carry over to any use of this test.

failure_map.reading: No beneficiary-level utilisation monitoring of any kind; all surveillance is provider-side, so members being used as billing vehicles across several providers are invisible because no single provider looks unusual.
A drug-management or overutilisation programme exists on paper with case criteria but no case volume — check whether any beneficiary was actually reviewed in the period.
Monitoring covers only the drug dimension MC-14 names and stops at the boundary of the pharmacy benefit, so service-side overutilisation has no owner at all.

Flags are generated but routed exclusively to integrity review, so members with fragmented care are investigated rather than case-managed. This is a real harm, not merely an inefficiency, and it is the failure mode to look for first.
No record of the disposition split between care-management referral and integrity referral, so the programme cannot show it is not simply investigating sick people.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Institutional cost-per-day outlier and cost-report-to-claims divergence
tests.hypothesis: Facilities are paid from rates built on self-reported cost data, and the rate is set once and then paid on every day of every stay. That makes the facility surface structurally different from the professional surface: the money does not move because someone billed a wrong code, it moves because the input to a rate calculation was wrong years earlier and has been compounding ever since. Where no independent cross-reference of self-reported cost data exists, the observable signature is divergence — a facility whose claims-derived cost per patient-day drifts away from its peer group in a direction and at a rate that its case mix does not explain, and whose reported costs move in the categories that carry the most rate weight.
tests.check: Compute claims-derived paid dollars per patient-day per facility, adjusted for the acuity mix the facility itself reports, and compare against peers grouped by facility type, bed size band and region. Then compare the trajectory: the ratio of the facility's current-period cost per day to its own prior-period cost per day, against the same ratio for its peer group. A facility moving away from its peers over time is a stronger candidate than one that has simply always been expensive.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 7 - Institutional cost-per-day outlier plus trajectory versus peers
-- Pattern only. Review candidates, not dispositions.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :prior_start, :prior_end, :min_days (500), :z_cut (2.5), :growth_cut (0.10)
-- Portability: GROUP BY 5 is an ordinal (repeat the CASE expression where ordinals are not accepted); STDDEV is STDDEV_SAMP; NULLS LAST: sort on (col IS NULL) first.

WITH fac_period AS (
  SELECT
      cl.facility_id,
      f.facility_type,                                 -- SNF / NF / ICF / IRF / LTACH / hospice
      f.bed_size_band,
      f.region_code,
      CASE WHEN cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end THEN 'CURRENT'
           WHEN cl.service_date BETWEEN :prior_start  AND :prior_end  THEN 'PRIOR'
      END                                              AS period_label,
      SUM(cl.covered_days)                             AS patient_days,
      COUNT(DISTINCT cl.beneficiary_id)                AS residents,
      SUM(cl.paid_amount)                              AS paid_total,
      AVG(cl.case_mix_index)                           AS mean_cmi   -- as reported by the facility
  FROM institutional_claims cl
  JOIN facility_reference f ON f.facility_id = cl.facility_id
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :prior_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  GROUP BY cl.facility_id, f.facility_type, f.bed_size_band, f.region_code, 5
  HAVING SUM(cl.covered_days) >= :min_days
),
pivoted AS (
  SELECT facility_id, facility_type, bed_size_band, region_code,
         MAX(CASE WHEN period_label = 'CURRENT'
                  THEN paid_total / NULLIF(patient_days, 0) / NULLIF(mean_cmi, 0) END) AS cur_cost_day,
         MAX(CASE WHEN period_label = 'PRIOR'
                  THEN paid_total / NULLIF(patient_days, 0) / NULLIF(mean_cmi, 0) END) AS pri_cost_day,
         -- the same cost with NO case-mix adjustment: the pass a facility cannot move by
         -- changing the acuity it reports
         MAX(CASE WHEN period_label = 'CURRENT'
                  THEN paid_total / NULLIF(patient_days, 0) END)                       AS cur_raw_cost_day,
         MAX(CASE WHEN period_label = 'CURRENT' THEN patient_days END)                 AS cur_days,
         MAX(CASE WHEN period_label = 'CURRENT' THEN paid_total   END)                 AS cur_paid,
         MAX(CASE WHEN period_label = 'CURRENT' THEN mean_cmi     END)                 AS cur_cmi
  FROM fac_period
  GROUP BY facility_id, facility_type, bed_size_band, region_code
),
peer AS (
  SELECT facility_type, bed_size_band, region_code,
         AVG(cur_cost_day)                                        AS peer_mean,
         STDDEV(cur_cost_day)                                     AS peer_sd,
         AVG(cur_raw_cost_day)                                    AS peer_raw_mean,
         STDDEV(cur_raw_cost_day)                                 AS peer_raw_sd,
         AVG(cur_cmi)                                             AS peer_cmi,
         AVG(cur_cost_day / NULLIF(pri_cost_day, 0))              AS peer_growth
  FROM pivoted
  GROUP BY facility_type, bed_size_band, region_code
),
scored AS (
  SELECT
      p.facility_id, p.facility_type, p.bed_size_band, p.cur_days, p.cur_paid, p.cur_cmi,
      p.cur_cost_day, p.pri_cost_day, p.cur_raw_cost_day,
      pe.peer_growth,
      pe.peer_cmi,
      (p.cur_cost_day     - pe.peer_mean)     / NULLIF(pe.peer_sd, 0)      AS z_adj,
      (p.cur_raw_cost_day - pe.peer_raw_mean) / NULLIF(pe.peer_raw_sd, 0)  AS z_raw,
      (p.cur_cost_day / NULLIF(p.pri_cost_day, 0)) - pe.peer_growth        AS excess_growth
  FROM pivoted p
  JOIN peer pe ON pe.facility_type   = p.facility_type
              AND pe.bed_size_band   = p.bed_size_band
              AND pe.region_code     = p.region_code
)
SELECT
    facility_id,
    facility_type,
    bed_size_band,
    cur_days,
    cur_paid,
    ROUND(cur_cmi, 3)                                                      AS reported_cmi,
    ROUND(cur_cmi / NULLIF(peer_cmi, 0), 3)                                AS cmi_ratio_to_peer,
    ROUND(cur_cost_day, 2)                                                 AS cmi_adj_cost_per_day,
    ROUND(z_adj, 2)                                                        AS z_score,
    ROUND(cur_raw_cost_day, 2)                                             AS raw_cost_per_day,
    ROUND(z_raw, 2)                                                        AS raw_z_score,
    ROUND(cur_cost_day / NULLIF(pri_cost_day, 0), 3)                       AS own_growth,
    ROUND(peer_growth, 3)                                                  AS peer_growth,
    ROUND(excess_growth, 3)                                                AS excess_growth,
    CASE
      WHEN z_adj > :z_cut AND z_raw > :z_cut THEN 'ADJUSTED_AND_UNADJUSTED'
      WHEN z_adj > :z_cut                    THEN 'CMI_ADJUSTED_ONLY'
      WHEN z_raw > :z_cut                    THEN 'UNADJUSTED_ONLY'   -- reported acuity absorbs the cost
      ELSE 'GROWTH_ONLY'
    END                                                                    AS outlier_basis
FROM scored
WHERE z_adj > :z_cut
   OR z_raw > :z_cut
   OR excess_growth > :growth_cut
ORDER BY excess_growth DESC NULLS LAST, z_score DESC;

-- Note the self-reference: the adjusted cost per day is divided by the case-mix index the
-- facility itself reports, so a facility that inflates its reported acuity LOWERS its own
-- adjusted cost and would hide from an adjusted-only test. The unadjusted pass above is
-- there to catch that. UNADJUSTED_ONLY means the reported case mix accounts for the whole
-- cost difference: that is either genuinely higher acuity or inflated acuity, and claims
-- cannot tell which. Check cmi_ratio_to_peer against clinical indicators before anything
-- else - rising CMI with flat clinical indicators is its own candidate list.
tests.threshold: :growth_cut = 0.10 (growing ten percentage points faster than the peer group year over year) is the number to tune first and the more informative of the two tests; a level outlier can reflect a legitimately different resident population, but divergence from an appropriate starting point usually cannot. Adjusting by self-reported case mix is a deliberate compromise recorded in the SQL comment: it controls for real acuity differences and simultaneously creates a defeat mechanism, so the query scores both the adjusted and the unadjusted cost and labels which one produced each row. An UNADJUSTED_ONLY row is a facility whose reported acuity explains its cost; the query cannot tell real acuity from inflated acuity, so that label is a prompt to verify the case mix, not a finding. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: **MD-23 — nursing-facility cost-report rate-setting integrity check, cross-referencing self-reported cost data against independent evidence.** This test is the claims-side half of that cross-reference: it cannot audit a cost report, but it can say which facilities' claims behaviour does not match the rate they are being paid. MD-11 (state-directed payment and capitation actuarial-soundness oversight) is the adjacent control where rate inputs are reviewed.

failure_map.reading: Cost reports are accepted and used for rate-setting with no independent cross-reference of any kind. The rate-setting cycle is annual and the error compounds, so the exposure is a multiple of a single period's divergence.
A desk-review procedure exists but reviews are not being completed within the rate cycle, so rates are set on unreviewed data and any correction lands too late to affect payment.
Review covers only facilities selected on a rotation or below a size threshold, and the largest facilities — where a rate error is worth the most — are reviewed least often.

Review verifies internal arithmetic and schedule completeness rather than the reasonableness of reported costs against independent evidence, which is the specific thing MD-23 asks for. Related-party transactions are the usual blind spot.
Adjustments were made to reported costs but the basis is not documented, so neither the facility nor a later auditor can reconstruct why the rate is what it is.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Capitation and directed-payment outlier — dollars per member the acuity does not explain
tests.hypothesis: Under capitation the money moves before any service does, so the provider-side tests in this family are blind to it: a plan or a delegated entity can be paid far above peers per member with no claim ever looking unusual. Where actuarial-soundness and directed-payment oversight is weak, the observable signature is a gap between what is being paid per member and what is being delivered per member — capitation and directed-payment dollars rising while encounter volume per member stays flat or falls. The same gap has an innocent explanation, incomplete encounter reporting, and distinguishing the two is the whole difficulty; that is why this test must be read alongside encounter-completeness monitoring rather than on its own.
