tests.check: For each plan or delegated entity and rating region, compute capitation plus directed-payment dollars per member month, and encounter-derived service volume and allowed value per member month. Compare both against peers in the same rating region and product line, and compute the ratio between them. Flag entities whose payment per member month is high relative to peers while their delivered value per member month is not — and cross-check every hit against that entity's encounter-completeness metrics before drawing any conclusion.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 8 - Capitation / directed-payment per member month versus delivered value
-- Pattern only. Review candidates, not dispositions. Read WITH encounter completeness.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :min_mm (5000), :z_cut (2.0), :gap_cut (1.25)
-- Portability: STDDEV is STDDEV_SAMP in standard SQL; where NULLS LAST is not accepted, sort on (col IS NULL), col DESC.

WITH pay AS (
  SELECT
      c.plan_id,
      c.entity_id,                                     -- delegated entity / sub-cap arrangement
      c.product_line,                                  -- MCO / PIHP / PAHP / D-SNP / etc.
      c.rating_region,
      SUM(c.member_months)                             AS member_months,
      SUM(c.capitation_paid)                           AS cap_paid,
      SUM(c.directed_payment_amount)                   AS directed_paid,
      AVG(c.mean_risk_score)                           AS mean_risk
  FROM capitation_payments c
  WHERE c.payment_month BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
  GROUP BY c.plan_id, c.entity_id, c.product_line, c.rating_region
  HAVING SUM(c.member_months) >= :min_mm
),
delivered AS (
  SELECT
      e.plan_id, e.entity_id,
      COUNT(*)                                         AS encounter_count,
      SUM(e.allowed_amount)                            AS encounter_value
  FROM encounter_records e                             -- T-MSIS OT/IP/LT encounter concepts
  WHERE e.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
  GROUP BY e.plan_id, e.entity_id
),
joined AS (
  SELECT
      p.*,
      COALESCE(d.encounter_count, 0)                                   AS encounter_count,
      -- encounters carry no region: allocate the entity's total across its region rows by
      -- member-month share so a multi-region entity is not credited with it in full each time
      COALESCE(d.encounter_value, 0) * p.member_months
        / NULLIF(SUM(p.member_months) OVER (PARTITION BY p.plan_id, p.entity_id), 0)
                                                                       AS encounter_value,
      (p.cap_paid + p.directed_paid) / NULLIF(p.member_months, 0)
        / NULLIF(p.mean_risk, 0)                                       AS adj_pmpm_paid,
      COALESCE(d.encounter_value, 0) / NULLIF(SUM(p.member_months) OVER (PARTITION BY p.plan_id, p.entity_id), 0)
        / NULLIF(p.mean_risk, 0)                                       AS adj_pmpm_delivered
  FROM pay p
  LEFT JOIN delivered d ON d.plan_id = p.plan_id AND d.entity_id = p.entity_id
),
peer AS (
  SELECT product_line, rating_region,
         AVG(adj_pmpm_paid)         AS peer_paid_mean,
         STDDEV(adj_pmpm_paid)      AS peer_paid_sd,
         AVG(adj_pmpm_delivered)    AS peer_delivered_mean
  FROM joined
  GROUP BY product_line, rating_region
)
SELECT
    j.plan_id,
    j.entity_id,
    j.product_line,
    j.rating_region,
    j.member_months,
    ROUND(j.adj_pmpm_paid, 2)                                             AS adj_pmpm_paid,
    ROUND(j.adj_pmpm_delivered, 2)                                        AS adj_pmpm_delivered,
    ROUND((j.adj_pmpm_paid - pe.peer_paid_mean)
          / NULLIF(pe.peer_paid_sd, 0), 2)                                AS paid_z,
    ROUND((j.adj_pmpm_paid / NULLIF(pe.peer_paid_mean, 0))
          / NULLIF(j.adj_pmpm_delivered
                   / NULLIF(pe.peer_delivered_mean, 0), 0), 2)            AS paid_to_delivered_gap,
    j.encounter_count,
    CASE WHEN j.encounter_count = 0 THEN 'NO_ENCOUNTERS_REPORTED'
         WHEN j.adj_pmpm_delivered < 0.5 * pe.peer_delivered_mean
              THEN 'DELIVERY_FAR_BELOW_PEER'
    END                                                                   AS delivery_flag
FROM joined j
JOIN peer pe ON pe.product_line = j.product_line AND pe.rating_region = j.rating_region
WHERE (j.adj_pmpm_paid - pe.peer_paid_mean) / NULLIF(pe.peer_paid_sd, 0) > :z_cut
   OR j.encounter_count = 0                  -- zero delivered value makes the gap ratio NULL
   OR (j.adj_pmpm_paid / NULLIF(pe.peer_paid_mean, 0))
      / NULLIF(j.adj_pmpm_delivered / NULLIF(pe.peer_delivered_mean, 0), 0) > :gap_cut
ORDER BY paid_to_delivered_gap DESC NULLS LAST;

-- MANDATORY companion: pull the same entities' encounter-completeness metrics before
-- interpreting anything. An entity that under-reports encounters looks identical here to
-- an entity that under-delivers care, and the remedy for the two is opposite.
tests.threshold: :z_cut = 2.0 is looser than elsewhere in this family because the population is small — there are tens of plans, not thousands of providers — and a strict cut on a small population finds nothing. :gap_cut = 1.25 says an entity is paid 25% more relative to peers than it delivers relative to peers; that is a starting point and is highly sensitive to encounter-data quality, which is the reason the companion check is marked mandatory rather than optional. Where encounter completeness is known to be poor, this test should be reported as a data-quality finding and not as a payment finding at all. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: **MD-11 — state-directed payment and capitation actuarial-soundness oversight.** The test asks the question MD-11 owns: is what we are paying per member defensible against what comparable entities are paid and what is being delivered. MD-17 (managed-care encounter/payment data completeness monitoring) is the control that makes the answer interpretable; MC-24 (favourable-selection detection) is the adjacent explanation when the risk mix rather than the rate is doing the work.

failure_map.reading: No comparative review of directed payments or capitation against delivered value; soundness is certified on the actuarial submission alone with no retrospective look-back.
Oversight is defined in the contract or state plan but the retrospective comparison was not performed for the rating period under review.
Review covers base capitation but excludes directed payments and pass-through arrangements, which is where the discretionary dollars and the growth actually are.

Review compares payments against the actuarial certification rather than against delivered value or peers, so an arrangement that was certified on optimistic assumptions is never revisited against what happened.

Encounter data is too incomplete to support any delivered-value comparison, so the oversight cannot be performed at all. Record this as an MD-17 evidence finding, not as an MD-11 payment finding — the distinction is the point.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Documentation-request aging and non-response — flags that never became evidence
tests.hypothesis: An outlier flag becomes a finding only if someone asks for records and the records arrive. Where documentation-request tracking is weak, requests are issued and then silently expire: the provider does not respond, the clock runs out, and the case is closed as unsubstantiated — which reads in the metrics as a false positive when it is actually an unanswered question. Two populations are diagnostic. Requests aged past the response deadline with no recorded response and no recorded escalation, and providers with a persistent non-response rate across multiple requests. The second is the more serious: a provider who reliably does not answer has learned that not answering works.
tests.check: For every documentation request issued in the period, compute days from issue to response or to today, whether a response was recorded, and whether the case was closed before or after the deadline. Aggregate to provider level to find persistent non-responders, and to programme level to find the share of requests that expired without escalation.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 9 - ADR / documentation-request aging and non-response
-- Runs on your audit-tracking system, not on claims. Two statements: A by programme, B by provider.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :response_days (45), :min_requests (3), :nonresponse_cut (0.30)
-- Portability: DATE_DIFF with a trailing DAY unit is BigQuery syntax (elsewhere DATEDIFF(day, earlier, later) or a date subtraction); for date + integer use DATEADD.

-- STATEMENT A: programme-level aging
WITH req AS (
  SELECT
      r.request_id,
      r.provider_npi,
      r.programme,                                     -- UPIC / RAC / CERT / MAC / internal SIU
      r.issue_date,
      r.response_due_date,
      r.response_received_date,
      r.case_status,
      r.case_closed_date,
      r.dollars_at_risk,
      COALESCE(DATE_DIFF(COALESCE(r.response_received_date, CURRENT_DATE), r.issue_date, DAY),
               0)                                      AS days_open,
      CASE WHEN r.response_received_date IS NULL
            AND COALESCE(r.response_due_date, r.issue_date + :response_days) < CURRENT_DATE
           THEN 1 ELSE 0 END                           AS expired_unanswered
  FROM documentation_requests r
  WHERE r.issue_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
)
SELECT
    programme,
    COUNT(*)                                                     AS requests,
    SUM(expired_unanswered)                                      AS expired_unanswered,
    ROUND(100.0 * SUM(expired_unanswered) / NULLIF(COUNT(*),0),1) AS pct_expired,
    SUM(CASE WHEN expired_unanswered = 1 THEN dollars_at_risk END) AS dollars_unresolved,
    -- the quiet failure: cases closed as unsubstantiated while the request was still
    -- unanswered. Count these separately; they are not false positives.
    SUM(CASE WHEN case_status = 'CLOSED_UNSUBSTANTIATED'
              AND response_received_date IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
                                                                 AS closed_unsubstantiated_unanswered,
    ROUND(AVG(days_open), 1)                                     AS mean_days_open
FROM req
GROUP BY programme
ORDER BY dollars_unresolved DESC NULLS LAST;

-- STATEMENT B: persistent non-responders - the population that matters most
WITH req AS (
  SELECT
      r.provider_npi,
      r.dollars_at_risk,
      CASE WHEN r.response_received_date IS NULL
            AND COALESCE(r.response_due_date, r.issue_date + :response_days) < CURRENT_DATE
           THEN 1 ELSE 0 END                           AS expired_unanswered
  FROM documentation_requests r
  WHERE r.issue_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
)
SELECT
    provider_npi,
    COUNT(*)                                             AS requests,
    SUM(expired_unanswered)                              AS unanswered,
    ROUND(1.0 * SUM(expired_unanswered) / COUNT(*), 3)   AS nonresponse_rate,
    SUM(dollars_at_risk)                                 AS exposure
FROM req
GROUP BY provider_npi
HAVING COUNT(*) >= :min_requests
   AND 1.0 * SUM(expired_unanswered) / COUNT(*) > :nonresponse_cut
ORDER BY exposure DESC;
tests.threshold: :response_days = 45 reflects a common documentation-request window but yours is set by programme and by contract — use the actual due date on the record wherever it exists and fall back to the parameter only where it does not. :nonresponse_cut = 0.30 across at least :min_requests = 3 requests is a starting point for 'persistent'; the number matters less than running the provider-level pass at all, since a single unanswered request is routine and a pattern of them is not. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: **PI-13 — contractor ADR-response tracking (UPIC/RAC/CERT/MAC).** The closed_unsubstantiated_unanswered column of statement A is the sharpest use of this test: cases closed as unsubstantiated while the request sat unanswered are being counted as analytics false positives, which quietly corrupts every precision metric in test 10 and can lead a programme to tune down a test that was working. PI-05 is the medical-review process the request serves; CD-14 is the insufficient-documentation root-cause loop.

failure_map.reading: No central tracking of documentation requests; each reviewer tracks their own, so no one can say how many requests are outstanding or what they are worth.
A tracking system exists but issue and response dates are not consistently populated, making aging uncomputable — check field completeness before interpreting any aging number.

Requests issued outside the tracked workflow — by email, or by a delegated vendor with its own system — are absent from the tracker entirely, so the measured non-response rate understates the real one.
Aging is tracked but expiry triggers no escalation, so the tracker faithfully records requests dying of old age. Look for the escalation field being uniformly null.
Responses were received but not linked to the request or the case, so the programme cannot demonstrate what evidence it had when it closed a case.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Flag-to-disposition yield — precision, cycle time and return by test
tests.hypothesis: An outlier programme that does not measure its own precision cannot improve and cannot be defended. The failure has a characteristic shape: flag volume is reported as an accomplishment, dollars identified are reported as a result, and the two numbers that actually matter — what share of flags became findings, and what share of identified dollars were recovered — are absent. Where performance reporting is absent or vanity-metric only, the observable signature is a programme whose flag volume is stable or growing while its finding rate is unmeasured, and whose oldest open flags are older than anyone realises.
tests.check: For each detection test or model that generates flags, compute flags generated, flags triaged, flags dispositioned, findings confirmed, dollars identified and dollars recovered, plus median cycle time from flag to disposition and the age of the oldest open flag. Report precision per test rather than in aggregate, because a single high-precision test can carry a programme average while every other test runs at near-zero yield.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 10 - Yield, precision and cycle time by detection test
-- Runs on your PI case-management system. This is the programme's self-measurement.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end
-- Portability: DATE_DIFF with a trailing DAY unit is BigQuery syntax; elsewhere use DATEDIFF(day, earlier, later) or a date subtraction.

WITH f AS (
  SELECT
      fl.flag_id,
      fl.detection_test_id,                             -- which query/model produced it
      fl.model_version,
      fl.generated_date,
      fl.triage_date,
      fl.disposition,                                   -- e.g. NO_ACTION / EDUCATION / AUDIT / REFERRAL
      fl.disposition_date,
      fl.finding_confirmed,                             -- boolean set at case closure
      fl.dollars_identified,
      fl.dollars_recovered
  FROM pi_flags fl
  WHERE fl.generated_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
)
SELECT
    detection_test_id,
    model_version,
    COUNT(*)                                                            AS flags_generated,
    SUM(CASE WHEN triage_date IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)            AS flags_triaged,
    SUM(CASE WHEN disposition IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)            AS flags_dispositioned,
    -- findings and precision count dispositioned flags only, so the numerator is a subset
    -- of the denominator and precision cannot pass 100
    SUM(CASE WHEN finding_confirmed AND disposition IS NOT NULL
             THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                                         AS findings,
    ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN finding_confirmed AND disposition IS NOT NULL
                           THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
          / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN disposition IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0), 1)
                                                                        AS precision_pct,
    -- data-quality column: a confirmed finding with no recorded disposition is a record
    -- error; it is shown here and kept out of precision
    SUM(CASE WHEN finding_confirmed AND disposition IS NULL
             THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                                         AS confirmed_without_disposition,
    SUM(dollars_identified)                                             AS dollars_identified,
    SUM(dollars_recovered)                                              AS dollars_recovered,
    ROUND(100.0 * SUM(dollars_recovered)
          / NULLIF(SUM(dollars_identified), 0), 1)                      AS recovery_pct,
    -- cycle time on dispositioned flags only, so an untouched backlog cannot flatter it
    ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN disposition_date IS NOT NULL
                   THEN DATE_DIFF(disposition_date, generated_date, DAY) END), 1)
                                                                        AS mean_days_to_disposition,
    MAX(CASE WHEN disposition IS NULL
             THEN DATE_DIFF(CURRENT_DATE, generated_date, DAY) END)     AS oldest_open_flag_days
FROM f
GROUP BY detection_test_id, model_version
ORDER BY dollars_identified DESC NULLS LAST;

-- Read precision and the untriaged backlog together. A test showing 90% precision on
-- twelve triaged flags out of nine hundred generated is not a precise test; it is an
-- untouched queue with a cherry-picked front. Always report flags_triaged/flags_generated
-- next to precision_pct, and never publish precision without it.
tests.threshold: There is no correct precision number and any published target would be misused — a high-precision programme may simply be running one narrow test and ignoring the rest of its exposure, and a low-precision one may be doing valuable exploratory work. What is diagnosable is the *shape*: precision that is unmeasured, precision reported without triage coverage, cycle times with no ceiling, and an oldest-open-flag age that exceeds the recovery look-back period, which converts an analytics backlog into an unrecoverable one. Set your own targets from your own baseline and revisit them when a model version changes. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: **PI-19 — PI performance reporting (recovery ROI, prevention metrics).** This test is PI-19 executing at test-level granularity rather than programme level, which is the granularity at which the numbers are actionable. It also feeds AG-01: precision by model version is the model-monitoring metric an analytics governance regime needs, and it cannot be produced unless the flag record carries the model version — which is the single most valuable field to add if it is missing.

failure_map.reading: No performance reporting exists; the programme reports activity (flags generated, audits opened) and never outcome. Ask for last year's precision figure and see whether one exists.
A reporting pack is defined but has not been produced for the period, or is produced for an executive audience only in a form that omits precision and backlog.

Reporting covers the tests that perform well and omits the rest, or resets the denominator each period so a growing backlog never appears. Check whether flags_generated reconciles to the detection runs.

Metrics are recovery-weighted only, so prevention — an edit that stops the claim, an education contact that changes behaviour — scores zero and gets defunded in favour of pay-and-chase. This is the failure mode with the largest long-run cost.
Flags are not linked to the test or model version that produced them, so no per-test precision can be computed at all and model monitoring is impossible.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Cross-programme duplication — the same provider-period audited more than once
tests.hypothesis: Outlier lists are generated independently by several programmes — internal SIU, a recovery contractor, a state unit, a plan's own analytics — and they all rank on roughly the same signal, so they converge on the same providers. Without de-duplication the same provider-period is requested, reviewed and sometimes recovered against more than once. This has three costs, and the third is the one that gets missed: wasted review capacity, an unreasonable burden on the provider, and a real risk of double recovery on the same dollars, which is a finding against the payer rather than the provider.
tests.check: Across all audit and review programmes, find provider-period combinations touched by more than one programme, and among those find any where recovered dollars overlap on the same claims. Report burden separately from double recovery — the first is an efficiency and fairness question, the second is a correction the payer owes.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 11 - Cross-programme audit duplication and potential double recovery
-- Runs on your audit-tracking and recovery systems.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end
-- Portability: DATE_TRUNC('quarter', d) and STRING_AGG(DISTINCT ...) vary by engine; use year and quarter columns and LISTAGG or GROUP_CONCAT.

WITH touches AS (
  SELECT
      a.provider_npi,
      DATE_TRUNC('quarter', a.service_period_start)     AS service_quarter,
      a.programme,
      a.audit_id,
      a.dollars_identified,
      a.dollars_recovered
  FROM audit_activity a
  WHERE a.activity_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
),
dupes AS (
  SELECT provider_npi, service_quarter,
         COUNT(DISTINCT programme)  AS programmes,
         COUNT(DISTINCT audit_id)   AS audits,
         SUM(dollars_identified)    AS total_identified,
         SUM(dollars_recovered)     AS total_recovered
  FROM touches
  GROUP BY provider_npi, service_quarter
  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT programme) > 1
)
SELECT
    d.provider_npi,
    d.service_quarter,
    d.programmes,
    d.audits,
    d.total_identified,
    d.total_recovered,
    STRING_AGG(DISTINCT t.programme, ', ')  AS programme_list
FROM dupes d
JOIN touches t
  ON t.provider_npi    = d.provider_npi
 AND t.service_quarter = d.service_quarter
GROUP BY d.provider_npi, d.service_quarter, d.programmes, d.audits,
         d.total_identified, d.total_recovered
ORDER BY d.audits DESC, d.total_recovered DESC;

-- The serious pass: same CLAIM recovered by two programmes. Run this one first if your
-- recovery records carry claim identifiers; a hit here is a payer-side correction.
--   SELECT r.claim_id, COUNT(DISTINCT r.programme) AS programmes,
--          SUM(r.amount_recovered) AS recovered_total
--   FROM recovery_detail r
--   WHERE r.recovery_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
--   GROUP BY r.claim_id
--   HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT r.programme) > 1
--   ORDER BY recovered_total DESC;
tests.threshold: Duplication is not a threshold test: any same-claim double recovery is a finding at a count of one and should be worked immediately. Provider-period overlap between programmes is expected at some level and only becomes a coordination finding when it is routine, so measure your own overlap rate first and set the trigger relative to that baseline rather than importing a number. A useful secondary measure is requests per provider per year across all programmes — the burden number, which nobody computes and every provider association can. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: **PI-15 — cross-contractor audit coordination and de-duplication.** The test is the direct measurement of what PI-15 exists to prevent. Note the asymmetry in how the findings resolve: overlap is a coordination fix, double recovery is a repayment the payer owes, and conflating them in a single report lets the second hide inside the first.

failure_map.reading: No coordination mechanism exists between programmes; each maintains its own worklist and there is no shared view of who is already under review.
A coordination log or clearance step is defined but is not being populated, so clearance checks pass trivially because the log is empty.
Coordination covers contractor programmes but not internal SIU work or delegated-entity audits, so the overlap simply moves to the uncovered channel.
De-duplication matches on provider and date range but not on claim, so two programmes can recover different amounts against the same claims without triggering anything.
Recovery records lack claim-level detail, so double recovery cannot be detected or disproved — which is also the state in which a provider's assertion of it cannot be rebutted.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Did the intervention work? Pre/post re-measurement of the flagged behaviour
tests.hypothesis: Corrective action is treated as complete when it is delivered rather than when it works. A provider is educated, an edit is installed, a recovery is taken — and no one returns to measure whether the underlying rate changed. Where the effectiveness re-measurement loop is absent, the observable signature is a set of providers whose post-intervention metric is statistically indistinguishable from their pre-intervention metric, sitting in a case system where every one of those cases is marked closed and effective. The mirror signature matters too: interventions that worked and were never credited, which is how effective prevention work loses its funding to recovery work.
tests.check: For each closed corrective action, recompute the provider's flagged metric over a matched window before and after the intervention date, and compare the change against the change in a peer group over the same calendar window — so a market-wide shift is not credited to the intervention. Classify each into improved, unchanged or worsened, and report the distribution by intervention type.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 12 - Pre/post effectiveness re-measurement with a peer-difference correction
-- Runs on your case system joined to the metric that produced the flag.
-- Params: :window_days (180), :improve_cut (0.20)
-- Portability: date +/- integer days is not universal; use DATEADD(day, n, d) or d + INTERVAL n DAY. NULLS LAST: sort on (col IS NULL) first.

WITH actions AS (
  SELECT ca.action_id, ca.provider_npi, ca.action_type,      -- EDUCATION / EDIT / RECOVERY / CAP
         ca.intervention_date, ca.metric_id, ca.closed_date, ca.closure_assessment
  FROM corrective_actions ca
  WHERE ca.closed_date IS NOT NULL
),
metric AS (
  -- provider_metric_history is whatever table stores the recurring value of a detection
  -- metric per provider per period. If you do not have one, build it: without a metric
  -- history this control cannot be tested at all, which is itself the finding.
  SELECT m.provider_npi, m.metric_id, m.period_end, m.metric_value, m.peer_mean
  FROM provider_metric_history m
),
prepost AS (
  SELECT
      a.action_id, a.provider_npi, a.action_type, a.intervention_date, a.closure_assessment,
      AVG(CASE WHEN m.period_end <  a.intervention_date
                AND m.period_end >= a.intervention_date - :window_days
               THEN m.metric_value END)                        AS pre_value,
      AVG(CASE WHEN m.period_end >  a.intervention_date
                AND m.period_end <= a.intervention_date + :window_days
               THEN m.metric_value END)                        AS post_value,
      AVG(CASE WHEN m.period_end <  a.intervention_date
                AND m.period_end >= a.intervention_date - :window_days
               THEN m.peer_mean END)                           AS pre_peer,
      AVG(CASE WHEN m.period_end >  a.intervention_date
                AND m.period_end <= a.intervention_date + :window_days
               THEN m.peer_mean END)                           AS post_peer
  FROM actions a
  JOIN metric m ON m.provider_npi = a.provider_npi AND m.metric_id = a.metric_id
  GROUP BY a.action_id, a.provider_npi, a.action_type, a.intervention_date, a.closure_assessment
)
SELECT
    action_id, provider_npi, action_type, intervention_date, closure_assessment,
    ROUND(pre_value, 3)   AS pre_value,
    ROUND(post_value, 3)  AS post_value,
    -- difference-in-differences: the provider's change net of the peer group's change
    ROUND((post_value - pre_value) - (post_peer - pre_peer), 3) AS peer_adjusted_change,
    CASE
      WHEN post_value IS NULL OR pre_value IS NULL THEN 'NOT_MEASURABLE'
      WHEN ((post_value - pre_value) - (post_peer - pre_peer))
           / NULLIF(pre_value, 0) <= -:improve_cut               THEN 'IMPROVED'
      WHEN ((post_value - pre_value) - (post_peer - pre_peer))
           / NULLIF(pre_value, 0) >=  :improve_cut               THEN 'WORSENED'
      ELSE 'UNCHANGED'
    END                                                          AS effectiveness,
    CASE WHEN closure_assessment = 'EFFECTIVE'
          AND (post_value IS NULL OR pre_value IS NULL
               OR ((post_value - pre_value) - (post_peer - pre_peer))
                  / NULLIF(pre_value, 0) > -:improve_cut)
         THEN 'CLOSURE_NOT_SUPPORTED' END                        AS closure_check
FROM prepost
ORDER BY peer_adjusted_change DESC NULLS LAST;

-- CLOSURE_NOT_SUPPORTED is the column to read first: cases the programme certified as
-- effective where the data does not show improvement. It is a finding about the closure
-- process, not about the provider.
tests.threshold: :window_days = 180 balances having enough post-intervention data against waiting so long that other changes intervene; shorten it for edits, which act immediately, and lengthen it for education, which does not. :improve_cut = 0.20 (a 20% peer-adjusted movement) is a starting point chosen to be larger than ordinary period-to-period noise — measure your metric's own volatility and set the cut above it, or the test will report improvement and deterioration at random. The peer-difference correction is not optional: without it, a market-wide coding change is credited to whatever intervention happened to precede it. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: **PI-11 — corrective-action effectiveness re-measurement (loop closure).** This is the control the whole family exists to serve: detection without effectiveness measurement is a treadmill. PI-10 is the root-cause workflow that produces the action; MD-13 is the Medicaid improper-payment CAP-to-closure requirement. Note that NOT_MEASURABLE rows are as informative as the rest — they identify actions taken against a metric that is not tracked over time, so effectiveness was never knowable.

failure_map.reading: No re-measurement occurs; cases close on delivery of the action. Look for closure assessments that are uniformly 'effective' with no supporting metric.
Re-measurement is defined in the PI plan at a stated interval but no re-measurement records exist for the period.
Re-measurement is performed for edits and system changes, where it is easy, and skipped for provider-level education, where most of the case volume is.
Re-measurement compares raw before and after with no peer adjustment, so it credits or blames the intervention for market-wide movement. The peer-adjusted column exists to expose exactly this.

No provider metric history is retained, so pre-intervention values cannot be reconstructed and the loop cannot be closed even retrospectively. Retaining the metric history is the cheapest remediation in this family.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Education without effect — repeat outliers across consecutive detection cycles
tests.hypothesis: Provider education is the cheapest corrective action and therefore the default one, which makes it the action most likely to be applied where it cannot work. Education addresses error; it does nothing about deliberate conduct and nothing about a structural incentive. Where the education-and-feedback control operates without an escalation rule, the signature is a small population of providers who appear on the outlier list every cycle, receive an education contact every cycle, and never move — and whose repeat appearances are counted as evidence the education programme is busy. The number of prior contacts is the variable that should drive escalation and usually is not recorded at all.
tests.check: Join the outlier list across consecutive detection cycles and count consecutive appearances per provider. For each repeat provider, count prior education contacts and any escalation beyond education. Flag providers above an appearance count who have received only education, and report the dollars flowing through them while the cycle repeats.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 13 - Repeat outliers who have received only education
-- Runs on the flag history joined to the contact/action log.
-- Params: :cycles_lookback (4), :repeat_cut (3), :education_cut (2)
-- Portability: LIMIT inside a subquery is not universal; use FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY, TOP n, or ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY cycle_end DESC) <= n.

WITH appearances AS (
  SELECT
      fl.provider_npi,
      fl.detection_cycle,                                -- e.g. 2026Q1, 2026Q2
      MAX(fl.dollars_at_risk)                            AS cycle_dollars
  FROM pi_flags fl
  WHERE fl.detection_cycle IN (SELECT cycle_id FROM detection_cycles
                               ORDER BY cycle_end DESC LIMIT :cycles_lookback)
  GROUP BY fl.provider_npi, fl.detection_cycle
),
repeats AS (
  SELECT provider_npi,
         COUNT(DISTINCT detection_cycle) AS cycles_flagged,
         SUM(cycle_dollars)              AS dollars_across_cycles
  FROM appearances
  GROUP BY provider_npi
  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT detection_cycle) >= :repeat_cut
),
actions AS (
  SELECT ca.provider_npi,
         SUM(CASE WHEN ca.action_type = 'EDUCATION' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS education_contacts,
         SUM(CASE WHEN ca.action_type IN ('AUDIT','RECOVERY','EDIT','REFERRAL','SUSPENSION')
                  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                                   AS escalated_actions,
         MAX(ca.intervention_date)                                     AS last_action_date
  FROM corrective_actions ca
  GROUP BY ca.provider_npi
)
SELECT
    r.provider_npi,
    r.cycles_flagged,
    r.dollars_across_cycles,
    COALESCE(a.education_contacts, 0)  AS education_contacts,
    COALESCE(a.escalated_actions, 0)   AS escalated_actions,
    a.last_action_date,
    CASE
      WHEN COALESCE(a.escalated_actions, 0) > 0                  THEN 'ESCALATED'
      WHEN COALESCE(a.education_contacts, 0) >= :education_cut   THEN 'EDUCATION_ONLY_REPEAT'
      WHEN COALESCE(a.education_contacts, 0) = 0                 THEN 'NO_ACTION_TAKEN'
      ELSE 'EDUCATION_BELOW_TRIGGER'   -- some education, fewer contacts than the trigger, nothing else
    END                                AS action_profile
FROM repeats r
LEFT JOIN actions a ON a.provider_npi = r.provider_npi
ORDER BY r.dollars_across_cycles DESC;

-- NO_ACTION_TAKEN is usually the larger population and the quieter problem: providers
-- flagged in three or four cycles with no recorded contact of any kind.
-- Report the two profiles separately; they have different remedies.
-- cycles_flagged counts distinct flagged cycles inside the lookback. It does not require
-- them to be consecutive; add a gap check if consecutive appearance matters to you.
tests.threshold: :repeat_cut = 3 consecutive-or-near-consecutive cycles is a starting point and depends entirely on cycle length — three quarterly cycles is nine months of unchanged behaviour, three monthly cycles is not much at all. The query counts flagged cycles inside the lookback and does not require them to be consecutive. :education_cut = 2 education contacts with no escalation is offered as the trigger for an escalation review, not as a rule that education has failed; some legitimate practice patterns will recur permanently and the right outcome for those is a documented exclusion rather than a third contact. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: **PI-12 — provider education and error-trend feedback.** The control is sound and the test is about its boundary: education is the correct response to error and the wrong response to everything else, so a programme with no escalation rule converts every case into an error case by default. Pair with PI-11 (was the education effective) and CB-19 (coding audit) as the usual next step.

failure_map.reading: No education or feedback programme exists; providers learn about their outlier status only through an audit, which is both more expensive and more adversarial than it needs to be.
An education programme is described in the compliance plan but no contacts were logged in the period.
Education is delivered to small providers and skipped for the large systems that generate the most dollars, usually because the relationship is managed elsewhere in the organisation.
Education is delivered repeatedly with no escalation criterion, so the same providers cycle indefinitely. EDUCATION_ONLY_REPEAT is the direct measurement of this failure.
Contacts are not logged against the provider record, so prior-contact count is unknown and escalation cannot be triggered by it even if a rule exists.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Identified but not recovered — overpayment aging against the look-back limit
tests.hypothesis: Dollars identified is the number every programme reports; dollars recovered is the number that changes the ledger, and the gap between them is where the recovery control fails silently. Two mechanisms produce the gap. Cases age past the reopening or look-back limit while sitting in a queue, at which point the money is gone as a matter of law rather than as a matter of collectability. And identified overpayments are recorded but never converted into a demand, so nothing ever starts. The second is harder to see because the case looks open and healthy right up until it expires.
tests.check: For each identified overpayment, compute age from identification, whether a demand was issued, days remaining against the applicable look-back or reopening limit, and amounts outstanding. Bucket by time-to-expiry and report dollars in each bucket, so the report says how much money will be lost in the next quarter if nothing changes.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 14 - Overpayment aging against the look-back limit
-- Runs on your overpayment / recovery tracking system.
-- Params: :lookback_days (1460 for a four-year reopening window - use YOUR applicable limit)
-- Portability: DATE_DIFF with a trailing DAY unit is BigQuery syntax (elsewhere DATEDIFF(day, earlier, later)); GROUP BY 2 is an ordinal, repeat the CASE where ordinals are not accepted.

WITH op AS (
  SELECT
      o.overpayment_id,
      o.provider_npi,
      o.source,                                        -- SELF_REPORTED / AUDIT / ANALYTICS / CONTRACTOR
      o.service_period_end,
      o.identified_date,
      o.demand_issued_date,
      o.amount_identified,
      COALESCE(o.amount_recovered, 0)                  AS amount_recovered,
      o.status,
      DATE_DIFF(CURRENT_DATE, o.identified_date, DAY)  AS days_since_identified,
      :lookback_days - DATE_DIFF(CURRENT_DATE, o.service_period_end, DAY)
                                                       AS days_to_lookback_expiry
  FROM overpayments o
  -- a NULL status is unknown, not recovered: keep the row (a bare <> would drop it)
  WHERE COALESCE(o.status, 'UNKNOWN') <> 'FULLY_RECOVERED'
)
SELECT
    source,
    CASE
      WHEN days_to_lookback_expiry <  0   THEN 'EXPIRED'
      WHEN days_to_lookback_expiry <  90  THEN 'EXPIRES_WITHIN_90D'
      WHEN days_to_lookback_expiry < 365  THEN 'EXPIRES_WITHIN_1Y'
      ELSE 'IN_WINDOW'
    END                                                        AS expiry_bucket,
    COUNT(*)                                                   AS cases,
    SUM(CASE WHEN status IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)            AS cases_status_unknown,
    SUM(amount_identified - amount_recovered)                  AS outstanding,
    SUM(CASE WHEN demand_issued_date IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS no_demand_issued,
    SUM(CASE WHEN demand_issued_date IS NULL
             THEN amount_identified - amount_recovered END)     AS outstanding_no_demand,
    ROUND(AVG(days_since_identified), 0)                        AS mean_age_days
FROM op
GROUP BY source, 2
ORDER BY outstanding DESC;

-- The line to act on is EXPIRES_WITHIN_90D with no demand issued. Everything in it is
-- recoverable today and unrecoverable next quarter, and nothing else in this pack has
-- that property.
--
-- Separately: the 60-day clock on self-identified overpayments (PI-07 / MC-19) runs from
-- identification, not from the look-back limit, and is much shorter. Report source =
-- 'SELF_REPORTED' against a 60-day age, not against this bucket scheme.
tests.threshold: :lookback_days must be replaced with your own applicable limit — reopening rules, state recovery statutes and contract terms all differ, and the four-year value used here is a placeholder chosen only to make the query runnable. The 90-day bucket is the operationally useful one because it matches a quarter of management attention. No threshold in this test is statistical; every one is a legal or contractual deadline, so confirm each against its source rather than tuning it. Where a demand tolls or extends the limit in your programme, model that explicitly rather than using identified date as a proxy.
tests.pair: **PI-09 — overpayment recovery tracking versus reopening / RAC look-back.** The test is a direct instrument for the control. PI-07 and MC-19 (60-day identify-report-return obligations) are the much tighter clock on self-identified overpayments and should be measured separately; mixing the two populations in one aging report is the most common way the 60-day exposure gets hidden inside a comfortable-looking four-year window.

failure_map.reading: No aging of identified overpayments against any limit; recovery is worked in whatever order cases arrive and expiry is discovered after the fact.
An aging report is specified but not produced, or is produced without the look-back comparison, which is the only part that matters.
Aging covers contractor-identified overpayments, which come with their own tracking, and omits internally identified and self-reported ones.

Aging runs from identification date rather than from the service period, so a case identified late looks young while its look-back window is already closing. Compare the two age columns; the divergence is the failure.

Demand issuance is not recorded against the overpayment, so it is impossible to show whether recovery was ever pursued — and equally impossible to defend the programme against a claim that it was not.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Payment velocity during an open investigation — exposure accruing while a case runs
tests.hypothesis: Between the moment a credible allegation exists and the moment anything is done about it, claims continue to pay at whatever rate they were paying. Where the payment-suspension control is absent or is treated as a last resort rather than a considered decision, the observable signature is measurable and rarely measured: dollars paid to providers with open high-severity cases, accruing over the life of the case. The right output is emphatically not a suspension recommendation — suspension is a serious action with due-process requirements, real consequences for beneficiary access, and a legal standard this query cannot evaluate. The output is the exposure number that should be in front of whoever makes that decision.
tests.check: For each open case at or above a defined severity, compute dollars paid to the subject provider between the case-open date and today, the daily payment rate, and whether a suspension, prepayment review or other mitigation was considered and recorded. Report accrued exposure and the decision record, not a recommendation.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 15 - Exposure accruing during open investigations
-- Runs on the case system joined to paid-claims totals. NOT a suspension recommendation.
-- Params: :severity_min ('HIGH'), :period_end
-- Portability: DATE_DIFF with a trailing DAY unit is BigQuery syntax (elsewhere DATEDIFF(day, earlier, later)); where there is no boolean type compare the flags to 1 and 0.

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT c.case_id, c.provider_npi, c.severity, c.opened_date,
         c.suspension_considered_flag, c.suspension_decision,
         c.prepay_review_flag, c.referral_date,
         -- severity is text: compare ranks, never the strings (alphabetically CRITICAL < HIGH < LOW < MEDIUM)
         -- adapt both lists to your severity scheme; a value on neither list ranks NULL
         CASE c.severity    WHEN 'LOW' THEN 1 WHEN 'MEDIUM' THEN 2 WHEN 'HIGH' THEN 3 WHEN 'CRITICAL' THEN 4 END AS severity_rank,
         CASE :severity_min WHEN 'LOW' THEN 1 WHEN 'MEDIUM' THEN 2 WHEN 'HIGH' THEN 3 WHEN 'CRITICAL' THEN 4 END AS min_rank
  FROM pi_cases c
  WHERE c.status = 'OPEN'
),
open_cases AS (
  SELECT case_id, provider_npi, severity, opened_date,
         suspension_considered_flag, suspension_decision, prepay_review_flag, referral_date,
         CASE WHEN min_rank IS NULL      THEN 'SEVERITY_MIN_NOT_RECOGNISED'
              WHEN severity_rank IS NULL THEN 'UNKNOWN_SEVERITY'
              ELSE 'OK' END                            AS severity_check
  FROM ranked
  WHERE severity_rank >= min_rank
     OR severity_rank IS NULL     -- missing or unlisted severity: kept and labelled, never dropped
     OR min_rank IS NULL          -- unlisted :severity_min: nothing is filtered and every row says so
),
paid_since AS (
  SELECT oc.case_id,
         SUM(cl.paid_amount)                                     AS paid_since_open,
         COUNT(*)                                                AS lines_since_open,
         MIN(cl.service_date)                                    AS first_service,
         MAX(cl.service_date)                                    AS last_service
  FROM open_cases oc
  JOIN claim_lines cl
    ON cl.billing_npi = oc.provider_npi
   AND cl.paid_date BETWEEN oc.opened_date AND :period_end
   AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  GROUP BY oc.case_id
)
SELECT
    oc.case_id,
    oc.provider_npi,
    oc.severity,
    oc.severity_check,
    oc.opened_date,
    DATE_DIFF(:period_end, oc.opened_date, DAY)                          AS case_age_days,
    COALESCE(p.paid_since_open, 0)                                       AS paid_since_open,
    ROUND(COALESCE(p.paid_since_open, 0)
          / NULLIF(DATE_DIFF(:period_end, oc.opened_date, DAY), 0), 2)   AS daily_accrual,
    p.lines_since_open,
    oc.suspension_considered_flag,
    oc.suspension_decision,
    oc.prepay_review_flag,
    oc.referral_date,
    CASE WHEN COALESCE(oc.suspension_considered_flag, FALSE) = FALSE
          AND COALESCE(oc.prepay_review_flag, FALSE) = FALSE
         THEN 'NO_MITIGATION_RECORDED' END                                AS mitigation_gap
FROM open_cases oc
LEFT JOIN paid_since p ON p.case_id = oc.case_id
ORDER BY paid_since_open DESC NULLS LAST;

-- Read mitigation_gap as a DOCUMENTATION finding. A decision not to suspend is a
-- legitimate and often correct decision; a case where nobody recorded making the
-- decision either way is the finding. The regulation contemplates good-cause exceptions
-- and they must be documented to exist.
-- Read severity_check before anything else: UNKNOWN_SEVERITY rows carry a severity this
-- query does not rank (fix the record or the list), and SEVERITY_MIN_NOT_RECOGNISED means
-- the parameter itself is not on the list, so the severity filter did not run at all.
tests.threshold: There is no dollar threshold here on purpose. Any figure would read as an implicit trigger for suspension, and suspension is not a threshold decision — it turns on the credibility of the allegation and on documented good-cause considerations, neither of which is in claims data. What can be set locally is a review trigger: an accrued exposure or case age at which the mitigation decision must be revisited and recorded. Also worth measuring is the distribution of case age at severity, because the real problem is usually case cycle time rather than the suspension decision itself. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: **PI-16 — payment suspension on credible allegation of fraud.** Note the direction of the pairing carefully: the test does not measure whether suspension happened, it measures whether the decision was made and recorded, and what it cost while it was pending. MD-18 is the Medicaid credible-allegation suspension and MFCU referral control; PI-14 is the law-enforcement referral pathway, and the referral date column is included because a pending referral is one of the recognised good-cause grounds for not suspending.

failure_map.reading: No suspension authority is operationalised — the control exists in regulation but there is no internal process to invoke it, so the option is never on the table.
A suspension process exists but has not been invoked or formally declined in any case in the period; check whether the consideration step appears anywhere in the case workflow.
Suspension is considered only on referred cases and never on internally developed ones, or is routinely deferred pending a referral that is not pursued.
Suspension decisions are made so late in the case lifecycle that most of the exposure has already accrued. The daily-accrual column times the median case age is the size of this failure.
Neither the decision nor the good-cause rationale is recorded, so the payer cannot show it considered suspension — the position that is hardest to defend afterwards, whichever way the decision went.

tests.family_title: Peer-group cost-per-beneficiary outlier — and the program around it
tests.name: Detection coverage map — which spend has no test looking at it
tests.hypothesis: Detection programmes accrete. Tests are written in response to whatever went wrong last, so coverage follows history rather than exposure, and the categories that have never produced a scandal are the categories nobody watches. Where the programme has no coverage map, the signature is straightforward and slightly uncomfortable to look at: rank spend by service category, mark which categories had a detection test run against them in the period, and read the unmarked rows. That list is the programme's blind spot, and it is usually larger and more expensive than the people running the programme expect — not because anyone decided not to look, but because nobody ever laid the two lists side by side.
tests.check: Aggregate paid dollars by service category and provider type for the period. Join to the inventory of detection tests actually executed, by the category each test covers. Report every category with material spend and no executed test, ranked by dollars, and compute the share of total spend under active detection coverage.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 16 - Coverage map: spend by category against detection tests actually run
-- Runs on claims aggregates joined to your detection-test inventory/run log.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :material_pct (0.005)
-- Portability: STRING_AGG(DISTINCT ...) is LISTAGG or GROUP_CONCAT on other engines.

WITH spend AS (
  SELECT
      cl.service_category,
      cl.provider_type,
      SUM(cl.paid_amount)                                       AS paid_total,
      COUNT(DISTINCT cl.billing_npi)                            AS providers,
      SUM(cl.paid_amount) / SUM(SUM(cl.paid_amount)) OVER ()    AS share_of_spend
  FROM claim_lines cl
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
  GROUP BY cl.service_category, cl.provider_type
),
covered AS (
  SELECT tc.service_category, tc.provider_type,
         COUNT(DISTINCT tr.run_id)  AS runs_in_period,
         MAX(tr.run_date)           AS last_run_date,
         -- only tests with a run in the period count as covering; the rest are listed apart
         STRING_AGG(DISTINCT CASE WHEN tr.run_id IS NOT NULL THEN tc.detection_test_id END, ', ')
                                    AS tests_run,
         STRING_AGG(DISTINCT CASE WHEN tr.run_id IS NULL THEN tc.detection_test_id END, ', ')
                                    AS tests_not_run
  FROM detection_test_coverage tc                     -- which categories each test covers
  LEFT JOIN detection_test_runs tr
         ON tr.detection_test_id = tc.detection_test_id
        AND tr.run_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
  GROUP BY tc.service_category, tc.provider_type
)
SELECT
    s.service_category,
    s.provider_type,
    s.paid_total,
    s.providers,
    ROUND(100.0 * s.share_of_spend, 2)                 AS pct_of_spend,
    COALESCE(c.runs_in_period, 0)                      AS detection_runs,
    c.last_run_date,
    COALESCE(c.tests_run, '(none)')                    AS tests_covering,
    COALESCE(c.tests_not_run, '(none)')                AS tests_defined_not_run,
    CASE
      WHEN c.service_category IS NULL              THEN 'NO_TEST_DEFINED'
      WHEN COALESCE(c.runs_in_period, 0) = 0       THEN 'TEST_DEFINED_NOT_RUN'
      ELSE 'COVERED'
    END                                                AS coverage_status
FROM spend s
LEFT JOIN covered c
       ON c.service_category = s.service_category
      AND c.provider_type    = s.provider_type
WHERE s.share_of_spend >= :material_pct
ORDER BY s.paid_total DESC;

-- Headline number worth putting on one slide: the share of paid dollars in categories
-- with coverage_status = 'COVERED'. Most programmes have never computed it, and the
-- first computation of it is usually the most useful output of this entire pack.
tests.threshold: :material_pct = 0.005 (half a percent of total spend) keeps the map readable while still surfacing categories large enough to matter; lower it once the obvious gaps are closed. Do not set a coverage target — a programme can reach high nominal coverage by defining one weak test per category, and the honest reading of this map is qualitative: which uncovered categories carry both material dollars and known scheme risk. Cross-reference the uncovered list against the case base and against the other six families in this pack before deciding what to build next. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: **MD-19 — CMIP-aligned programme-integrity unit with analytics and UPIC coordination.** Coverage is the question a PI unit's design has to answer and the one least often asked of it: not whether the analytics are good, but whether they point at the money. PI-18 (PI/SIU governance, segregation of duties, independence from payment) is the secondary because a coverage map is only credible if the unit producing it is independent of the operations whose blind spots it reports.

failure_map.reading: No detection-test inventory exists, so coverage cannot be stated at all and this query cannot be run. Building the inventory is the remediation and it is largely a documentation exercise.
An inventory exists but no run log, so tests defined years ago cannot be distinguished from tests running today. TEST_DEFINED_NOT_RUN is the population to look at.

Coverage is claimed at the programme level while whole delegated or carved-out benefits — behavioural health, dental, transport, pharmacy under a PBM — sit outside the analytics environment entirely and never appear in the spend denominator either.
Coverage is broad and shallow: every category has a test, and most of those tests are threshold reports nobody works. Read this test with test 10 — coverage without yield is coverage on paper.
Test runs are not logged, so the programme cannot demonstrate what surveillance was in place during any past period, which is precisely the question asked after a scheme surfaces.

tests.family_title: Prior authorisation and claims processing
tests.name: Duplicate payment — the four keys that a single duplicate rule cannot see
tests.hypothesis: Duplicate detection is almost never absent; it is almost always keyed too narrowly. A rule keyed on (claim number, line, provider, date, code, units) catches only resubmission of an identical claim. It does not catch the same service billed under a different NPI in the same group, under a different but clinically equivalent code, across a professional and a facility claim, or across an FFS claim and an encounter already covered by capitation. Each of those is a real duplicate with a different key, and each survives adjudication cleanly.
tests.check: Run four passes over the same paid population with four progressively looser keys, and report each pass separately with its own count and exposure — never merged. The point is not a single duplicate list; it is the shape of the gap between what the production rule catches and what each looser key finds. That gap is the control finding, and it is stated in dollars.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 1 - Duplicate payment across four keys
-- Pattern only. Run on your own warehouse. Output = review candidates, not dispositions.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :window_days (0 = same day only; 1 to 3 also reports exact-key repeats that many days apart)

WITH paid AS (
  SELECT cl.claim_line_id, cl.claim_id, cl.beneficiary_id, cl.service_date,
         cl.hcpcs, cl.modifier_1, cl.units, cl.paid_amount,
         cl.rendering_npi, cl.billing_npi, cl.group_tin,
         cl.claim_type,              -- 'PROFESSIONAL' | 'INSTITUTIONAL'
         cl.payer_program            -- 'FFS' | 'MANAGED_CARE' | waiver code
  FROM claim_lines cl
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status = 'PAID'
),

-- KEY 1 - exact duplicate: what your production rule should already catch.
-- Its purpose here is to establish the baseline. If this returns rows, the
-- production rule is not running, and no other pass means anything yet.
k1 AS (
  SELECT beneficiary_id, service_date, hcpcs, modifier_1, units,
         rendering_npi, billing_npi,
         COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(paid_amount) AS paid, MIN(claim_line_id) AS keep_line
  FROM paid
  GROUP BY beneficiary_id, service_date, hcpcs, modifier_1, units, rendering_npi, billing_npi
  HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
),

-- KEY 1, date drift - the exact key again, on service dates up to :window_days apart.
-- Reported as its own row so KEY1_EXACT stays arithmetic. Each row is a later line that
-- repeats an earlier one; with :window_days = 0 it returns nothing.
-- Date minus date gives days here (PostgreSQL, DuckDB, Oracle); elsewhere use DATEDIFF(day, a, b).
k1_drift AS (
  SELECT b.claim_line_id, b.paid_amount
  FROM paid b
  WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM paid a
                WHERE a.beneficiary_id = b.beneficiary_id
                  AND a.hcpcs          = b.hcpcs
                  AND COALESCE(a.modifier_1, '') = COALESCE(b.modifier_1, '')
                  AND a.units          = b.units
                  AND a.rendering_npi  = b.rendering_npi
                  AND a.billing_npi    = b.billing_npi
                  AND a.service_date   < b.service_date
                  AND b.service_date - a.service_date <= :window_days)
),

-- KEY 2 - same service, different rendering NPI inside one group/TIN.
-- The classic locum, cross-cover and "billed by both partners" duplicate.
k2 AS (
  SELECT beneficiary_id, service_date, hcpcs, group_tin,
         COUNT(DISTINCT rendering_npi) AS distinct_renderers,
         COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(paid_amount) AS paid
  FROM paid
  WHERE group_tin IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY beneficiary_id, service_date, hcpcs, group_tin
  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT rendering_npi) > 1
),

-- KEY 3 - professional/institutional pairing for the same service.
-- Legitimate for split professional/technical component billing; the
-- discriminator is whether the modifiers (26 / TC) are present and consistent.
k3 AS (
  SELECT p.beneficiary_id, p.service_date, p.hcpcs,
         MAX(CASE WHEN p.claim_type = 'PROFESSIONAL'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS has_prof,
         MAX(CASE WHEN p.claim_type = 'INSTITUTIONAL' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS has_inst,
         MAX(CASE WHEN p.modifier_1 IN ('26','TC')    THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS has_component_mod,
         SUM(p.paid_amount) AS paid, COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM paid p
  GROUP BY p.beneficiary_id, p.service_date, p.hcpcs
  HAVING MAX(CASE WHEN p.claim_type = 'PROFESSIONAL'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1
     AND MAX(CASE WHEN p.claim_type = 'INSTITUTIONAL' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1
),

-- KEY 4 - FFS claim paid for a service already inside a capitated arrangement.
-- Usually the largest single bucket in a managed-care programme and the one
-- least likely to have any rule at all, because the two payment streams are
-- often held in different systems that are never joined.
k4 AS (
  SELECT p.beneficiary_id, p.service_date, p.hcpcs, p.paid_amount, p.claim_line_id
  FROM paid p
  JOIN capitation_enrollment ce
    ON  ce.beneficiary_id = p.beneficiary_id
    AND p.service_date BETWEEN ce.coverage_start AND COALESCE(ce.coverage_end, DATE '9999-12-31')
  WHERE p.payer_program = 'FFS'
    AND p.hcpcs IN (SELECT hcpcs FROM capitated_benefit_package WHERE package_id = ce.package_id)
)

-- Report each key separately. Do NOT union these into one duplicate list:
-- key 1 is an error, keys 2-4 are questions, and merging them destroys that.
SELECT 'KEY1_EXACT'          AS dup_key, COUNT(*) AS groups, SUM(paid) AS exposure FROM k1
UNION ALL
SELECT 'KEY1_DATE_DRIFT', COUNT(*), SUM(paid_amount) FROM k1_drift   -- counts later lines, not groups
UNION ALL
SELECT 'KEY2_CROSS_NPI_SAME_TIN', COUNT(*), SUM(paid) FROM k2
UNION ALL
SELECT 'KEY3_PROF_INST_PAIR',      COUNT(*), SUM(paid) FROM k3 WHERE has_component_mod = 0
UNION ALL
SELECT 'KEY4_FFS_INSIDE_CAPITATION', COUNT(*), SUM(paid_amount) FROM k4;

-- Then drill into whichever key carries material exposure. The control finding is
-- the SHAPE of the gap: "the production key catches KEY1 and nothing else, and
-- KEY4 carries $X" is a specification defect stated in dollars.
tests.threshold: No statistical threshold — KEY1 is arithmetic and any row is an error. The tunable :window_days = 0 assumes clean service dates; set 1–3 only if your warehouse carries known date drift, and expect the false-positive volume to rise sharply because genuinely repeated services (a daily injection, twice-daily therapy) then collide. The window applies to the exact key only and is reported as its own KEY1_DATE_DRIFT row, so KEY1_EXACT stays arithmetic; KEY2 and KEY3 remain same-day keys. KEY2 and KEY3 are questions, not findings: cross-cover and split-component billing are both legitimate, and the discriminating evidence is the modifier, not the count. KEY4 is the one to run first if you have any capitated population at all — it is usually the largest bucket and often has no rule behind it. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: CB-15 (Duplicate claim / line detection). Secondary: CB-18 (Pre-submission claim scrubber, provider side), MD-12 (PERM / MEQC sampling with error-rate measurement — duplicates are a data-processing error category).

failure_map.reading: No duplicate rule beyond exact claim resubmission. Build KEY2 and KEY4 first; they carry the exposure.
CB-15's duplicate-hit disposition log is empty or absent for the period, so no rule fired at all.
Duplicate hits were overridden at adjudication in bulk to clear a backlog, with no per-override rationale.
The key is too narrow. This is the defining defect for this test and the one the four-key report is built to prove — the rule works exactly as specified, and the specification is the problem.
Hits are suppressed at the edit engine with no retained disposition log, so the rule's precision cannot be assessed at all.

tests.family_title: Prior authorisation and claims processing
tests.name: Medicaid NCCI — which of the six methodologies is actually firing
tests.hypothesis: Medicaid NCCI comprises six methodologies (practitioner and outpatient-hospital PTP; practitioner, outpatient-hospital and DME MUE; and the associated add-on code edits). A state or plan can attest to implementation while in practice only one or two are wired into adjudication, because the quarterly edit files are loaded for one claim type and not the others. The signature is an edit-hit rate that is normal for one methodology and effectively zero for another, on claim volume that should produce hits.
tests.check: Count edit hits and denials per methodology per quarter alongside the claim volume each methodology should have been applied to. A methodology with material eligible volume and a near-zero hit rate is not a clean population — it is an edit file that was never loaded. Cross-check the loaded edit-file version dates against the CMS quarterly release dates.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 2 - Medicaid NCCI six-methodology coverage
-- Reference: CMS Medicaid NCCI, https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/ncci-medicaid
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :min_eligible_lines, :min_expected_hit_rate

WITH eligible_volume AS (
  SELECT
      CASE
        WHEN cl.claim_type = 'PROFESSIONAL'  AND cl.service_category <> 'dme' THEN 'PRACTITIONER'
        WHEN cl.claim_type = 'INSTITUTIONAL' AND cl.bill_type LIKE '13%'      THEN 'OUTPATIENT_HOSPITAL'
        WHEN cl.service_category = 'dme'                                       THEN 'DME'
        ELSE 'OTHER'
      END                                     AS methodology_population,
      DATE_TRUNC('quarter', cl.service_date)  AS svc_quarter,
      COUNT(*)                                AS eligible_lines,
      SUM(cl.paid_amount)                     AS paid_amount
  FROM claim_lines cl
  WHERE cl.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
    AND cl.adjudication_status IN ('PAID','DENIED')
  GROUP BY 1, 2
),
edit_activity AS (
  SELECT
      eh.methodology,                 -- your edit engine's methodology tag
      eh.edit_family,                 -- 'PTP' | 'MUE' | 'ADD_ON'
      DATE_TRUNC('quarter', eh.service_date) AS svc_quarter,
      COUNT(*)                                AS edit_hits,
      SUM(CASE WHEN eh.outcome = 'DENIED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS edit_denials,
      SUM(CASE WHEN eh.outcome = 'OVERRIDDEN' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS edit_overrides,
      MAX(eh.edit_file_version_date)          AS edit_file_version_used
  FROM edit_hit eh
  WHERE eh.service_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
)
SELECT
    v.svc_quarter,
    v.methodology_population,
    a.edit_family,
    v.eligible_lines,
    v.paid_amount,
    COALESCE(a.edit_hits, 0)    AS edit_hits,
    COALESCE(a.edit_denials, 0) AS edit_denials,
    COALESCE(a.edit_overrides, 0) AS edit_overrides,
    ROUND(COALESCE(a.edit_hits, 0) * 1.0 / NULLIF(v.eligible_lines, 0), 5) AS hit_rate,
    a.edit_file_version_used,
    CASE
      WHEN a.edit_hits IS NULL AND v.eligible_lines > :min_eligible_lines
        THEN 'METHODOLOGY_NOT_FIRING'
      WHEN COALESCE(a.edit_hits,0) * 1.0 / NULLIF(v.eligible_lines,0) < :min_expected_hit_rate
        THEN 'HIT_RATE_IMPLAUSIBLY_LOW'
      ELSE 'ACTIVE'
    END AS coverage_class
FROM eligible_volume v
LEFT JOIN edit_activity a
       ON a.svc_quarter = v.svc_quarter
      AND a.methodology = v.methodology_population
WHERE v.methodology_population <> 'OTHER'
  AND v.eligible_lines >= :min_eligible_lines
ORDER BY v.svc_quarter, v.methodology_population;

-- Companion, and the cheaper of the two: compare edit_file_version_used against
-- the CMS quarterly release dates. A version more than one quarter stale is a
-- finding on its own and needs no claim analysis to state.
tests.threshold: :min_expected_hit_rate has no importable value — derive it from your own history. Take each methodology's hit rate in a quarter you have reason to trust and flag any later quarter below roughly half of it. :min_eligible_lines = 1000 keeps thin populations out of the report. Read the override column alongside the denial column: a high hit rate with a high override rate is not a working edit, it is an edit being routed around, and it appears healthy on a hit-rate metric alone. The edit-file version check needs no threshold at all and should be run first. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: CB-06 (Medicaid NCCI six-methodology implementation). Secondary: CB-04 (NCCI PTP edit enforcement pre-submission), CB-07 (MUE units-of-service edit enforcement).

failure_map.reading: One or more methodologies were never implemented. CB-06's quarterly methodology attestation covers a state of affairs that does not exist.
The quarterly edit files were not loaded for one or more quarters in the period — the version-date companion proves this without any claim analysis.
Edits fire and are overridden at volume. Check the override rate before concluding the methodology is working.
Edits are loaded for the practitioner population only and never applied to outpatient-hospital or DME claim types, so two-thirds of the methodology set is decorative.
The attestation exists but names no file version and no hit statistics, so implementation cannot be verified from the artifact.

tests.family_title: Prior authorisation and claims processing
tests.name: Clean-claim rate and the rework loop — the scrubber's real yield
tests.hypothesis: A pre-submission scrubber that reports a high clean-claim rate may be measuring the wrong thing: claims that pass the scrubber and are then denied by the payer for a reason the scrubber could have caught. The signature is a denial-reason distribution concentrated in categories the scrubber claims to cover, and a rework loop — the same claim submitted, denied, corrected and resubmitted — carrying real administrative cost that nobody has priced.
tests.check: Join submitted claims to their scrubber disposition and their eventual adjudication outcome. Report the denial rate among scrubber-passed claims by denial-reason category, and separately count resubmission chains and the days they add to the payment cycle.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 3 - Scrubber yield and the rework loop
-- Provider-side control, but equally runnable by a payer against its own denial stream.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :min_pass_denial_rate (about 0.02, i.e. 1 in 50)

WITH submissions AS (
  SELECT c.claim_id, c.beneficiary_id, c.billing_npi,
         c.submission_date, c.original_claim_id,
         s.scrubber_outcome,            -- 'PASS' | 'EDIT_FIXED' | 'EDIT_OVERRIDDEN'
         a.adjudication_status, a.denial_reason_code, a.denial_reason_category,
         a.adjudication_date, a.paid_amount
  FROM claim c
  LEFT JOIN scrubber_result s ON s.claim_id = c.claim_id
  LEFT JOIN adjudication  a ON a.claim_id = c.claim_id
  WHERE c.submission_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
),
scrubber_yield AS (
  SELECT
      scrubber_outcome,
      denial_reason_category,
      COUNT(*) AS claims,
      SUM(CASE WHEN adjudication_status = 'DENIED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS denied
  FROM submissions
  GROUP BY scrubber_outcome, denial_reason_category
),
scrubber_yield_rated AS (
  SELECT y.*,
         SUM(y.claims) OVER (PARTITION BY y.scrubber_outcome) AS outcome_claims
  FROM scrubber_yield y
),
-- A chain is the original submission plus every resubmission that points at it, so the
-- original's own submission date starts the clock. The original is read from claim without
-- the period filter, because it may have been submitted before the period began.
-- Assumes original_claim_id always names the first submission of the chain; if your data
-- chains resubmission to resubmission, resolve the root first.
chain AS (
  SELECT COALESCE(c.original_claim_id, c.claim_id) AS chain_id,
         c.submission_date, a.adjudication_date, a.paid_amount
  FROM claim c
  LEFT JOIN adjudication a ON a.claim_id = c.claim_id
),
rework AS (
  SELECT
      chain_id,
      COUNT(*)                                  AS submissions_in_chain,  -- original included
      MIN(submission_date)                      AS first_submitted,       -- the original's date
      MAX(adjudication_date)                    AS finally_adjudicated,
      -- date minus date gives days (PostgreSQL, DuckDB, Oracle); elsewhere use DATEDIFF(day, a, b)
      MAX(adjudication_date) - MIN(submission_date) AS days_to_resolution,
      MAX(paid_amount)                          AS eventual_paid
  FROM chain
  GROUP BY chain_id
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3                          -- the original plus two or more resubmissions
     AND SUM(CASE WHEN submission_date BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
                  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0        -- at least one submission inside the period
)
SELECT 'SCRUBBER_YIELD' AS report, scrubber_outcome AS k1, denial_reason_category AS k2,
       claims AS n, denied AS m,
       ROUND(denied * 1.0 / NULLIF(outcome_claims, 0), 4) AS rate  -- denied / ALL scrubber-passed claims
FROM scrubber_yield_rated
WHERE scrubber_outcome = 'PASS' AND denied > 0
  AND denied * 1.0 / NULLIF(outcome_claims, 0) > :min_pass_denial_rate

UNION ALL

SELECT 'REWORK_LOOP', CAST(submissions_in_chain AS VARCHAR), NULL,
       COUNT(*), SUM(eventual_paid), AVG(days_to_resolution)
FROM rework
GROUP BY submissions_in_chain
ORDER BY 1, 6 DESC;

-- The number worth carrying to a governance meeting is not the clean-claim rate.
-- It is: claims that PASSED the scrubber and were then denied for a reason the
-- scrubber covers, times the fully-loaded cost of a rework cycle.
tests.threshold: There is no external benchmark for a clean-claim rate that means anything across organisations, so do not import one. The internally meaningful metric is the scrubber-passed denial rate by reason category, and the only threshold worth setting is relative: any category where scrubber-passed claims are denied more often than roughly 1 in 50 is a rule the scrubber should already have. Chains of three or more submissions are worth reading individually — they are usually one specific edit misconfigured, not a general quality problem. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
tests.pair: CB-18 (Pre-submission claim scrubber, provider side). Secondary: CB-04 (NCCI PTP edit enforcement pre-submission), PA-08 (Item-category documentation-eligibility checklists).

failure_map.reading: No pre-submission scrubbing at all; the payer's edit engine is the first check any claim meets.
The scrubber is licensed and installed but its rule set has not been updated in the period, so it enforces a stale code set.
EDIT_OVERRIDDEN is a material share of submissions and no override rationale is retained — the scrubber is advisory in name only.
The clean-claim rate is high because the scrubber checks format and eligibility but not coding policy, so it passes exactly the claims that will be denied.
No scrubber disposition is retained per claim, so scrubber-passed denials cannot be measured and this test cannot be run at all — which is itself the finding.

tests.family_title: Prior authorisation and claims processing
tests.name: PA decision timeliness — and what happens when the clock runs out
tests.hypothesis: Where the decision-timeliness SLA control is absent or measures only the cases it closed, prior-authorisation decisions run past the standard and expedited limits. Two distinct failures hide behind one average: requests decided late, and requests never decided at all — still open past the limit and therefore invisible to any metric computed over closed cases. A third pattern is subtler and worse: a spike of denials clustered in the final hours before the clock expires.
tests.check: Compute elapsed time from a complete request to a communicated decision, split by standard and expedited track, and include still-open requests in the denominator. Then look at the distribution of decisions within the allowed window — a mass of determinations in the last few hours is a queue-management artifact, and whether those determinations skew toward denial is the question worth asking.
tests.sql:
-- TEST 4 - PA decision timeliness, including never-decided requests
-- Anchors: 42 CFR 419 Subpart I; CMS-0057-F. Confirm the limits that bind YOUR line
-- of business before setting parameters - they differ by programme and have changed.
-- Params: :period_start, :period_end, :standard_limit_days (7), :expedited_limit_hours (72)

WITH requests AS (
  SELECT pa.pa_request_id, pa.beneficiary_id, pa.requesting_npi, pa.service_code,
         pa.track,                       -- 'STANDARD' | 'EXPEDITED'
         pa.received_datetime,
         pa.complete_datetime,           -- when the package became complete
         pa.decision_datetime,
         pa.decision,                    -- 'AFFIRMED' | 'NON_AFFIRMED' | 'PARTIAL' | NULL if open
         pa.notice_sent_datetime
  FROM pa_request pa
  WHERE pa.received_datetime BETWEEN :period_start AND :period_end
),
timed AS (
  SELECT r.*,
         COALESCE(r.decision_datetime, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) AS clock_stop,
         EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (COALESCE(r.decision_datetime, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)
                             - COALESCE(r.complete_datetime, r.received_datetime))) / 3600.0
           AS elapsed_hours,
         CASE WHEN r.track = 'EXPEDITED' THEN :expedited_limit_hours
              ELSE :standard_limit_days * 24 END AS limit_hours
  FROM requests r
)
SELECT
    track,
    CASE
      WHEN decision IS NULL AND elapsed_hours > limit_hours THEN 'OPEN_PAST_LIMIT'
      WHEN decision IS NULL                                  THEN 'OPEN_WITHIN_LIMIT'
      WHEN elapsed_hours > limit_hours                       THEN 'DECIDED_LATE'
      WHEN elapsed_hours > limit_hours * 0.9                 THEN 'DECIDED_IN_FINAL_TENTH'
      ELSE 'DECIDED_ON_TIME'
    END AS timeliness_class,
    COUNT(*)                                                        AS requests,
    ROUND(AVG(elapsed_hours), 1)                                    AS mean_elapsed_hours,
    SUM(CASE WHEN decision = 'NON_AFFIRMED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)      AS non_affirmed,
    ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN decision = 'NON_AFFIRMED' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END)
          / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 4)                                 AS non_affirm_rate,
    -- notice lag is a separate obligation from the decision itself
    ROUND(AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (notice_sent_datetime - decision_datetime)) / 3600.0), 1)
          AS mean_notice_lag_hours
FROM timed
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY track, timeliness_class;

-- Read DECIDED_IN_FINAL_TENTH's non_affirm_rate against DECIDED_ON_TIME's.
-- A materially higher denial rate in the last tenth of the window is a queue
-- artifact, not a clinical pattern, and it is a control finding about the
-- workflow rather than about any individual determination.
tests.threshold: The limits are regulatory, not tunable — but they differ by programme, line of business and state, and CMS-0057-F changed several of them, so read the rule that binds you rather than the defaults above. What is tunable is the final-tenth window: 0.9 is a starting cut, and the comparison that matters is between denial rates inside and outside it, not the raw count. OPEN_PAST_LIMIT should be zero and any non-zero count is a finding; it is also the number most likely to be missing from an existing timeliness report, because reports built over closed cases cannot see it. Tune to your population; a starting point, not a standard.
